Hour caps, exception processes, and life-sharing matches without language are not culturally neutral.

Child welfare: help-seeking that becomes a report is part of this history. Mandated reporting still exists. So does the duty not to treat a whole community as a risk score.

Notices and comment: an eList and an English PDF is not how this community was reached. Empty follow-up cells are theater. Nations are governments — they are not this page — but the same comment period that BCCs a tribe and skips Maay has already chosen who counts.

Workforce: Somali staff are not the interpreter pool and not the community.

Legislation, funding, rule: you cannot advocate for a channel you will not study. This cultural intelligence exists so the 40% has a household in it — not a paternalistic program designed in a building that never learned the names.

sections.heading: A Note on This Guide
sections.body:
This brief is about Hmong people — Hmoob in White Hmong, Moob in Green Hmong / Mong Leng. It is a people with ancient roots in southern China, a highland life in Laos, and a Minnesota community built after 1975. Pronounce it mung. The H is silent. If you say Huh-mong in a lobby, you have already told the household you did not study.

### Who this is

Minnesota Compass (ACS 2019–2023) puts Hmong ancestry near 99,900. About 94 percent Twin Cities, about 6 percent Greater Minnesota. About 38 percent age 17 or younger. About 33 percent foreign-born — which means a majority of this community was born here. Pew (May 2025, 2021–2023 ACS) put Minnesota near 95,000 on a Hmong-alone count and named it the second-largest state community after California. Date the number you use. A rate is not the person.

St. Paul is a national hub. It is not the map. Frogtown, the East Side, Little Mekong on University Avenue, Hmongtown Marketplace, Hmong Village, Brooklyn Center, Maplewood, and a smaller Greater Minnesota share are not one client.

The diversity inside this people is the point. A Secret War veteran who came through Ban Vinai, a Christian grandmother, a txiv neeb (traditional healer) whose altar is in the living room, a U.S.-born nurse, a farmer at the summer market, a college student who uses English with friends and Hmong with an elder, a person who left clan obligation and still shows up at New Year — share a people and do not share a Tuesday.

### Who this is not

This is not a Census “Asian” mash. It is not Chinese New Year. It is not Karen, Vietnamese, Lao as a synonym, Cambodian, or a generic Southeast Asian interpreter. Shared continent is not shared culture.

### How to read this

Read it as an orientation. A full mosaic is not a stereotype. A stereotype is when this page becomes the person in the lobby. Always defer to the person in front of you. This page is a hypothesis you still test on this family.

The facts that follow are meant to help you meet people well — how family is named, what respect looks like, what a greeting carries, what a form may land on. Counts are dated. History is here so the meeting is clearer, not so you deliver a lecture.

sections.heading: Origins and the Founding of a People
sections.body:
Hmong peoplehood is older than Laos, older than the CIA file, and older than the refugee camp. Oral history and scholarship place origin in southern China; movement into the highlands of what became Laos, Vietnam, and Thailand under pressure from imperial states. Statelessness is a political fact, not a personality.

### Clan, language, writing

There is no Hmong nation-state. Clan, language, agriculture, and ritual organized life without a capital city. Writing systems came late. The Romanized Popular Alphabet (RPA), developed in the 1950s in Laos, is the common Latin script in Minnesota. Historically the language was oral. Paj ntaub / paaj ntaub — story cloth and embroidery — carried memory when paper did not.

### White Hmong and Green Hmong

Two large dialect-and-dress groups live in Minnesota: White Hmong (Hmoob Dawb) and Green Hmong, also called Blue Hmong or Mong Leng (Hmoob Leeg / Moob). The names come from dress, not politics. The dialects are close and not always interchangeable in an interpreter. Green Hmong often write the people-name without the H: Moob. That is the same instruction as this page: say mung.

### What people brought

Clan, ancestor obligation, shamanic healing and Christianity both, farming knowledge, oral skill, a memory of being recruited to fight someone else’s war and then left. What they met in Minnesota: an English form, one “Asian” checkbox, and often one interpreter labeled “Hmong.”

sections.heading: The Geography of the Hmong World
sections.body:
Homeland is not one flag. Southern China remains a Hmong (Miao) geography. The Laos highlands — Xieng Khouang, Long Tieng, the places named in veteran stories — are the origin of most Minnesota families.

### Diaspora

There are Hmong communities in Vietnam, Thailand, Burma/Myanmar, and a global diaspora: California, Minnesota, Wisconsin, North Carolina, France, Australia.

Pew (May 2025): California is the largest U.S. state community; Minnesota second; Wisconsin third. Fresno and Sacramento sit next to Minneapolis–St. Paul as sister maps. Secondary migration built Minnesota. Church sponsors scattered people; clan pulled them back together.

### In Minnesota

St. Paul is the national urban hub. East Side. Frogtown. University Avenue / Little Mekong. Ramsey County. Brooklyn Center and inner-ring suburbs. A small Greater Minnesota share. Frogtown is not the whole. The person in front of you may not have been to Laos.

sections.heading: The Secret War, 1975, and the Camps — Foundational Event
sections.body:
If the Great Migration is the foundational demographic event of modern Black America, and 1991 of Somali Minnesota, the Secret War and 1975 are the foundational event of Hmong Minnesota.

### The Secret War

From 1961 to 1975 the United States, through the CIA, recruited Hmong forces under General Vang Pao to fight in Laos — a war the Geneva Accords had said should not be there. Hmong soldiers blocked supply lines and died in large numbers. Boys were recruited. When the United States left in 1975, the Pathet Lao and Vietnamese forces treated Hmong allied families as the enemy.

### Airlift, walk, camps

May 12–14, 1975: airlift from Long Tieng. About 2,500 people in those days. General Vang Pao left May 14. Minnesota later marked that date. Most people were not on the planes. They walked. Thai camps followed — Ban Vinai among the named ones. Years. Then resettlement.

### Minnesota

The first Hmong family in Minnesota, Dang Her and Shoua Moua, arrived in December 1975. Church and voluntary-agency sponsors (Lutheran, Catholic, and others) placed people across the country so no one state would “take too many.” Clan and secondary migration undid the scatter. St. Paul became a hub because people chose each other.

U.S. policy at first treated Hmong people as “too primitive” for asylum. The Indochina Migration and Refugee Assistance Act had to be amended. That sentence is literacy for the meeting. It is not a speech you give the family.

sections.heading: Family
sections.body:
Clan organizes family. About 18 clans are commonly named among Hmong from Laos now in the United States. The clan name is the last name: Chang, Cheng, Chue, Fang, Hang, Her, Khang, Kong, Kue, Lee, Lor, Moua, Pha, Thao, Vang, Vue, Xiong, Yang — English spellings of Hmong names. Same last name often means same clan. Marriage is supposed to be outside the clan.

### Household size

Households are larger than a nuclear English form. Compass: average household size about 4.4. Elders, in-laws, adult children, and clan obligation sit in the same week. Who cares for the child may not match the waiver checkbox.

### Marriage and labor

Bride wealth and clan negotiation are real in some marriages. Minnesota law still stands. A wedding custom is not a crime scene. Mandated reporting still stands.

Women’s labor — market, factory, farm, professional second generation — sits next to a patrilineal clan. Both can be true in the same room. Ask who should be in the room.

sections.heading: Minnesota and Hmong History
sections.body:
St. Paul is one of the largest urban Hmong communities in the world. That is why this page has to be as complete as the African American and Somali intelligences — because this department will meet this community on waivers, child welfare, health care, cash, food, aging, and employment.

### Places, not a blob

East Side St. Paul; Frogtown; University Avenue and Little Mekong; Hmongtown Marketplace (opened 2004, a former lumberyard); Hmong Village (2010, Johnson Parkway); Brooklyn Center; Maplewood; a small Greater Minnesota share. Compass: about 94 percent Twin Cities.

### Institutions

Partners include Hmong American Partnership; Hmong Cultural Center of Minnesota; Hmong Museum; Center for Hmong Studies (Concordia); Hmong 18 Council and clan structures some families name; CECLC as a department door — not the whole community.

Public calendar: Hmong New Year in St. Paul (weekend near the end of November, RiverCentre in recent years; held since 1977); Hmong International Freedom Festival at Como Park — sport, not consultation. Hmong American Day / May 14 is literacy. A calendar click is not community engagement.

Hmong staff are colleagues, not a stand-in for the community. A New Year visit is optional professional development. You are a guest. It does not make you the expert.

sections.heading: Hmoob / Moob — the heart of a people
sections.body:
To be Hmong is to be a people without a state and with a long memory of being used by states.

### In Minnesota

In Minnesota it sits inside another fact: many Hmong Minnesotans are Asian in a U.S. racial order that files them under a checkbox that also holds Chinese, Indian, and Korean histories they do not share; veterans of a war the United States ran and then classified; Christians and traditionalists in the same cousin-line.

### Kwvtij

Kwvtij — clan-kin — is not a metaphor. Face, ancestor obligation, and not shaming the name travel into a waiver meeting. Harmony can look like agreement and then a plan nobody follows. Ask whether they agree. A smile is not consent.

This guide is a working orientation. Individual variation always supersedes group generalization.

sections.heading: Core Concepts
sections.body:
These concepts recur. They express differently by clan, church, generation, and how this family lives ritual. They are hypotheses — not a script for the person in front of you.

### Clan

About 18. Patrilineal. Exogamous. The last name is not a decoration. Staff do not use it as an icebreaker. If the family names it, you listen.

### Ancestors

Household ritual, soul, and funeral are not extras. A missed funeral obligation can be a crisis in the family when the English form thinks the crisis is a missed appointment.

### Txiv neeb

Traditional healer / shaman. An altar in a living room is not a case plan and not a museum. If they name a healer, listen. The healer is the case plan when they asked. A soul-calling is not DHS programming.

### Christianity

Catholic, Protestant, evangelical streams are large in Minnesota Hmong life. Church can be the information channel. It is not “the community.”

### Face and harmony

Direct refusal may be costly. A yes that is courtesy is not a signature. Ask again, plainly, without humiliation.

### Hu plig / poob plig

Soul-calling and soul-loss are meaning systems some families use for illness, fright, and developmental difference. They can sit next to a fierce wish for services. You can hold both.

### Farming and market

Garden plots, farmers markets, and the two St. Paul markets are economy and culture. A food-court visit is not consultation.

sections.heading: Religion and Healing
sections.body:
Traditional Hmong religion is household-centered: ancestors, spirits (dab), shamanic healing, soul. It is not a Sunday service you can BCC. Christianity arrived through mission and camp and is now ordinary in Minnesota — sometimes in the same extended family as a traditional altar.

### Pastor and healer

A pastor or a txiv neeb is the case plan when this family asked. Traditional practice is not witchcraft. Church is not the evolved version.

### Funerals

Funerals can last days and gather clan. Burial timing, animal offering in traditional practice, and who must be there are not delays for your convenience. You still keep medical and legal time. You name the conflict instead of punishing it.

Illness meaning may not be the DSM sentence. MDH’s 2014 qualitative work with Hmong parents on autism: unclear meaning of the word, stigma, waiting to share concerns, professionals who were not responsive. Late identification is a gate. Stigma is a gate. English-only is a gate.

sections.heading: Greetings
sections.body:
Elders first. A slight bow or nod with an older person is safer than a hard handshake you assume is universal. Many second-generation people will shake hands in English-language rooms. Follow this room.

### Names

Nyob zoo is a common White Hmong greeting. English “hello” is ordinary. Say the name. The clan name is the last name; it is not optional.

Somali right-hand rules and the Black nod are not this page. This is not those grammars.

Physical contact: ask the room. Cross-gender touch with elders is not a default.

sections.heading: Naming Conventions
sections.body:
The last name is a clan name. Eighteen common clans. People who share it may be kin in a way the database cannot see — or strangers who still should not marry. Every Lee is not related. Two Lees in a household are not automatically a married couple; they may be clan-kin of a kind your form does not have a box for.

### Given names

Given names may be Hmong, English, or both. Soul names, nicknames, and generation names exist. The form that demands first-middle-last and a hyphen will invent a person.

Pronounce it. Ask. “Too many Vangs” is a closed door, not a joke.

Women may or may not take a husband’s clan name in U.S. records. Ask how to file. A mother and child who do not share a last name is not a fraud signal until you have a reason.

sections.heading: Dates of Significance
sections.body:
Hmong New Year — traditionally after harvest; in St. Paul a public weekend near the end of November since 1977. Courtship ball-toss (pov pob) is public history at the celebration, not a file. Guest, not researcher.

### May 14 and public life

May 14 — General Vang Pao’s 1975 departure from Laos; marked in Minnesota as Hmong American / Hmong-Lao veterans memory. Literacy.

Fourth of July / Freedom Festival soccer and sport at Como Park — community public life, not consultation.

Lunar and household ritual dates vary by family and by traditional vs Christian practice. Ask. “Asian holiday” does not belong on a case note.

sections.heading: Education
sections.body:
Compass (ACS 2019–2023): among Hmong Minnesotans 25 and older, about 80 percent high school or higher; about 26 percent bachelor’s or higher. A majority of children are U.S.-born and in English-dominant schools. The IEP still has to reach the parent who does not read it.

### Language at the door

White Hmong and Mong Leng are not always interchangeable on an interpreter line. English-only parent forms are a gate. A parent who speaks fluent Hmong and limited English is not illiterate.

Second-generation educational mobility is real. So is a gap that a room which treats everyone the same will call “culture” instead of language access plus poverty plus a school that never learned the name.

sections.heading: Etiquette
sections.body:
Shoes off in many homes. Accept a little food if offered. Elders first. Feet pointed at an altar or a person, in a traditional household, is not the default.

### Time and the plan

Hospitality is a virtue. You still keep medical and legal time.

A living room is not a photograph of the altar. Ritual objects are not for touching. An elder is not entertainment explaining shamanism.

On-time for appointments. Traffic and multi-household logistics are real. So is a pattern of courtesy-yes then no-show when the plan was never agreed. Ask whether they agree. Confirm in the language they use.

sections.heading: Language and Communication
sections.body:
White Hmong and Green Hmong / Mong Leng. Confirm the variety. An interpreter labeled Hmong who does not speak this household’s dialect is still a closed door. RPA is the common written form; many elders do not read it. Second-generation English is common. Compass: among those 5 and older, about 77 percent speak a language other than English; about 31 percent speak English less than “very well.” Date the number.

### Tone and yes

Hmong is tonal. The doubled vowels in RPA mark tone, not extra sound. You do not need to become a linguist. You need to put the variety on the interpreter request.

A long answer may be story. A short English yes may be exhaustion or courtesy. A smile is not consent. Ask whether they agree with the plan.

A Hmong coworker is not the interpreter.

sections.heading: Other Considerations
sections.body:
Unvarnished, because Minnesota Nice is how a room that treats everyone the same deletes facts.

### Marriage, disability, status

Early marriage and bride-wealth patterns exist in history and in some present families. Minnesota age-of-consent and forced-marriage law still stand. You follow the law. You still see a family, not a crime scene walking in.

Disability stigma and late autism identification are documented (MDH 2014; later qualitative work). Under-identification is the Hmong pattern in Minnesota autism surveillance; Somali over-concern is a different page. The two are not the same.

Deportation to Laos of people with certain convictions — including people who have lived here since childhood — is current structure, not folklore. It changes who opens the door, who signs, and who will not put a relative’s name on a form. Collect the status the work requires, not more. Fear is not noncompliance.

### History that still sits in the room

1990s youth violence in some St. Paul neighborhoods is a history some families carry. A clan last name is not a gang file.

LGBTQ Hmong Minnesotans exist. You use the name. Outing someone to kin is not culture.

Employee groups may fact-check this page. A hard fact still belongs here.

sections.heading: Health
sections.body:
MDH 2014 qualitative study with Hmong community partners: parents unclear what autism meant, delayed sharing concerns, stigma, professionals who were not responsive. Late identification is the finding. Identification is not a community personality. Date the study.

### Under-count

Later Minnesota ADDM-style work has reported lower autism prevalence among Hmong children than among white and non-Somali Black children. Under-count, measurement, and meaning can sit together. Inventing a rate does not help. Skipping screening because “Hmong families don’t have that” does not help.

Chronic disease, trauma, and aging veterans of the Secret War sit in the same clinics as U.S.-born children. Traditional healing and biomedicine are often both in the household. Ask. Co-create. An altar is not a joke. A healer in the story is not a reason to skip the waiver.

Gender match may be requested in maternal and intimate care. Offer it.

Believe reported pain. This history is not Tuskegee and not a generic “Asian stoicism” slide.

sections.heading: LGBTQ
sections.body:
Queer and trans Hmong Minnesotans exist. Conservative clan and church climates can mean silence or exile. Some people live a public English life and a private Hmong life. You use the name they use. Outing them to an elder is not cultural humility.

### Law

Minnesota’s Human Rights Act still applies. A whole people is not a family-values exhibit.

sections.heading: Hair, Dress, and Body
sections.body:
Traditional dress is public at New Year and not a daily uniform. Second generation looks like Minnesota. “Still wears the costume” is not a clinic question.

### Hair and silver

Hair and head: follow this person. Hair is not for touching. Silver, embroidery, and paj ntaub are art and history, not a mascot for the unit’s Heritage Month table.

sections.heading: Music
sections.body:
The qeej (reed pipe) is ritual and art, especially at funerals. New Year stages hold dance, pop, and Christian music.

### Not entertainment

A playlist is not engagement. A funeral qeej is not entertainment for staff.

sections.heading: Sports
sections.body:
Soccer and the Freedom Festival matter in public Hmong Minnesota life. Volleyball, flag football, and school sport are ordinary for the second generation.

### Not a case plan

Sport clubs are not language access and not a case plan.

sections.heading: Literature
sections.body:
Oral literature first: proverb, funeral text, clan narrative. RPA made a written public possible.

### Letters

Minnesota and U.S. Hmong writers, scholars, and journalists exist. You do not need to quote a novel. You need to know this is not a people without letters.

sections.heading: Art
sections.body:
Paj ntaub / paaj ntaub — story cloth, reverse appliqué, memory sewn when camps and exile made paper unsafe or unavailable. Hmong Cultural Center. Hmong Museum. 2025 Minnesota History Center exhibit on fifty years.

### Guest

Guest. A story cloth is not a case plan. A museum visit is not consultation.

sections.heading: Conflict, War, and the State
sections.body:
The Secret War, the walk to Thailand, Ban Vinai, dispersal, secondary migration, and a United States that recruited then delayed asylum — that is the political event. Later: policing, youth violence in some 1990s neighborhoods, and deportation of people with records. A DHS badge is not automatically help.

### Not a personality

1975 is not a personality. A veteran is not a narrator of killing for your professional development.

sections.heading: Work, Markets, and Government
sections.body:
Factory, farm, small business, professional second generation, public employment. Hmongtown and Hmong Village are commercial hubs. Hmong staff inside the department are not unpaid interpreters and not the community. Identity is not a staffing plan.

### Relationship and the notice

Relationship may precede a signature. That is not permission to skip a notice. It is a reason the first visit may not be the decision.

sections.heading: Health-care and Human-service Encounters
sections.body:
Language and dialect. Who is in the room. Gender. An altar or a pastor in the story. Late developmental concern. Deportation climate. A nuclear form that cannot see clan.

### In the encounter

Confirm the variety. Offer gender match. Ask who should hear. Staff are not the interpreter. If they name a healer, listen. Mandated reporting still exists.

sections.heading: Adjacent Peoples — Do Not Mash
sections.body:
Not Karen. Not Lao as a synonym. Not Vietnamese. Not Chinese. Not “Asian American” as the file.

### Open the right page

Open the Karen brief for Karen. Open this for Hmong. Some households are mixed. Ask this household.

Miao in China is a related but not identical administrative story. A St. Paul family does not need a lecture on Chinese taxonomy.

sections.heading: Counts, Dated
sections.body:
Minnesota Compass, ACS 2019–2023, Hmong cultural community: about 99,912; Twin Cities 94.4%; Greater Minnesota 5.6%; age 17 or younger 38.3%; 65+ about 3.7%; foreign-born 33.4%; language other than English (age 5+) 77.3%; English less than “very well” 31.1%; high school or higher (25+) 80.3%; bachelor’s or higher 26.4%; median household income about $90,000 (2022 dollars, averaged); poverty 9.1%; owner-occupied 63.2%; average household size 4.40.

### Other counts

Pew, May 2025 (2021–2023 ACS / 2023): U.S. Hmong-alone about 330,000; including combinations about 360,000; Minnesota about 95,000 on that count; median age about 26.8.

Counts disagree because definitions disagree. Date the number. A young age structure is not a personality. A poverty rate that fell over decades is not proof the gates closed.

sections.heading: Doors and Sources
sections.body:
Minnesota Compass Hmong profile (ACS 2019–2023). Pew fact sheet on Hmong in the U.S. (May 2025). Minnesota Historical Society / MNHS Hmong in Minnesota; MNopedia. Hmong Cultural Center of Minnesota. Hmong Museum. Hmong American Partnership. Center for Hmong Studies, Concordia University, St. Paul. MDH 2014 qualitative autism study with community partners. Chaxiong 2022. EthnoMed Hmong page for clan-name spellings — a clinical literacy door, not a bible.

### Learn on your own time

CECLC is a door, not the whole community. Learn on your own time. A Hmong colleague is not an unpaid tutor. Pay partners.

sections.heading: How it hits DHS gates — the 40%
sections.body:
Workplace culture and service delivery are both candidates.

Language: an interpreter labeled Hmong who does not speak White Hmong or Mong Leng as this household speaks it is a closed door. Gender match may be requested in maternal and intimate care.

Names: the last name is a clan name. The database that cannot see unmatched last names without a fraud flag is a gate.

Hour caps, exception processes, and life-sharing matches without language are not culturally neutral.

Child welfare and disability: late identification and stigma are documented. Help-seeking that becomes a report is part of why people wait. Mandated reporting still exists. So does the duty not to treat a whole community as a risk score.

Deportation climate: people skip clinic, school, and waiver meetings when a relative can be moved. That is not noncompliance. Do not collect status you do not need.

Notices and comment: an eList and an English PDF is not how this community was reached. Empty follow-up cells are theater.

Workforce: Hmong staff are not the interpreter pool and not the community.

Legislation, funding, rule: you cannot advocate for a channel you will not study. This cultural intelligence exists so the 40% has a household in it — not a paternalistic program designed in a building that never learned to say mung.

sections.heading: A Note on This Guide
sections.body:
This brief is about Karen people — Kayin; pronounce kah-REN — as a people from the hills of what became Burma/Myanmar, with generations in Thai camps and a Minnesota community built from mid-2000s resettlement. This is not Burmese. This is not Hmong. This is not a Census “Asian” mash. Shared continent is not shared culture. A full mosaic is not a stereotype. A stereotype is when this page becomes the person in the lobby.

### Who this is

S’gaw and Pwo are not one interpreter. Burmese and English may also be in the home. Put the dialect on the line. An interpreter labeled Karen who does not speak this household’s variety is still a closed door. Literacy in the language of the form is not guaranteed. Camp years are structure.

### Who this is not

There is no Minnesota Compass “Karen” row. Compass Burmese 17,123 (ACS 2019–2023) is not this people. Do not file them under that count. Coalition of Asian American Leaders (CAAL) has named Karen the largest recent Southeast Asian population to arrive in Minnesota, from 2004, as political refugees. Community and media estimates have been cited near 20,000 statewide — date those as estimates, not Compass. Pattern: Karen Organization of Minnesota and school-language data. Date counts when you have them. Do not invent a rate.

Twin Cities AND Greater Minnesota. Worthington, Albert Lea, and other southern towns are not an afterthought. Church is often the information channel. A smile is not consent to the plan.

The diversity inside this people is the point. A Mae La elder who does not read the English form, a Baptist deacon, a Buddhist household, a Pwo speaker who was given a S’gaw interpreter, a U.S.-born teenager, a night-shift worker in a southern plant — share a people and do not share a Tuesday.

### How to read this

Always defer to the person in front of you. This page is a hypothesis you still test on this family.

sections.heading: Origins and the Founding of a People
sections.body:
Karen (Kayin) peoplehood is older than Burma, older than the British colonial border, and older than the camp file. Oral history and scholarship place Karen peoples in the hills of what became eastern Burma/Myanmar and adjacent Thailand. There is no Karen nation-state they control. British colonial administration drew borders and recruited; independent Burmese states continued a long conflict with Karen armed and civilian communities.

### History for the meeting

S’gaw and Pwo are the large language groups you will meet in Minnesota. They are not always interchangeable in an interpreter. Other Karen groups exist. Do not flatten them into “Burmese.” Do not flatten them into “Asian.”

### What people brought

Baptist Christianity arrived through mission and is now ordinary in many Minnesota Karen communities. Buddhist and traditional/animist practice also live here. That split is Minnesota fact, not a ranking.

What people brought: language, church or temple, agricultural knowledge, a memory of being a people inside a state that made war on them, and years of camp time. What they met in Minnesota: an English form, one “Asian” checkbox, and often one interpreter labeled “Karen” or, worse, “Burmese.”

sections.heading: The Geography of the Karen World
sections.body:
Homeland is Kayin State and adjacent hills, not a tourism map. Thai border camps — Mae La among the named ones — were home for years or for a generation. That geography is still in the room when a form assumes continuous schooling and a stable address history.

### Homeland

U.S. resettlement scattered people; secondary migration and church pulled some together. Minnesota became a large community. St. Paul / Ramsey County is a hub. It is not the map.

### Minnesota

Greater Minnesota is on this page: Worthington, Albert Lea, and other southern and plant towns. Jobs and housing pulled people out of the metro. Rural isolation is a service fact — interpreter scarcity, no Karen-language print in the county office, a church that is the only channel. Do not assume St. Paul. Do not assume they have been to Mae La.

sections.heading: Camps and Resettlement from 2004 — Foundational Event
sections.body:
If 1975 is Hmong Minnesota’s foundational year, Karen Minnesota’s visible U.S. chapter is the mid-2000s. Conflict with the Burmese state produced generations in Thai camps. Camp is not a weekend. Camp is school interrupted, papers that do not match, a smile you give authority, and a clock that is not the county’s.

### Foundational events

U.S. resettlement of Karen refugees scaled in the mid-2000s. CAAL has named Karen the largest recent Southeast Asian population to arrive in Minnesota, from 2004, as political refugees. Date that claim as CAAL. Secondary migration followed jobs and housing into Greater Minnesota.

### Who you meet

The first years were voluntary-agency and church. Karen Organization of Minnesota was founded by Karen refugees and became a national first: a social-services agency built by this people, not only for them. Partner. Do not extract.

A smile at the resettlement office was survival. A smile in your lobby is not consent to the plan. Ask whether they agree.

sections.heading: Family
sections.body:
Extended household is the default hypothesis. Elders, adult siblings, cousins, and church kin may sit in the same week. Who cares for the child may not match the waiver checkbox. Ask who should be in the room. The form’s “family” may be too small.

### Who is in the household

Church is kin-like for some Baptist households — not a metaphor. A deacon or a church sister may be the person who can actually bring the child. That is not permission to make the church the case plan unless this family asked.

### Who speaks

Marriage, bride arrangements, and age are Minnesota law. You follow the law. You still see a family, not a crime scene walking in. Do not skip mandated reporting and call it culture.

Women’s labor in plants, churches, and second-generation school sits next to elder authority. Both can be true in the same room.

sections.heading: Minnesota and Karen History
sections.body:
This department will meet this community on waivers, child welfare, health care, cash, food, aging, employment, and school-linked services — in Ramsey County and in southern towns.

### Places

Karen Organization of Minnesota (KOM), https://www.mnkaren.org/, is the first social-services agency in the country founded by Karen refugees from Burma. Most staff and board have been of this community. Pay. Report back. Do not BCC and stop. Do not invent a Burma briefing when KOM already exists.

### Partners

Church networks — often Baptist — are the information channel in metro and rural sites. Sunday is operations for scheduling. A notice that lands on Saturday night in English is a closed door.

Public calendar: Karen New Year (often early January; confirm locally). Guest if you go, not researcher. Karen staff are not unpaid interpreters and not the community. Identity is not a staffing plan. A New Year visit does not make you the expert.

sections.heading: Kayin — not Burmese
sections.body:
To be Karen in Minnesota is to be a people without a state they control, filed under a checkbox that also holds Hmong, Chinese, and Korean histories they do not share, and often filed again under “Burmese” because the sending country had that name.

### In this state

Camp years sit in the body: time, literacy, trust of a badge. Quiet endurance can look like agreement and then a plan nobody follows. Harmony can be survival. Ask whether they agree. Do not take a smile as consent.

Baptist and Buddhist streams share a people and do not share a Sunday. Youth born here sit between camp parents and U.S. school. That is not a personality. That is a Tuesday.

This guide is a working orientation. Individual variation always supersedes group generalization.

sections.heading: Core Concepts
sections.body:
S’gaw vs Pwo. Put the dialect on the line. “Karen interpreter” is not always the dialect in the room.

### Camp literacy

Interrupted schooling is structure. The English form is a gate. So is a Karen written notice if this person does not read it.

### Church as channel

Baptist majority in many MN communities. Not the case plan unless they asked. Sunday is operations.

### Reciprocity

Showing up, bringing food, returning a favor. Not a delay tactic.

### Quiet endurance

A smile, a nod, a yes that is courtesy. Ask again, plainly, without humiliation.

### Greater Minnesota

Worthington, Albert Lea, and other towns. Print in the office. An eList is not how you reached them.

sections.heading: Religion
sections.body:
Baptist Christianity is the majority stream in many Minnesota Karen communities. Church is often the information channel, the mutual aid, and the Sunday calendar. It is not “the community.” It is not the case plan unless this family asked.

### Streams

Buddhist streams live here too. Animist and traditional practice live here too. Do not treat church as the evolved version. Do not treat traditional practice as folklore.

### Practice

Funerals, baptisms, and New Year gather people. You still keep medical and legal time. You name the conflict instead of punishing it.

Do not make a pastor the interpreter, the case manager, or the mandated reporter’s substitute. Partner if they name the church. Pay. Report back.

sections.heading: Greetings
sections.body:
Elders first. A slight bow or nod with an older person is safer than a hard handshake you assume is universal. Many people will shake hands in English-language rooms. Follow this room.

### Titles

A smile is common. A smile is not consent to the plan. Say the name. Ask how to say it.

### This room

Do not import Hmong clan-name rules, Somali right-hand rules, or the Black nod onto this page. This is not those grammars.

Physical contact: ask the room. Cross-gender touch with elders is not a default.

sections.heading: Naming Conventions
sections.body:
Karen names may not match first-middle-last. A person may have several given names. A family name may be absent, invented by a camp or a U.S. form, or shared in a way the database cannot see. Burmese-style names and Karen-style names both appear. Ask how to say it. Ask how to file it.

### How to file

Do not invent a last name and then flag the household when it does not match the child’s school record. Do not treat unmatched last names as fraud by default.

Pronounce kah-REN for the people. Pronounce this person’s name. Do not joke about “difficult” names. That joke is a closed door.

Women may or may not share a last name with a spouse or child in U.S. records. Ask how to file.

sections.heading: Dates of Significance
sections.body:
Karen New Year — traditionally on the lunar calendar, often celebrated in Minnesota in early January; confirm locally. Public community day. Guest, not researcher. A tunic on a stage is not a file.

### Calendar

Karen Martyrs’ Day — August 12, marking the 1950 killing of Saw Ba U Gyi. Literacy for the desk. Not a day off the work. Not a speech.

Christmas is operations in many Baptist streams. Buddhist holy days are operations in Buddhist streams. Ask this family. Do not put “Asian holiday” on a case note.

A calendar click is not community engagement.

sections.heading: Education
sections.body:
Interrupted schooling in camps is structure. Literacy in English, in Burmese, or in written S’gaw or Pwo is not guaranteed. A parent who speaks fluent S’gaw and limited English is not illiterate. The English-only IEP is the gate.

### School and language

U.S.-born children sit in English-dominant schools. Youth between camp parents and U.S. school is a documented tension in community reporting. Do not make it a personality. Put the dialect on the interpreter line for the meeting the parent has to understand.

Do not invent a Minnesota Karen attainment rate. Compass has no Karen row. Date school-language data when a district has it.

Second-generation educational mobility is real. So is a gap that a room that treats everyone the same will call “culture” instead of language access plus camp years plus a rural office that never learned to say kah-REN.

sections.heading: Etiquette
sections.body:
Elders first. Shoes off in some homes. Accept a little food if offered. You still keep medical and legal time.

### In the home

Sunday church is operations. Do not schedule the only waiver slot through the service and then write “no-show.”

### Time

Quiet disagreement may look like yes. Courtesy is survival from camp and from a badge. Ask whether they agree. Confirm in the dialect they use.

Do not photograph people at New Year as research. Do not walk into a living room and treat dress or an altar as content. Do not force first-name familiarity on an elder.

sections.heading: Language and Communication
sections.body:
S’gaw Karen and Pwo Karen are not one interpreter. Confirm the variety. An interpreter labeled Karen who does not speak this household’s dialect is a closed door. Burmese may be in the home — a second language from the sending state, not the same as Karen. English may be in the home. Literacy in any of those written forms is not guaranteed.

### Language

Put the dialect on the request. Gender match may be requested in maternal and intimate care. CLAS says do not use untrained people or minors. A child who “speaks English” is not the interpreter.

A long answer may be story. A short English yes may be exhaustion or courtesy. Do not take a smile as consent. Ask whether they agree with the plan.

Do not make a Karen coworker the interpreter.

sections.heading: Other Considerations
sections.body:
Unvarnished, because Minnesota Nice is how a room that treats everyone the same deletes facts.

### Named harms

Trauma and quiet endurance will be misread as agreement, as “easy clients,” as a people who do not complain. Ask. A plan nobody follows is a closed door you did not hear shut.

Greater Minnesota isolation: no dialect on the county line, no print notice, a plant shift that cannot make a 10 a.m. St. Paul appointment. Rural is not an afterthought.

Youth between camp parents and U.S. school: language, dress, church, and a county that files the family under Burmese or Asian. Do not make the teenager the interpreter and the culture broker.

LGBTQ Karen Minnesotans exist. You use the name. You do not out someone to church as culture. Do not file under Burmese. Do not file under Hmong. Do not invent a Burma briefing from a news clip.

Staff who share this community may add facts. They do not get to delete a fact because it is hard to say.

sections.heading: Health
sections.body:
Camp and refugee health histories — including interrupted care, immunization records that do not match the form, and chronic conditions identified late — are structure. Date Minnesota rates when a professional has them. Do not invent a rate. Pattern of language barriers now.

### Access

Literacy of the form is a health gate. A signed English consent is not consent if they could not read it and the interpreter was the wrong dialect.

Mental health: trauma is in the history of this people. Do not skip screening. Do not make camp a personality. Do not assume a Baptist household will refuse a counselor. Do not assume they will accept one.

Gender match may be requested in maternal and intimate care. Offer it. Believe reported pain. Do not fold this history into a generic “Asian stoicism” slide. If they name a healer or a pastor, listen. Do not make that person the case plan unless they asked.

sections.heading: LGBTQ
sections.body:
Queer and trans Karen Minnesotans exist. Conservative Baptist climates can mean silence or exile. Buddhist and traditional households vary. Some people live a public English life and a private Karen life. You use the name they use. You do not out them to an elder or a pastor as cultural humility.

### This person

Minnesota’s Human Rights Act still applies. So does the duty not to treat a whole people as a church-values exhibit.

Greater Minnesota isolation can make a closed church the only room. That is not permission to out someone. Ask this person. Defer.

sections.heading: Hair, Dress, and Body
sections.body:
Traditional dress is public at New Year and not a daily uniform. Second generation looks like Minnesota — including in Worthington. Do not ask a woman in clinic whether she “still wears the costume.”

### Dress

Hair and head: follow this person. Do not touch. Do not photograph a tunic as content.

Do not mash Karen dress with Hmong paj ntaub on the unit’s Heritage Month table.

sections.heading: Music
sections.body:
Church music is ordinary in Baptist streams — choir, guitar, hymnody that is operations on Sunday. New Year stages hold dance and song. Traditional instruments exist. None of this is a soundtrack for the unit.

### Variation

A playlist is not engagement. A funeral or a church service is not staff entertainment.

Do not ask a staff person to sing.

sections.heading: Sports
sections.body:
Soccer is public in some Karen Minnesota life. Ordinary school sport is ordinary for the second generation, metro and Greater Minnesota. Neither is language access.

### Not the whole person

Sport clubs are not a case plan. A Saturday league is not consultation.

A parent in the stands who does not read the English IEP still needs S’gaw or Pwo on the line. Book it.

sections.heading: Literature
sections.body:
S’gaw and Pwo have writing systems. Oral tradition is older than the camp school. Interrupted literacy is structure: a person may speak fluently and not read the notice you printed in “their” language.

### Literacy in the lobby

Minnesota Karen students, church writers, and oral-history participants exist (MNHS Karen Community Oral History Project). You do not need to quote a text. You need to know this is not a people without letters, and not a people who can all read the flyer.

Do not put a proverb on a brochure and call it CLAS.

sections.heading: Art
sections.body:
Weaving, dress, and New Year performance are public culture. Guest. A tunic is not a case plan. A museum visit is not consultation.

### Guest

Do not mash with Hmong story cloth or a generic “Southeast Asian” craft table.

KOM and church stages are doors if they name them. Pay. Do not extract photographs.

sections.heading: Conflict, War, and the State
sections.body:
British colonial borders, a long conflict with the Burmese state, generations in Thai camps, and U.S. resettlement from the mid-2000s — that is the political event. Later: a badge in a Minnesota lobby. A DHS badge is not automatically help.

### The badge

Do not invent a Burma briefing from a news clip. The news is not this family’s Tuesday. Do not use camp years as a personality. Do not ask a person to narrate killing, rape, or flight for your professional development.

Filing this household under Burmese in a database is a state act. It is a closed gate with a polite label.

sections.heading: Work, Plants, and Government
sections.body:
Food processing and other Greater Minnesota work drew people to Worthington, Albert Lea, and other towns. Night shifts are operations. A 10 a.m. St. Paul appointment is a gate. Second generation in school, college, and public employment is real.

### Work

KOM employment programs are a partner door. Pay. Do not treat KOM as unpaid county staff.

### Staff

Karen employees inside the department are not unpaid interpreters and not the community. Identity is not a staffing plan.

sections.heading: Health-care and Human-service Encounters
sections.body:
S’gaw or Pwo. Literacy of the form. Who is in the room. Gender. A pastor in the story. Camp health history. Distance from a southern town. A smile that is not consent.

### Language

Confirm the dialect. Ask whether they agree. Offer gender match. Believe reported pain. Do not make staff the interpreter. Do not use a child as interpreter. Mandated reporting still exists.

### The meeting

A signed English page is not consent if they could not read it. Name who the form was built for. Sunday is operations — do not write “no-show” through church.

sections.heading: Adjacent Peoples — Do Not Mash
sections.body:
Not Hmong. Not Burmese. Not Chin. Not Karenni unless they are. Not Rohingya unless they are. Not Vietnamese. Not “Asian American” as the file. Open the Hmong CI for Hmong. Open this for Karen. Some households are mixed. Ask this household.

### Adjacent doors

Compass Burmese 17,123 is a different door. If the household needs Burmese, book Burmese. If the household is Karen, put S’gaw or Pwo on the line. “Burmese” on a form can erase them.

Never one Asian module.

sections.heading: Counts, Dated — and what you may not invent
sections.body:
There is no Minnesota Compass cultural-community row for Karen. Compass Burmese, ACS 2019–2023: 17,123. That count is not this people. Do not file Karen under it. Do not subtract or add your way to a Karen number from that row.

### Counts

CAAL (cited 2021 in community reporting): Karen as the largest recent Southeast Asian population to arrive in Minnesota, from 2004, as political refugees. Date that as CAAL.

### What the count is not

Community and media estimates have been cited near 20,000 Karen in Minnesota (including Wikipedia-style round numbers and local news). Date them as estimates. They are not Compass. School-language counts in St. Paul and southern districts are a pattern when a professional has them. Date those. Do not invent a poverty rate, an LEP rate, or an autism rate for this page.

A young school-age population is visible in classrooms. That is not a Compass age structure. Do not invent one.

sections.heading: Doors and Sources
sections.body:
Karen Organization of Minnesota — https://www.mnkaren.org/. First U.S. social-services agency founded by Karen refugees from Burma. Pay. Report back. Guest at New Year.

### Public doors

CAAL reporting on Asian Minnesotans and the 2004 Karen arrival. Minnesota Historical Society Karen Community Oral History Project. CLAS fifteen: Karen. Put S’gaw or Pwo on the line. The five standing written languages are not the ceiling. A vital notice is still a vital notice.

### Learn on your own time

CECLC is a door, not the whole community. Learn on your own time. Do not make a Karen colleague your unpaid tutor. Greater Minnesota print still matters. An eList is not how you reached Worthington.

sections.heading: How it hits DHS gates — the 40%
sections.body:
Workplace culture and service delivery are both candidates.

Language: an interpreter labeled Karen who does not speak S’gaw or Pwo as this household speaks it is a closed door. Burmese is not Karen. Gender match may be requested in maternal and intimate care. Literacy in the form language is not guaranteed — a signed page is not consent.

Names: the database that invents a last name is a gate that follows the person.

Hour caps, exception processes, and life-sharing matches without dialect and without a rural clock are not culturally neutral. An English IEP is a closed door. A 10 a.m. metro appointment for a night-shift plant household is a closed door.

Child welfare and disability: help-seeking that becomes a report is part of why people wait. Quiet endurance is not safety. Mandated reporting still exists. So does the duty not to treat a whole community as a risk score.

Greater Minnesota: print in the office still matters. An eList and an English PDF is not how Worthington or Albert Lea was reached. Empty follow-up cells are theater.

Filing under Burmese or under Asian is a closed gate with a polite label.

Workforce: Karen staff are not the interpreter pool and not the community.

Legislation, funding, rule: you cannot advocate for a channel you will not study. This cultural intelligence exists so the 40% has a household in it — not a paternalistic program designed in a building that never learned to say kah-REN.

sections.heading: A Note on This Guide
sections.body:
This brief is about African Americans — also called Black Americans. It is the cultural community whose history in this country runs through enslavement in what became the United States, Reconstruction, Jim Crow, the Great Migration, the Civil Rights Movement, and Black life in Minnesota today.

### Who this is

Descendants of Africans enslaved here, and the community that grew from that history across four centuries. About 42.9 million people nationwide (U.S. Census, July 2024), or about 12.6 percent of the country.

Some people in this community use other names for the same historic lineage. This brief uses African American and Black American.

### Who this is not

It is not a brief about every Black person in Minnesota. Somali, Nigerian, Liberian, Ethiopian, Eritrean, Ghanaian, Haitian, Cuban, and other African and Afro-Caribbean communities have their own pages. Census “Black” mixes those stories. This page does not.

### How to read this

Read it as an orientation. A church mother, a physician in St. Paul, a teenager in North Minneapolis, a producer in Atlanta, and a law professor share a history. They do not live one life. There is no single Black culture. Always defer to the person in front of you.

The facts that follow are meant to help you meet people well — how family is named, what respect looks like, what a greeting carries, what a form may land on. Counts are dated. History is here so the meeting is clearer, not so you deliver a lecture.

What shaped this culture includes West and Central African inheritances; enslavement in North America (1619–1865); Reconstruction and Jim Crow; the Great Migration (1916–1970); the Civil Rights Movement and what followed; and a cultural life — music, literature, church, food, language, sport — that has shaped the United States and the world.

sections.heading: Origins and the Founding of a People
sections.body:
African Americans came into being through one of the largest forced migrations in history, and then through life in North America that no other large enslaved population in the Americas matched: the community grew here.

### Across the Atlantic

Between 1525 and 1866 about 12.5 million enslaved Africans were carried across the Atlantic. About 388,000 were brought directly to British North America and the United States. By 1860, on the eve of the Civil War, about four million people lived in slavery in the United States, with about 488,000 free Black Americans, mainly in the North and in free communities in the South.

### West and Central Africa

People came mainly from West and West-Central Africa: Senegambia (Wolof, Mandinka, Fulani); Sierra Leone and the Windward Coast (Mende, Temne, Vai); the Gold Coast (Akan, Asante, Fante); the Bight of Benin (Yoruba, Fon, Ewe); the Bight of Biafra (Igbo, Ibibio, Efik); and West-Central Africa (Kongo, Mbundu, Ovimbundu, Loango). Igbo, Kongo, and Akan were among the largest groups in the British colonies.

They spoke many languages. They practiced traditional African religions, and some practiced Islam. They came from agricultural societies with music, foodways, naming traditions, craft, and knowledge that survived the Middle Passage.

### What they brought

That inheritance is not a museum label. It is in the music, the church, the food, the names, and the way family is held. History here is literacy for the meeting. It is not a speech you give the household.

sections.heading: The Geography of African America
sections.body:
For the first 250 years of African American history — roughly 1660 to 1910 — the vast majority of African Americans lived in the South: Virginia, North Carolina, South Carolina, Georgia, Florida, Alabama, Mississippi, Louisiana, Tennessee, Kentucky, Arkansas, Texas, and Maryland — on plantations, in cities, and after 1865 as sharecroppers, tenant farmers, and small landowners. In 1910, about 90 percent of Black Americans lived in the South.

### After the Great Migration

Then came the Great Migration, taken up in the next chapter. By 1970, only about 53 percent of African Americans lived in the South. By 2020 the share had stabilized at roughly 55 percent as the Reverse Migration (1970s–present) brought Black Americans from Northern cities back to Atlanta, Charlotte, Houston, Dallas, and other Southern metros of the New South.

### Regions now

Pew Research Center’s Facts About the U.S. Black Population:

The South, about 55 percent — especially Atlanta, Houston, Dallas–Fort Worth, Washington, D.C., Miami, Charlotte, the Mississippi Delta, the Black Belt, the Carolinas, the historic Tidewater.

The Midwest, about 17 percent — Chicago, Detroit, Cleveland, St. Louis, Milwaukee, Indianapolis, Cincinnati, Minneapolis–St. Paul, Kansas City, Columbus.

The Northeast, about 17 percent — New York, Philadelphia, Baltimore, Boston, Newark, Pittsburgh, the Hudson Valley.

The West, about 10 percent — Los Angeles, Oakland–San Francisco, Seattle, Las Vegas, Phoenix, Denver, San Diego, Sacramento.

Largest concentrations include New York City (about 2 million), Atlanta (about 2 million), Chicago (about 1.5 million), Washington, D.C. (about 1.5 million), Miami, Dallas, Houston, Detroit, Philadelphia, Los Angeles, Baltimore.

sections.heading: The Great Migration — Foundational Demographic Event
sections.body:
The Great Migration (1916–1970), per the National Archives, was “one of the largest movements of people in United States history. Approximately six million Black people moved from the American South to Northern, Midwestern, and Western states roughly from the 1910s until the 1970s. The driving force behind the mass movement was to escape racial violence, pursue economic and educational opportunities, and obtain freedom from the oppression of Jim Crow.”

It is the foundational demographic event of modern Black America.

### What it transformed

Geography — from 90 percent Southern to roughly 55 percent Southern.

Urban character — from rural agrarian to urban industrial, then urban post-industrial.

Economic structure — from sharecropping and domestic service to factory work, then later professional, white-collar, and entrepreneurial occupations.

Cultural production — the Harlem Renaissance (1920s), Chicago blues (1940s), Motown (1960s Detroit), Philly soul (1970s), New York hip-hop (1970s), Los Angeles gangsta rap (1980s), Atlanta trap (2000s). Every major Black cultural movement traces to the Migration.

Political power — Black voters in Northern and Midwestern cities became decisive in U.S. elections, shifting from Republican (Lincoln’s party) to Democratic (1936–present) and producing the modern civil rights coalition.

Family structure — Migration disrupted Southern extended family networks while creating new urban kinship and community structures.

Harvard’s Great Migration in-focus piece (March 2026): “Between 1916 and 1970, the promise of non-agricultural work, higher wages, educational opportunities, and an escape from racial violence led six million courageous Black Americans to uproot their entire lives and migrate to industrial cities in the West and North.”

sections.heading: Family
sections.body:
The African American family has been among the most resilient and the most embattled institutions in Black America — surviving slavery’s deliberate destruction of family bonds, Jim Crow’s economic and political subjugation, the Great Migration’s geographic dispersal, mass incarceration’s removal of millions of fathers and brothers, and persistent structural inequality. The Black family has continually reinvented itself in forms that have sustained the community.

### Kinship, not only biology

Niara Sudarkasa, cited in EBSCO on African American families: commitment to the family is the most important factor in the socialization of African American children. Reliance on the extended family for emotional, social, and financial support is well documented, and reflects both lasting African inheritances and the experience of slavery. “It takes a village to raise a child” names shared family and community responsibility.

Because of Them We Can on Black traditions: family has nothing to do with biology alone. Black folks have a long history in kinship. People who may not have been blood were family. There are no such things as half-siblings or step-parents in that grammar, and aunties and cousins may or may not be biologically related.

The Black family is extended, fictive, and flexible. Multi-generational households are common, especially with grandparents. Play cousins, play aunties, play uncles — non-biological kin treated as family. Big Mama / Mama / Madea — the matriarchal grandmother who anchors families. First cousins are often more like siblings. Othermothers, a term from Patricia Hill Collins — women who take active roles in raising children not biologically theirs. Co-parenting across households — children raised by multiple households and relatives.

Ask who should be in the room.

### What the numbers miss

African American families are far from homogeneous in structure. In the early twenty-first century more African American children have been born to unwed mothers than to married women — a fact often misread. Many children formally counted as living with a single mother are being raised by extended kinship networks including grandmothers, aunts, fathers (even if not co-residing), godparents, and community elders.

A University of Minnesota study on African American family structure: two distinctive features are well known — Black children have been more likely than white children to reside without one or both parents, and Black households have had a consistently higher percentage of extended households. From 1880 through 1960, Black children were two to three times more likely to reside without one or both parents than were white children. Those patterns reflect the legacy of slavery, economic exclusion, mass incarceration, and different cultural values around extended-family commitment and shared child-rearing.

### Black matriarchs

The Black grandmother — Big Mama, Mama, Madea, Grams, Grandma, Granny, MawMaw — is one of the most powerful figures in African American culture. She often raises grandchildren during parents’ absence or in addition to parents; holds family wisdom and history; anchors Sunday dinners, holidays, and major events; provides moral and spiritual guidance; cooks the family recipes. Big Mama’s house as the family gathering place appears across Black literature, film, and lived experience.

### Fatherhood

The portrayal of “absent Black fathers” is significantly misleading. CDC and academic studies, especially the 2013 NCHS report, find Black fathers more likely than white or Hispanic fathers to be involved in daily activities with their children when controlling for whether they live with the children. Many fathers who do not live with the children’s mothers maintain active involvement.

Mass incarceration of Black men has produced real father-absence at scale. The community has responded with father figures — uncles, grandfathers, coaches, pastors, mentors; Black fatherhood activism including the Million Man March (1995); and many Black men raising children alone.

### Authority and children

Patterns of authority in two-parent African American households are more frequently egalitarian, with flexible rather than traditional gender roles. Children’s responsibilities have long been driven by age and birth order rather than gender. That egalitarianism is partly West African inheritance, partly necessity — Black women have always had to work outside the home — and partly post–Civil Rights and feminist evolution.

Child-rearing has historically been strict, loving, and oriented toward survival in a hostile world. High expectations: respectful, helpful, well-behaved, representing the family well. Corporal punishment has been more accepted in some Black families than in some other communities — “whoopin’” for serious misbehavior — and is increasingly contested in younger generations. Mandatory reporters still distinguish physical discipline from abuse, with cultural literacy. “You’ll have to be twice as good” is a message many Black children receive. Education as the path to freedom. Religious upbringing — Sunday school, vacation Bible school, youth choir. Traditional “children are seen and not heard,” increasingly relaxed. Love expressed through care, food, and presence as much as verbal affirmation in some families.

### Marriage and homegoing

Marriage rates among African Americans are lower than among other racial groups, for economic, demographic (gender imbalance tied to mass incarceration), and cultural reasons. Black marriage celebrations are often elaborate and multi-generational. Jumping the broom — a wedding ritual dating to slavery, when enslaved people could not legally marry — has been revived; many Black couples include it. Co-parenting and partnership across multiple households are normalized.

African American funerals — homegoing services in the Christian tradition — are among the most distinctive cultural events. Because of Them We Can: nobody does homegoing services like Black folks. The death of a community member is sacred. There will be gathering and songs; it may be two to eight hours; there might be a color theme; professional, preferably Black-owned funeral homes matter.

The wake or viewing — open casket, family receives mourners, often the night before. The funeral — often two to four hours, with multiple speakers, choirs, soloists, scripture, eulogy. The repast — after burial, an enormous communal meal at the church or family home. Color theme — families sometimes specify (all white, blue, the deceased’s favorite color). The obituary — often long, detailed, an act of family honor. Birthdays and death anniversaries are remembered.

### Elders

Elders — Mother [Name], Big Mama, Granddaddy, Mr./Mrs. [Name], the OG — are revered. The Black church mother holds particular authority. Sending elders to nursing homes carries stigma, though it is increasingly accepted out of necessity. Adult children are expected to provide care, financial support, and frequent visits. Daughters, granddaughters, nieces, and church sisters often shoulder elder support.

sections.heading: Minnesota and African American History
sections.body:
Minnesota’s African American population is modest in absolute terms — about 350,000 Black Minnesotans as of 2024, or about 6 percent of the state — and culturally significant and historically deep.

### Places

Minneapolis — especially North Minneapolis (the Near North side: Hawthorne, Jordan, Near North, Willard-Hay, Sumner-Glenwood, Harrison), the Black cultural and demographic heart of Minneapolis since the 1910s. MNopedia: the Near North community “has had a major African American presence since the early 1900s.”

South Minneapolis — historically a smaller Black community; Bryant, Bryn Mawr, Field-Regina-Northrop, Powderhorn, Phillips, and Central have all had significant Black populations. The murder of George Floyd at 38th and Chicago in May 2020 put South Minneapolis at the global epicenter of racial justice consciousness.

St. Paul — Rondo was the historic Black community of St. Paul, destroyed by I-94 construction in the 1960s — a generational trauma Black St. Paul still commemorates annually with Rondo Days (the third Saturday of July). Frogtown, Summit-University, and Dayton’s Bluff continue to have significant Black populations.

Brooklyn Park, Brooklyn Center, Robbinsdale, Crystal, New Hope — rapidly diversifying first-ring northwest suburbs, now home to large and growing Black communities, both African American and East African. Eden Prairie, Plymouth, Maple Grove — outer-ring suburbs with growing Black middle-class populations. Duluth, St. Cloud, Rochester — smaller but distinct Black communities, often university or healthcare related.

### Minnesota’s Black history includes

Dred and Harriett Scott — enslaved by Dr. John Emerson at Fort Snelling (1830s–1840s); Dred Scott v. Sandford (1857) was a critical step toward the Civil War.

Roy Wilkins — born in St. Louis, raised in St. Paul; long-time executive secretary of the NAACP.

Lena O. Smith — Minnesota’s first Black female attorney (1921); civil rights pioneer.

Nellie Stone Johnson — labor and civil rights leader; first Black person elected to a city office in Minneapolis (1945).

Prince Rogers Nelson — born in North Minneapolis, 1958; one of the greatest musicians in American history.

August Wilson — playwright, raised in Pittsburgh, spent significant years in St. Paul; two Pulitzer Prizes.

Sharon Sayles Belton — first Black woman mayor of Minneapolis (1994–2001). Melvin Carter III — first Black mayor of St. Paul (2018–present). Andrea Jenkins — first openly transgender Black woman elected to public office in the United States (Minneapolis City Council). Keith Ellison — Minnesota Attorney General; first Muslim elected to Congress (2007); prosecuted the George Floyd case. Toni Carter, Rena Moran, and other contemporary African American political leaders. East African Minnesotans in public office, including Ilhan Omar, have their own community pages; shared race in the United States is not shared culture.

Walter “Fritz” Mondale and Hubert Humphrey — white Minnesota political leaders whose civil-rights advocacy was profoundly shaped by Black Minnesota organizing.

The 2020 murder of George Floyd by Minneapolis police, the subsequent uprising, and the global Black Lives Matter mobilization centered Minnesota in American racial discourse. Minnesota’s racial story is now globally known. The state’s African American community navigates both the legacy of the Migration generation and the weight of being where Floyd died.

sections.heading: The Heart of the People
sections.body:
W.E.B. Du Bois, the foundational African American sociologist and intellectual (1868–1963), wrote in The Souls of Black Folk (1903):

“The history of the American Negro is the history of this strife — this longing to attain self-conscious manhood, to merge his double self into a better and truer self. In this merging he wishes neither of the older selves to be lost. He would not Africanize America, for America has too much to teach the world and Africa. He would not bleach his Negro soul in a flood of white Americanism, for he knows that Negro blood has a message for the world. He simply wishes to make it possible for a man to be both a Negro and an American.”

### Double consciousness

Being both Black and American — sharing in the American story while standing outside the dominant white narrative of it — is foundational to African American identity. Understanding African American culture means understanding this double consciousness: the ongoing tension and synthesis between full participation in American life and the maintenance of a distinct, valued, deeply rooted Black cultural identity.

### Not one life

What follows is a generalization. Individual variation always supersedes it. Diversity within Black America — across region, class, age, education, religion, sexuality, generation, urban and rural, political orientation — is vast. Always defer to the person in front of you.

sections.heading: Core Concepts
sections.body:
These concepts and values recur across African American culture. They express themselves differently across regions, classes, religious communities, generations, and individual circumstances. They are hypotheses — not a script for the person in front of you.

### Blackness

To be Black in America is to live in a culture where racial identity has been a central organizing fact of social existence since 1619. Blackness is at once a racial ascription imposed by a society that categorized people of African descent as “other”; a self-claimed identity affirmed through Black is Beautiful (1960s), natural hair, African heritage, and distinct cultural forms; a political solidarity that crosses class, region, religion, and generation; and a cultural inheritance of music, language, food, religion, family, art, sport, and intellectual tradition.

Blackness is not monolithic, and it is shared. African Americans of all classes, regions, and walks of life recognize each other across difference through the Black nod — the silent acknowledgment between Black strangers in white spaces — the shared vocabulary of references, the common touchstones of Black history.

### The race

Older Black Americans, especially those raised before the 1970s, often refer to “the race” — Black people collectively. The usage carries a Du Boisian sense of collective consciousness: that one is responsible to and for the race, that individual successes and failures matter to the race, that one carries the race into white spaces. Racial uplift, sometimes called the “talented tenth” mentality after Du Bois’s controversial term for the educated Black leadership class, shapes much Black middle-class life: “making the race look good,” “representing,” “lifting as we climb” (the motto of the National Association of Colored Women, 1896).

### Soul

Soul is one of the most important and least translatable Black cultural concepts. Coined in the 1960s but reflecting a much older sensibility, soul names distinctive emotional depth, expressive authenticity, communal feeling, and spiritual resonance. Soul food, soul music, soul brother / soul sister, having soul — the concept pervades Black self-description. To have soul is to be authentic, to feel deeply, to express truthfully, to be in genuine connection with the community and the ancestors. To lack soul is to be cold, fake, disconnected, or assimilated past recognition.

### Respect

Respect is among the most important values in Black social life. To be disrespected — by police, employers, teachers, strangers, family — is a foundational injury. Respect is earned and also fundamentally owed: every human being deserves baseline respect for their personhood. “Respect my Black” names the demand for acknowledgment of full humanity.

Interpersonal respect is signaled through titles and last name (Mr. Johnson, Mrs. Brown, Sister, Brother) until invited otherwise; listening when elders speak; acknowledging people’s presence; not embarrassing people in public; honoring lineage. Aretha Franklin’s “Respect” (1967) became an anthem because it articulated this demand.

### Ubuntu

W.E.B. Du Bois devoted considerable time to cooperative economics, an approach rooted in African traditions such as ubuntu — often translated as “I am, because we are.” African American thinkers have embraced the South African / Bantu concept as articulating a sensibility that runs through Black American life: individual flourishing through collective flourishing.

### Making a way out of no way

A foundational Black American expression — the recognition that African Americans have survived and even thrived through 400 years of conditions designed to destroy them. The capacity to endure, adapt, improvise, and find joy in hardship is celebrated as a core cultural strength. Black resilience is not stoic suffering but creative survival — making something out of nothing, turning pain into art, dancing at the funeral, laughing through the storm. The Black church song “We’ve Come This Far by Faith” captures it: faith as lived practice of getting through what should not have been gotten through.

### Black Excellence

A term that crystallized in the 2010s but expresses a much older sensibility — the celebration of Black achievement in fields where systemic barriers have made achievement extraordinarily hard. It is not assimilationist. It is affirmative: look what we have done despite everything. Invoked at graduations, weddings, professional milestones, and communal — our excellence, not just mine.

### Code-switching

The practice of shifting language, demeanor, accent, and presentation between Black and non-Black spaces is a near-universal experience for Black Americans navigating predominantly white institutions. It can mean speaking African American Vernacular English at home and Standard American English at work; wearing professional hair in white workspaces and natural hair at home; adjusting humor, references, tone, volume, body language. It is a survival skill, an art form, and often a source of fatigue. Younger generations increasingly resist it, asserting the right to show up as fully Black in all spaces.

### The hustle

Entrepreneurial, multi-job, side-business resourcefulness is a recognized cultural pattern, rooted in centuries of exclusion from mainstream employment and capital. Hustle culture is celebrated in hip-hop. The concept honors economic creativity born of necessity.

### Sankofa

The Akan (Ghanaian) word sankofa — “go back and fetch it,” symbolized by a bird looking backward — has been adopted across the African American cultural community as a touchstone for knowing one’s history and honoring ancestors in order to move forward. It appears on Black cultural institutions, in HBCU graduation regalia, in Black bookstores, and in everyday discourse about heritage.

### The ancestors

Honoring those who came before — particularly the enslaved generations whose labor and survival made the present possible — is a quietly central practice. “The ancestors are watching” or “do it for the ancestors” invokes their moral presence. Pouring libations — a small amount of water, juice, or alcohol on the ground while naming ancestors — is observed at weddings, funerals, Kwanzaa, and other significant events. Visiting historic Black sites (Tuskegee, Selma, the cotton fields of the Black Belt, the African Burial Ground in New York, the Whitney Plantation, the National Museum of African American History and Culture) is a contemporary form of pilgrimage.

### Joy as resistance

Black joy — celebration, pleasure, laughter, dance, beauty, and play — is increasingly named as resistance. To be joyful as a Black person in a society that has tried for centuries to make Blackness synonymous with suffering is itself a political act. The cookout, the family reunion, the wedding, the homecoming, the praise dance, Saturday morning music — all are expressions of joy as resistance.

### The Talk

The conversation Black parents have with their children, particularly Black boys, about how to interact safely with police is a tragic and central cultural ritual. Every Black American parent has some version of it: keep your hands visible; do not run; do not reach for your wallet; address officers as Officer and Sir/Ma’am; do not argue; comply first, complain later; come home alive. That the Talk is universal is itself a commentary on the racialized texture of American life.

### The cookout

Cultural shorthand for Black community gathering and inclusion. To be “invited to the cookout” means to be accepted as a welcome guest in Black social life. Because of Them We Can: whether Labor Day, Memorial Day, or Independence Day, it means a cookout. No gathering is more sacred; there must be a Spades table.

### The Black vote

Black Americans are the most politically cohesive racial-ethnic voting bloc in U.S. politics — voting Democratic at rates around 85–95 percent in presidential elections since 1964. That cohesion reflects the Civil Rights Movement and the Voting Rights Act (1965); shared experience of structural racism across class; the strength of Black political institutions — the Black church, the NAACP, the Urban League, the Congressional Black Caucus, the Divine Nine, Black media; and lived political consciousness around policing, housing, education, healthcare, and economic justice.

### Pride in Black institutions

Fierce pride in institutions built within and against a hostile society: HBCUs — Howard, Spelman, Morehouse, Hampton, Tuskegee, Fisk, Florida A&M, North Carolina A&T, Xavier, Dillard, and 100-plus others. Black churches, taken up in Religion. The Divine Nine — Alpha Phi Alpha, Alpha Kappa Alpha, Kappa Alpha Psi, Omega Psi Phi, Delta Sigma Theta, Phi Beta Sigma, Zeta Phi Beta, Sigma Gamma Rho, Iota Phi Theta — central to Black professional and political life. Black-owned businesses — barbershops, beauty salons, restaurants, funeral homes, banks, newspapers, radio stations, publishing houses. Black media — Ebony, Jet (historic), Essence, The Root, BET, The Defender, The Amsterdam News, hundreds of Black newspapers, podcasts, YouTube channels. The NAACP (1909), the National Urban League (1910), SCLC (1957), Black Lives Matter (2013), the Movement for Black Lives.

sections.heading: Religion
sections.body:
The Black church is, per PBS American Experience: The Black Church, “a safe haven for black Christians in a nation shadowed by the legacy of slavery and a society that remains defined by race and class” — and it has been so for over 300 years.

Religious demographics of African Americans: Christian about 73 percent; religiously unaffiliated (“nones”) about 22 percent; non-Christian religious (Muslim, Buddhist, Jewish, and others) about 4 percent.

### The Black church

The most significant institution in African American history.
