sections.heading: A Note on This Guide — a language door, not one people
sections.body:
This brief is about Russian as a language door on the department’s CLAS five-language standing written list — with Hmong, Somali, Spanish, and Vietnamese — not as one people. If you invent a single “Russian community” from that list, you have already left this door. A list is not the person and not the dialect. Still book a qualified interpreter.

### Who this is

Disaggregate before you open a file. Ethnic Russians. Soviet Jews of the 1970s–90s refusenik / Jackson-Vanik stream. Ukrainian households who use Russian — not the Ukrainian people-page; Compass Ukrainian is about 22,570 (ACS 2019–2023); do not mash. Belarusian, Central Asian, and Caucasian Russian-speakers. Evangelical and Baptist Russians, including some Greater Minnesota towns. Recent arrivals versus 1990s versus a third generation that may not need you to speak Russian at all.

### Who this is not

A full mosaic is not a stereotype. A stereotype is when this page becomes the person in the lobby. Shared language is not shared origin, not shared religion, and not shared politics. The Ukraine war is current structure for some households and a trap if you assume every Russian speaker is a combatant or a Putin voter.

There is no Minnesota Compass cultural-community profile titled Russian. Compass immigration table: about 6,483 foreign-born from Russia — date the table you open; that is not a count of speakers. ACS language-at-home figures disagree across vintages. Star Tribune (31 July 2025): Russian is among languages each representing about 2% of Minnesotans who speak a language other than English at home. Minnesota Secretary of State voter materials include Russian. Date the number. Do not invent a community population.

The diversity inside this language is the point. A Jewish grandmother who left on an exit visa in 1989, an Orthodox parishioner, a Belarusian family that uses Russian at the table, a Ukrainian household that will not accept a “former Soviet” interpreter after 2022, a Baptist family in a Greater Minnesota town, a professional who does not need an interpreter and whose elder does — share a language on a form and do not share a Tuesday.

### How to read this

Always defer to the person in front of you. This page is a hypothesis you still test on this household.

sections.heading: Origins — empire, Soviet, and named streams
sections.body:
There is no single founding of “Russian-speaking Minnesota.” Ethnic Russian peoplehood is older than the Soviet Union and older than this department. It is not the whole door. Other peoples used Russian as an imperial and Soviet language of school, army, and office. That history is why a language list is not a census of who counts.

### History for the meeting

Late-imperial emigration included Jews fleeing pogroms and others leaving the Russian Empire. Some of that older Jewish Minnesota is English-dominant now and is not this CLAS door. Do not mash a 1910 synagogue story onto a 1994 arrival and call it one community.

### What people brought

The Soviet period produced later streams: dissidents, Jews denied exit (refuseniks) until Jackson-Vanik and the years that followed opened a way, and then the 1991 collapse of the USSR, which moved people for work, family, and survival. Evangelical Protestants — Baptists and related churches — left in named waves as well. Central Asian and Caucasian families may carry Russian as a public language beside another home language.

What people brought is not one kit: Orthodox practice, Jewish peoplehood, evangelical church, Soviet official atheism, Cyrillic literacy, professional skill the U.S. did not always recognize, and a memory of a state that surveilled. What they met in Minnesota: an English form, a racial order that may file them as white and skip the interpreter, and often one interpreter labeled “Russian.”

sections.heading: The Geography of Russian-Speaking Worlds
sections.body:
Homeland is not one flag. The Russian Federation is a geography some families name. Ukraine is another — and a Ukrainian household that uses Russian is still not this page’s invented people. Belarus, Kazakhstan and other Central Asian states, the Caucasus, the Baltics: Russian as a Soviet-era public language still sits in some of those rooms. Do not referee borders in a waiver meeting. Listen if they name a place.

### Homeland

The diaspora is global: Israel and Germany for large Jewish streams, the United States, Canada, and Europe. Brighton Beach is not Minnesota. Brooklyn, northern New Jersey, and California sit on a different map. Secondary migration and church networks built some of what you will meet here.

### Minnesota

In Minnesota: Twin Cities households; some inner-ring suburbs; Orthodox parishes and synagogues as named places, not a blob; evangelical and Baptist congregations in some towns, including Greater Minnesota. Do not assume Northeast Minneapolis. Do not assume the person in front of you has been to Russia. Do not assume a Greater Minnesota town has no Russian-speaking church.

sections.heading: Emigration Waves — Foundational Events, Not One Flight
sections.body:
If 1975 is the foundational event of Hmong Minnesota and 1991 of Somali Minnesota, Russian-speaking Minnesota does not get one year. It gets a stack, and you will misread the room if you pick the wrong one.

### Foundational events

Late-imperial flight. Soviet emigration in drips and then in named openings. The 1970s–90s Jewish stream — refuseniks, Jackson-Vanik (1974) as U.S. law tying trade to emigration, then the late-1980s and 1990s movement — built part of Twin Cities Jewish life. That stream is Jewish peoplehood meeting Minnesota synagogues and a JCC, not a nesting-doll exhibit. 1991 and the collapse of the USSR moved others: ethnic Russians, mixed families, professionals, people from republics that were suddenly different countries.

### Who you meet

Evangelical and Baptist Russians arrived in church-sponsored patterns that sometimes landed in Greater Minnesota, not only in Minneapolis. Later family and employment streams are ordinary immigration, not a refugee poster.

2022 and the war on Ukraine is current structure for some households in this language: relatives under fire, mixed families, people who will not accept a Russian-language flyer that looks like Moscow. It is a trap if you treat every Russian speaker as a combatant or a Putin voter. It is also a trap if you pretend the war is not in the room when they name it. Literacy for the desk. Not a speech you give the family.

sections.heading: Family
sections.body:
Family is not one size. Some households look nuclear on an English form and still carry obligation to a parent who does not drive and does not read the form. Some are three generations in one week. Some are a single elder whose children live in another metro. Elder isolation is a named harm in this language door. It is not a cultural virtue.

### Who is in the household

The patronymic — a name built from the father — is how a person is fully named in Russian. A form that keeps only first and last has already dropped a who. Ask how to file. Ask who should be in the room.

### Who speaks

Adult children may speak for an elder in English. That is a hypothesis, not permission to skip the interpreter or to use a child. CLAS still stands. A sixteen-year-old in the lobby is not the qualified interpreter.

Women’s labor and professional second generation sit next to older gender patterns in some rooms. Both can be true. Minnesota law still stands on violence, neglect, and who may consent. Do not skip mandated reporting and call it culture.

sections.heading: Minnesota and Russian-Speaking History
sections.body:
Minnesota put Russian on the CLAS five because the building already knew it would meet this language on notices, health care, cash, food, aging, and voting — not because Compass drew a people-blob titled Russian. That is the honest origin of this spine. A language list is operations. It is not a census.

### Places

Places, not a blob: Twin Cities; inner-ring suburbs; some Greater Minnesota towns with evangelical churches. Do not write “the Russian neighborhood” onto a map you do not have. Pattern now. Date a geography when a controlling source exists.

### Partners

Partners: synagogues and Jewish Community Centers for some of the Jewish stream; Russian Orthodox parishes some families name; evangelical and Baptist churches in some towns; no single “Russian community center” as the whole. CECLC is a department door — not the community. Pay the partner this household actually uses.

Do not extract Russian-speaking staff as the interpreter or as “the community.” They may be Jewish, Ukrainian, Belarusian, or a third generation that does not want to be your culture desk. A liturgy or a JCC visit is optional professional development. You are a guest. It does not make you the expert.

sections.heading: A Language Door — not a people you invented
sections.body:
The heart of this intelligence is a refusal. Russian on the five is a door onto many peoples. Ethnic Russian peoplehood is real — language, literature, Orthodox memory for some, a state that did harm and a state some people still defend. It is not permission to file a Ukrainian, a Tajik, or a Soviet Jew under one folk costume.

### In this state

Jewish peoplehood in the 1970s–90s stream is not “Russian culture with a menorah.” Ukrainian households that use Russian are not a round-up for this page. Evangelical Russians may organize life around a church in a town that has never heard the word CLAS.

In Minnesota another fact sits on the same desk: many of these households are read as white. The building’s unmarked default will skip the interpreter, skip the Cyrillic notice, and call that fairness. That skip is the gate. White appearance is not English proficiency and not the absence of a people.

This guide is a working orientation. Individual variation always supersedes group generalization. Always defer to the person in front of you.

sections.heading: Core Concepts
sections.body:
Disaggregation. The first grammar. If you cannot name the stream, you do not have a household yet.

### Patronymic

Given name, father’s name as a middle element, family name. Dropping it invents a person. Filing it wrong invents a person. Ask.

### Formality and titles

First name plus patronymic is respectful address in Russian. First name only can be too familiar with an elder. English “hi guys” is not a translation.

### Hospitality

Tea, food, time in some rooms. Refusing everything can read as cold. You still keep medical and legal clocks.

### State memory

For some, a Soviet past means you do not volunteer extra facts to a government desk. For some, the Russian Federation is still the frame. For some, 2022 ended that sentence. You do not interrogate loyalty. You do the form.

### Church, synagogue, none

A parish, a shul, or a Baptist church may be the actual information channel. It is not “the community.” Do not make clergy the case plan unless this family asked.

### Directness

Some Russian-speaking rooms will say the hard sentence without Minnesota Nice. That is not hostility. Follow this room. Do not punish candor and do not invent a Slavic personality.

sections.heading: Religion — Orthodox, Jewish, evangelical, none
sections.body:
Ask. Do not assume Russian Orthodox because the language is Russian. Russian Orthodox, Jewish, evangelical Protestant, and none all live in this door. Soviet official atheism left a mark in some families that still keep a holiday table.

### Streams

The parish is a center of liturgy, memorial, and sometimes mutual aid. It is not the community. Do not BCC one priest and call it consultation. Icons in a home are not a case plan and not a museum.

### Practice

Jewish households in the 1970s–90s stream may be secular in the Soviet sense and still Jewish in peoplehood — synagogue, JCC, kosher as a maybe, Hebrew school as a maybe. Do not give them an Orthodox Christian flyer and call it language access. Do not give them a “Russian culture night” and call it Jewish.

Evangelical and Baptist congregations — some in Greater Minnesota — can be the whole public life of a household. Church English and home Russian may sit together. Do not make the pastor the case plan unless they asked.

Do not rank piety. A person who left the church or the synagogue is still this language door if that is the language they need.

sections.heading: Greetings
sections.body:
Handshake is common in many rooms — men, and often women in professional space. Follow this room. Some older Orthodox or observant Jewish settings will change the rule. You nod if a hand is not offered. You do not make a scene in the lobby.

### Titles

Titles matter. First name plus patronymic is the respectful Russian address for an adult you do not know well. English Mr./Ms. plus family name is a decent substitute if you cannot produce the patronymic. Do not use a first name with an elder because the form printed it.

### This room

Zdravstvuyte is the formal hello. English “hello” is ordinary, especially with the second generation. Say the name. Ask how to say it.

Do not import Somali right-hand rules or the Black nod onto this page. This is not those grammars. Physical contact: follow this person. A hug from staff is not warmth if the household did not offer it.

sections.heading: Naming — given name, patronymic, family name
sections.body:
A common Russian pattern is given name, patronymic, family name: a person is Ivan Petrovich Sokolov because his father is Petr. Maria Ivanovna Sokolova because her father is Ivan. The patronymic is not a middle name you may drop for convenience. Databases that drop it invent a person. That invented person then fails a match in MHCP, child welfare, and school.

### How to file

Family names may take a gendered ending. Sokolov / Sokolova is the same family. The form that flags the difference as fraud has already chosen a household type. Ask how to file. Ask how this person wants the English record to read.

Jewish, Ukrainian, Belarusian, Central Asian, and Caucasian names in this language door will not all look like Ivan and Maria. Do not “correct” a name toward a Russian textbook. Pronounce it. Ask.

The form that demands first-middle-last and a hyphen will invent a person. Do not invent a last name, and do not invent a middle initial from a patronymic without asking. Three people in one household may not share a “last name” the way a Swedish Minnesota form expects. That is not fraud until you have a reason.

sections.heading: Dates of Significance
sections.body:
Orthodox Nativity and Pascha follow the Julian calendar for many Russian Orthodox households — often later than Western Christmas and Easter. Schedule around them when you can. They are not a day off the work. They are literacy.

### Calendar

Jewish High Holidays, Passover, and other calendar days matter in the Jewish stream. They are not “Russian holidays.” Open the Jewish calendar if that is the household.

9 May — Victory Day in Soviet and Russian memory of 1945 — is real for some elders and a political fight for others after 2022. Listen. Do not put a victory parade on a case note. Do not lecture.

1991 is literacy, not a holiday. 24 February 2022 is current structure for some families. Do not put “Fall of Saigon party” energy — or a Ukraine-war slogan — on a case note.

New Year’s Eve (Novy God) was the large Soviet winter holiday and still is for some secular families. A calendar click on this program is literacy for scheduling. It is not community engagement.

sections.heading: Education
sections.body:
There is no Compass education table for “Russian speakers.” Pattern now — date the number when a controlling source exists. Do not invent a rate.

### School and language

Soviet and post-Soviet credentials were often high — engineering, medicine, teaching — and not always recognized here. A person who was a professional in 1994 and a warehouse worker in 1996 is not a personality. Children of that stream may be in English-dominant schools with a parent who still cannot run an IEP in English.

Elders may be LEP and fully literate in Cyrillic. Professionals and the U.S.-born may not need an interpreter and may still have a parent who does. Do not skip the interpreter because the adult in the lobby is white, employed, or accent-light.

A parent who speaks fluent Russian and limited English is not illiterate. The English-only form is the gate. Put Russian on the line. Confirm it is Russian, not Ukrainian.

sections.heading: Etiquette
sections.body:
Shoes off in some homes. Follow the household. Accept a little tea or food if offered. Hospitality is a virtue. You still keep medical and legal time.

### In the home

Elders first. Formal address until invited. Flowers in odd numbers for some living-room visits is a pattern you do not need to perform; you do need to not mock it.

### Time

Do not walk into a living room and photograph an icon corner, a Sabbath table, or a family photograph wall. Do not touch ritual objects.

On-time for appointments. Traffic and multi-household logistics are real. Courtesy-yes then no-show happens when the plan was never agreed. Ask whether they agree. Confirm in the language they use.

Do not enter a parish, synagogue, or church as a researcher. Guest, if invited.

sections.heading: Language and Communication
sections.body:
Russian is on the five. It is not Ukrainian. It is not Belarusian. It is not “former Soviet.” An interpreter labeled Russian who is the wrong language for this household is still a closed door — and after 2022, a political door. Confirm. CLAS: still book a qualified interpreter. A list is not the person and not the dialect.

### Language

Cyrillic literacy and Latin literacy are not the same. Many elders read Russian in Cyrillic and do not read the English PDF. Some U.S.-born adults do not read Cyrillic. A “Russian notice” in Latin transliteration can still be a closed door. Put the language they read on the line.

Elders may be LEP. Professionals may not be. White appearance is not English. Do not take a light accent as “no interpreter needed” without asking.

A direct answer may be the point, not rudeness. A short English yes may be exhaustion or courtesy. Do not take a smile as consent. Ask whether they agree with the plan.

Do not make a Russian-speaking coworker the interpreter.

sections.heading: Other Considerations — unvarnished, not Minnesota Nice
sections.body:
Unvarnished, because Minnesota Nice is how a room that treats everyone the same deletes facts.

### Named harms

Alcohol harm and family violence exist in some households in this language door. They are not “the culture.” They are not a Slavic joke. You follow the law. You still see a household, not a crime scene walking in. Do not skip mandated reporting and call it humility.

Elder isolation is real for some post-Soviet elders: thin English, adult children at work, winter, no single community center that holds everyone. A missed appointment can be a bus and a language, not noncompliance.

The Russian Federation’s anti-LGBTQ legal climate is current structure for some families. Queer and trans Russian-speakers exist in Minnesota. Minnesota’s Human Rights Act still applies. You use the name. You do not out someone to kin and call it culture.

Immigration status fear is real for some recent arrivals. Do not collect status you do not need. Do not treat fear as noncompliance.

Do not treat every Russian speaker as one origin or one politics. Staff who share this community may add facts. They do not get to delete a fact because it is hard to say.

sections.heading: Health
sections.body:
There is no Compass health profile for this language door. Pattern now — date a rate when a controlling source exists. Do not invent one to fill the spine.

### Access

Elder isolation, depression, and alcohol harm sit in some rooms. War and displacement sit in others. Soviet-era medical culture was biomedical and hierarchical for many; “traditional Slavic medicine” as a staff story is often tourism. Ask what this person uses. Co-create. Do not mock. Do not skip the waiver because a home remedy is in the story.

Mental-health stigma exists in some families. Naming a counselor is not the same as a family accepting one. A smile is not a PHQ-9.

Believe reported pain. Do not invent a Slavic or “European stoicism” slide. Do not fold this into Tuskegee or into an Asian mash.

Gender match may be requested in maternal and intimate care. Offer it. Book the interpreter even if the person is white. Confirm Russian, not a “former Soviet” default.

sections.heading: LGBTQ
sections.body:
Queer and trans Russian-speakers exist in Minnesota. Conservative Orthodox, evangelical, and some family climates can mean silence or exile. The Russian Federation’s laws targeting LGBTQ people are current structure for some households and irrelevant in others. You do not assume either.

### This person

Staff duty is the same as on the other spines: use the name they use; do not out them to an elder as cultural humility; Minnesota Human Rights Act still applies.

Do not use this chapter to raid a household. Do not pretend the tension is not there. Do not treat RF propaganda law as Minnesota practice.

sections.heading: Hair, Dress, and Body
sections.body:
There is no daily Russian costume in the lobby. Second generation looks like Minnesota. Do not ask whether they “still dress Russian.” Head covering happens in some Orthodox churches, some Jewish settings, some evangelical rooms. It is not a security threat and not a consent problem.

### Dress

White appearance is not the absence of a language gate and not the absence of a body that staff may still other. Do not touch. Do not comment on gold, a cross, a magen david, or a headscarf as a case note.

Winter dress is Minnesota. It is not ethnography.

sections.heading: Music
sections.body:
Orthodox chant is liturgy, not a playlist. Jewish music — liturgical and popular — belongs to the Jewish stream, not to a “Russian mix.” Bard song, Soviet-era popular music, and contemporary pop exist. Evangelical rooms have their own hymn and chorus life.

### Variation

A playlist is not engagement. A funeral or a liturgy is not staff entertainment. Knowing that music splits along stream will stop you from putting one YouTube mix on a Heritage Month table and calling it this door.

Named variation is the point. An Orthodox memorial, a Jewish wedding, and a Baptist hymn night are not one “Russian culture night” you can BCC.

sections.heading: Sports
sections.body:
Hockey, soccer, figure skating, and chess carry prestige in some post-Soviet families. Ordinary school sport is ordinary for the second generation. Do not assume the kid plays. Do not make sport the only excellence you can see.

### Not the whole person

Sport clubs are social infrastructure for some. They are not language access and not a case plan. A hockey sticker on a minivan is not proof the elder reads English.

Greater Minnesota and Twin Cities both play. A club flyer in English is still a closed door for the parent who needs Russian on the line.

sections.heading: Literature
sections.body:
Russian is a major written language with a long literature. That fact is literacy: this is not a people without letters. It is not a prompt to quote Tolstoy in the lobby. Jewish, Ukrainian, and other literatures sit in some of the same households. Do not mash them.

### Literacy in the lobby

Cyrillic literacy for many elders is the actual operations fact. A notice that exists only in English, or only in Latin letters, is a closed door. U.S.-born adults may not read Cyrillic and may still be the person who has to explain the form.

You do not need a novel. You need the language this person reads.

sections.heading: Art
sections.body:
Icons are liturgical art in Orthodox homes and parishes — not décor for a unit bulletin board. Soviet visual culture, contemporary work, and Jewish arts in the 1970s–90s stream are not one exhibit.

### Guest

There is no single Minnesota museum that is this whole door. Guest. An icon is not a case plan. A festival is not consultation. Do not photograph a sanctuary as professional development without being asked.

Heritage Month tables that mash matryoshka, a menorah, and a Ukrainian vyshyvanka into one “Eastern European” booth have already mashed what this brief asks you to keep apart.

sections.heading: War, the State, and the Ukraine Trap
sections.body:
Empire, Soviet surveillance, collapse, Jewish emigration under Jackson-Vanik, and later enforcement climate for some arrivals — that is the political stack. A DHS badge is not automatically help. For some people, a government form is a thing you survive. That is not “paranoia.” It is pattern.

### The badge

The war on Ukraine is current structure for some households in this language: family under fire, mixed marriages, people who left Russia, people who did not, people who will not speak politics in a lobby. It is a trap if you assume every Russian speaker is a combatant or a Putin voter. It is also a trap if you punish someone for not performing the politics you prefer.

Do not use 1991 or 2022 as a personality. Do not ask a person to narrate a war for your professional development. Do not collect status you do not need.

sections.heading: Work and Government
sections.body:
Professional work, trades, small business, public employment, and under-recognized Soviet credentials all live here. A small-business owner and a waiver recipient may be the same extended family.

### Work

Russian-speaking staff exist inside DHS and counties. They are not unpaid interpreters and not “the community.” Identity is not a staffing plan.

### Staff

Relationship and hospitality may precede a signature. That is not permission to skip a notice. It is a reason the first visit may not be the decision. The notice still has to exist in Russian, in a script they can read.

An English eList comment period is not how this language door was reached.

sections.heading: Health-care and Human-service Encounters
sections.body:
Language. Interpreter. Cyrillic. Patronymic. Who is in the room. Assuming English because the person is white. Elder isolation. Enforcement climate for some. Alcohol and family violence as facts, not folklore.

### Language

Confirm it is Russian. Still book a qualified interpreter. Offer gender match. Ask who should hear. Ask how to file the name. Do not make staff the interpreter.

### The meeting

Believe reported pain. Do not invent stoicism. Mandated reporting still exists. So does the duty not to treat a whole language as a risk score. Do not collect status you do not need.

sections.heading: Adjacent Peoples — Do Not Mash
sections.body:
Not Ukrainian. Compass Ukrainian cultural community is about 22,570 (ACS 2019–2023). Open that people-page for a Ukrainian household. A Ukrainian family that uses Russian still gets to name their people. Ask. A Russian interpreter can still be the wrong door.

### Adjacent doors

Not Belarusian mash. Not a “former Soviet” interpreter for a Kazakh or Georgian household that needs another language. Not Somali. Not the African American CI. Not “white = no cultural intelligence.”

Historic German- and Scandinavian-Minnesota unmarked culture is the European American door, not this one. A white face in the lobby does not tell you which spine to open.

Some households are mixed. Ask this household. Never one East-European module.

sections.heading: Counts, Dated — no invented population
sections.body:
There is no Minnesota Compass cultural-community profile for Russian. Do not invent one to make this spine look like Hmong or Somali.

### Counts

Minnesota Compass immigration table: about 6,483 foreign-born from Russia. Date the table you open. That is not a count of Russian speakers. It is not Jewish. It is not Ukrainian. It is not the third generation born here.

### What the count is not

Star Tribune, 31 July 2025, on languages spoken at home: German, French, Chinese, Russian, and Arabic each represent about 2% of Minnesotans who speak a language other than English at home. The same reporting said Vietnamese, Chinese, and Russian home-speaker populations had stayed about the same. Date that article. ACS vintages disagree. Date the vintage.

Minnesota Secretary of State voter materials include Russian. That is operations evidence that the state already treats this language as a public-contact fact. It is not a population.

Compass Ukrainian: about 22,570 (ACS 2019–2023). Do not add it to 6,483 and call the sum “Russian-speaking Minnesota.” A rate is not the person. Pattern now — date the number when a controlling source exists.

sections.heading: Doors and Sources
sections.body:
DHS Equal Opportunity and Access LEP resources — five primary written languages: Hmong, Russian, Somali, Spanish, Vietnamese. The ten-language block and the fifteen interpreter cards also include Russian. A list is not the notice and not the interpreter.

### Public doors

Minnesota Compass immigration table (Russian immigrants ~6,483 — date it). Minnesota Compass Ukrainian cultural community profile — adjacent, not this page. Star Tribune, 31 July 2025, languages at home. Minnesota Secretary of State multilingual voter materials.

### Learn on your own time

Synagogues and Jewish Community Centers some Jewish households name. Orthodox parishes some families name. Evangelical and Baptist churches in some towns. CECLC is a door, not the community.

Learn on your own time. Do not make a Russian-speaking colleague your unpaid tutor. Do not BCC one priest or one rabbi and call it consultation. Pay partners you actually have. Report back.

sections.heading: How it hits DHS gates — the 40%
sections.body:
Workplace culture and service delivery are both candidates.

Language: Russian is on the five. An interpreter labeled “former Soviet” is a closed door. Ukrainian is a different language and a different brief. Still book a qualified interpreter. A list is not the person and not the dialect. Cyrillic is not optional decoration on a notice that actually has to be read.

Names: given name, patronymic, family name. The database that drops the patronymic or flags Sokolov / Sokolova as unmatched fraud is a gate that follows the person.

Assuming English because the person is white is a CLAS failure wearing Minnesota Nice.

Hour caps, exception processes, and life-sharing matches without language are not culturally neutral.

Enforcement climate: some recent arrivals skip clinic, school, and waiver meetings. That is not noncompliance. Do not collect status you do not need.

Notices and comment: an eList and an English PDF is not how this language door was reached. Empty follow-up cells are theater. SOS already prints Russian for voters. The packet can too.

Workforce: Russian-speaking staff are not the interpreter pool and not the community. Staff are colleagues, not the curriculum. Do not treat  them.

Legislation, funding, rule: you cannot advocate for a channel you will not study. This cultural intelligence exists so the 40% has a household in it — not a paternalistic program designed in a building that treated a white face as no CI and a language list as a people.

sections.heading: A Note on This Guide
sections.body:
This brief is a language door. Arabic sits on the CLAS ten-language block and the fifteen-language interpreter cards at this department. It is not an Arab module. It is not a Muslim module. If you open Somali Minnesota because Arabic is on the card, you have already closed the door.

### Who this is

Arabic is a first language in Lebanese, Iraqi, Syrian, Palestinian, Egyptian, Sudanese, Yemeni, Gulf, and Maghrebi households in this state. It is a liturgical and religious language in some Somali, Oromo, and other Muslim households — recitation, not the interview. Ask which language this family needs. Confirm whether Arabic is actually spoken at home.

### Who this is not

There is no dated total “Arab Minnesota” population on this page. Do not invent one. Minnesota Compass (ACS 2019–2023) puts Lebanese Minnesota near 6,959 — one stream, not the whole door. Star Tribune (31 July 2025, citing ACS 2017–2021): Arabic is about 2 percent of Minnesotans who speak a language other than English at home, grouped with German, French, Chinese, and Russian. Date the number you use. A language share is not a people-count.

### How to read this

Christian and Muslim Arabs both live here. Lebanese Christian streams are real and older in some Minnesota families. Do not assume mosque. Do not assume hijab. Druze: no dated Minnesota count — do not invent one. If this family is Druze, defer.

Always defer to the person in front of you. This page is a hypothesis you still test on this family.

sections.heading: Origins — a language, not a people
sections.body:
Arabic is an Afro-Asiatic language with a written standard (Modern Standard Arabic / fuṣḥā) and many spoken varieties that are not interchangeable in an interpreter. The language spread with trade, empire, and Islam — and it was already in the Levant and Egypt before that sentence. This is literacy for the desk. It is not a speech you give the family.

### History for the meeting

Peoples who use Arabic as a first language do not share one origin story. A Lebanese Maronite household, an Iraqi Chaldean household, a Palestinian family, an Egyptian Copt, a Sudanese Muslim family, a Yemeni household, a Maghrebi household — share a language family and do not share a Tuesday.

### What people brought

Do not found “the Arabs” in a waiver meeting. Do not lecture a Christian family about the Prophet. Do not file a Black Sudanese or Nubian Arabic speaker under a Levantine picture. Shared language is not shared culture.

What people brought: a dialect, a church or a mosque or neither, kinship, and a memory of states and wars that are not one war. What they met in Minnesota: an English form, one “Arabic interpreter,” and often a Somali default because the building already has that page.

sections.heading: The Geography of Arabic
sections.body:
The Arabic-speaking world is not one flag and not one race. Levant (Lebanon, Syria, Palestine, Jordan), Egypt, Iraq, Sudan and the Nile, the Maghreb, the Gulf, Yemen. Each has dialects, churches, mosques, and class that do not travel as a blob.

### Homeland

In the United States, Dearborn and the Detroit metro, southern California, New York, New Jersey, and Texas hold large communities. Minnesota is not Dearborn. Do not import a Michigan picture onto a Ramsey County lobby.

### Minnesota

In Minnesota: Twin Cities and Greater Minnesota both. Compass Lebanese: 81 percent Twin Cities, 19 percent Greater Minnesota (ACS 2019–2023). Other Arabic-speaking streams are not in that profile. Do not assume Minneapolis. Do not assume the person in front of you has been to the country on the passport copy.

sections.heading: Many arrivals — no single foundational year
sections.body:
If 1975 is Hmong Minnesota and 1991 is Somali Minnesota, Arabic-speaking Minnesota has no single foundational year. That is the point. Collapse is how a module gets written.

### Foundational events

Lebanese and other Levantine Christian streams include families with deep U.S. roots; Compass Lebanese foreign-born is 8.5 percent (ACS 2019–2023) — dated, one stream. Palestinian displacement is a twentieth-century and present fact. Iraqi arrival after 1991 and after 2003. Syrian after 2011. Sudanese streams. Yemeni. Maghrebi and Gulf smaller here. Secondary migration from other states.

### Who you meet

The desk in 2026 meets U.S.-born children in every stream, elders who need a dialect, and people who use Arabic only at church or only in Qurʾan school. If you only know “refugee” or only know “Muslim,” you will miss this room.

Distrust of government has sources that are not one source: 9/11-era surveillance, wars the United States ran, Gaza-era harassment, and ordinary ICE. A DHS badge is not automatically help.

sections.heading: Family
sections.body:
Who is in the household varies by stream, class, and generation. Some rooms are extended. Some are nuclear in the English way. Compass Lebanese average household size about 2.14 (ACS 2019–2023) is one stream — often smaller, older, more English-dominant. Do not copy it onto a Sudanese or Iraqi waiver household.

### Who is in the household

Ask who should be in the room. A nuclear English form already has a who. Elders, in-laws, and adult children may sit in the same week.

### Who speaks

Do not invent a last name because the database wants one. Do not treat unmatched last names as fraud by default. Patronymic and three-part patterns exist in some families; Westernized first-middle-last in others.

Women’s labor and men’s labor both live here. Gender norms are this family’s, not “Arab.” Ask.

sections.heading: Minnesota and Arabic as a door
sections.body:
Arabic is on the language block because the department already meets these households. That is operations, not a festival. There is no Cedar-Riverside of Arabic Minnesota. Named churches — Maronite, Antiochian and other Orthodox, Coptic — and named mosques and Islamic centers are partners if this family names them, not a list to extract from.

### Places

Compass Lebanese (ACS 2019–2023): about 6,959; 81.0 percent Twin Cities; 19.0 percent Greater Minnesota. Greater Minnesota is not an afterthought. Other Arabic-speaking streams are not inside that count.

### Partners

Arabic-speaking staff are not unpaid interpreters and not the community. Identity is not a staffing plan. A Heritage Month table is not consultation. You are a guest. It does not make you the expert.

CECLC is a door, not the whole. Pay partners. Report back.

sections.heading: A language door — not a heart to perform
sections.body:
There is no single heart of “Arab Minnesota” to put on a poster. For some people, Arabic is the language of the grandmother and the church. For some, it is the language of the Qurʾan and not of the kitchen. For some, it is the only language that reaches an elder. For some U.S.-born children it is a class they do not speak.

### In this state

Race in the U.S. file fails this door in more than one direction. Levantine and Iraqi Christians have often been filed White. Sudanese Arabic speakers have been filed Black. “MENA” as an emerging box is still not a person. Somali is a different people. Do not fold this household into Somali Minnesota because both might be Muslim.

This guide is a working orientation. Individual variation always supersedes group generalization.

sections.heading: Core Concepts
sections.body:
Dialect. Levantine, Egyptian, Iraqi, Maghrebi, Sudanese, Gulf, MSA. An interpreter labeled Arabic who does not speak this household’s variety is a closed door. Confirm it on the line.

### Home language versus liturgy

Arabic on a Somali or Oromo Muslim card may be recitation. Book the interview language. Do not open this door and skip Somali or Oromo when those are the people.

### Christian and Muslim both

Do not assume the mosque. Do not assume the priest.

### Hospitality and family reputation exist in many rooms

They are not a module you perform. A yes that is courtesy is not a signature. Ask whether they agree.

MSA is school and media for some; it is not the kitchen. Do not test an elder in fuṣḥā and call it language access.

sections.heading: Religion — not the language
sections.body:
Islam is not Arabic. Arabic is not Islam. Christian Arabs — Maronite, Orthodox, Coptic, Protestant — live in this state. Muslim Arabs — Sunni and Shiʿa — live in this state. People who left both live in this state. Do not make a religion the case plan unless this family asked.

### Streams

Arabic as Qurʾanic language is liturgical. It is used that way in some Somali, Oromo, and other Muslim households whose interview language is not Arabic. Do not book an Arabic interpreter for a Maay grandmother because the building saw “Muslim.”

### Practice

Do not assume hijab. Do not rank covering as piety or oppression. Halal matters in some rooms and not in others.

Druze: no dated Minnesota count. Do not invent a community. If this family names Druze, listen. Defer.

Ramadan, Eid, Friday prayer, Christmas, Easter, Coptic fasts — ask. A calendar click is not engagement.

sections.heading: Greetings
sections.body:
Follow this room. As-salāmu ʿalaykum is ordinary in many Muslim rooms; the reply is wa-ʿalaykumu s-salām. It is not default in a Christian Arab room. Marḥaban, ahlan, and English hello are ordinary. Say the name.

### Titles

Elders first. A hard handshake you assume is universal is already a closed door for some women and some elders. Many second-generation people will shake hands in English-language rooms. If a hand is not offered, nod. Do not force it.

### This room

Do not import the Black nod onto this page. Do not import Somali greeting rules as if Arabic were Somali.

Physical contact: ask the room. Cross-gender touch is not a default in some families. It is ordinary in others.

sections.heading: Naming Conventions
sections.body:
Naming patterns vary. Some families use given name + father’s name + family name. Some three-part names look like Somali names and are not. Some Lebanese and other Christian streams use French or English given names and a family surname that the database can already see. Some people have Westernized on U.S. forms. Ask.

### How to file

Do not invent a last name because the screen requires one. That invented name becomes a gate.

Pronounce it. Ask. Do not joke about long names. Do not assume three Somali names. Do not assume a hyphen.

Women may or may not take a husband’s family name in U.S. records. Ask how to file. Do not “correct” a mother and child who do not share a last name as a fraud signal until you have a reason.

sections.heading: Dates of Significance
sections.body:
Ask this family. Muslim lunar dates — Ramadan, Eid al-Fitr, Eid al-Adha, Mawlid in some rooms — move on the Gregorian calendar. Christmas and Easter (Western, Orthodox, Coptic) in Christian rooms. National days some families name (and some refuse).

### Calendar

11 September 2001 is structure in this country, not a holiday and not a personality. Gaza-era harassment is current structure. Neither is a calendar click that makes you engaged.

Do not put “Arab holiday” or “Muslim holiday” on a case note without asking. A calendar click is literacy. It is not community engagement.

sections.heading: Education
sections.body:
Streams differ. Compass Lebanese (ACS 2019–2023), among those 25 and older: about 97.9 percent high school or higher; about 50.5 percent bachelor’s or higher. That is one stream, often English-dominant. Do not copy it onto a recently arrived Sudanese or Iraqi parent.

### School and language

A parent who speaks fluent Arabic and limited English is not illiterate. Literacy in Modern Standard Arabic is not guaranteed for every dialect speaker. The English-only IEP is the gate.

The child is not the interpreter. CLAS: untrained individuals and minors are not the plan. Put the dialect on the line.

Second-generation educational mobility is real in some streams. So is a gap a room that treats everyone the same will call “culture” instead of language access.

sections.heading: Etiquette
sections.body:
Hospitality is a virtue in many rooms. Accept a little tea if offered. You still keep medical and legal time.

### In the home

Shoes off in some homes. Right hand for food in some Muslim rooms. Do not import a rule you learned on the Somali page as automatic.

### Time

Do not assume a woman will or will not cover. Do not photograph a family and call it rapport. Do not enter a prayer space as a tour.

On-time for appointments. Multi-household logistics are real. So is a courtesy-yes then no-show when the plan was never agreed. Ask whether they agree. Confirm in the language they use.

sections.heading: Language and Communication
sections.body:
Levantine, Egyptian, Iraqi, Maghrebi, Sudanese, Gulf, Modern Standard Arabic. Confirm the variety. An interpreter labeled Arabic who does not speak this household’s dialect is still a closed door. Maghrebi and Levantine are not interchangeable because both are “Arabic.”

### Language

Confirm whether Arabic is the home language at all. On a Somali or Oromo Muslim card it may be religion. Book the interview language. Do not open Somali Minnesota by default because Arabic is on the card.

Star Tribune (31 July 2025, ACS 2017–2021): Arabic is about 2 percent of non-English-at-home speakers in Minnesota, grouped with German, French, Chinese, and Russian. Date that. It is not a people-count.

A short English yes may be exhaustion or courtesy. Do not take a smile as consent. Do not make a coworker the interpreter. The child is not the interpreter.

sections.heading: Other Considerations
sections.body:
Unvarnished, because Minnesota Nice is how a room that treats everyone the same deletes facts.

### Named harms

Islamophobia and anti-Arab racism after 11 September 2001 and after Gaza are structure in this country and in this state. They change who opens the door, who will not put a relative’s name on a form, and who reads a DHS badge as threat. That is not noncompliance.

Do not collect political speech as a risk score. Do not file a protest, a flag, or an opinion about Gaza or Iraq as a safety note. Enforcement climate is real for some streams. Do not collect status you do not need.

Queer and trans Arabs exist. You use the name. You do not out someone to kin and call it culture.

Do not assume hijab. Do not assume Muslim. Do not skip mandated reporting and call it humility.

Staff who share this community may add facts. They do not get to delete a fact because it is hard to say.

sections.heading: Health
sections.body:
No dated Minnesota-wide Arabic-speaking autism, diabetes, or PTSD rate belongs on this page. Do not invent one. War trauma sits in some Iraqi, Syrian, Sudanese, Palestinian, and Yemeni streams. It is not a personality and not every household.

### Access

sections.heading: A Note on This Guide
sections.body:
This brief is about Oromo people — Oromoo; the language Afaan Oromoo — as a Cushitic-speaking nation of the Horn and as a Minnesota community. Oromo is not Somali. Not Amharic. Not “Ethiopian” as a synonym. If you open Somali Minnesota or book an Amharic interpreter because the building heard East Africa, you have already closed the door.

### Who this is

Minnesota Compass (ACS 2019–2023) puts Ethiopian Minnesota near 40,324: 89.4 percent Twin Cities, 10.6 percent Greater Minnesota; 43.5 percent age 17 or younger; 61.7 percent foreign-born; language other than English (age 5+) 74.9 percent; LEP 30.4 percent. Compass note historically: respondents born in Ethiopia who list Somali ancestry are counted Somali, not Ethiopian. Ethiopian Compass is an umbrella — Amhara, Oromo, Tigrayan and others are not one file. Use Ethiopian numbers as dated context, not as an Oromo census.

### Who this is not

Oromo-specific counts disagree. MinnPost (19 May 2016): the Oromo Community of Minnesota estimated up to 40,000 Oromo in the state; the state demographer’s office nearer 8,500 using census plus school language. Star Tribune (31 July 2025): about 8,000 Minnesotans speak Oromo at home; Minnesota Department of Education: Oromo was the 8th most-common home language in K–12. Date the disagreement. Do not invent a midpoint. A rate is not the person.

### How to read this

Islam and Christianity (Orthodox, Protestant) and Waaqeffanna traditional practice all live here. Do not assume Muslim like Somali. Always defer to the person in front of you. This page is a hypothesis you still test on this family.

sections.heading: Origins and the Founding of a People
sections.body:
Oromo peoplehood — Oromummaa — is older than the Ethiopian empire’s file on it and older than the refugee camp. Oromo people are a Cushitic-speaking nation of the Horn, the largest nation in the region by language. There is no Oromo nation-state. Gadaa (generational / governance tradition) is literacy for the desk, not a speech you give the family, and not every household still lives it.

### History for the meeting

Afaan Oromoo is not Amharic. Amharic is a Semitic language and was the imperial state language. Latin Qubee script, adopted in the early 1990s after the fall of the Derg, is political and educational history: a people writing itself after suppression. That sentence is literacy. It is not a lecture in the lobby.

### What people brought

What people brought: language and dialect, Islam and Christianity and Waaqeffanna, kinship, oral art, a memory of imperial and 20th-century state violence. What they met in Minnesota: an English form, one “Ethiopian” checkbox, one “East African” interpreter, and often Somali because the building already has that page.

Do not assume Addis Ababa as identity. Many Oromo people name Oromia, a region, a village, a lineage — not the capital of the state that ruled them.

sections.heading: The Geography of the Oromo World
sections.body:
Homeland is Oromia and Oromo-inhabited country across the Horn — a map that does not match the Ethiopian state’s ethnic-federal drawing in every family’s mouth. Oromo communities also live in Kenya. A global diaspora: Middle East, Europe, North America. After Kenya, Minnesota has been named among the largest Oromo communities outside the homeland (MNHS / MNopedia). Twin Cities as Little Oromia is community naming, not a census.

### Homeland

Compass Ethiopian (ACS 2019–2023): 89.4 percent Twin Cities, 10.6 percent Greater Minnesota — umbrella, not an Oromo map. Do not assume Cedar-Riverside. That sentence is Somali geography unless this family lives there. Do not assume Addis.

### Minnesota

Do not assume the person in front of you has been to Oromia. Secondary migration built parts of this map. Greater Minnesota is still this people when they live there.

sections.heading: Imperial Violence, Struggle, and Secondary Migration — Foundational Event
sections.body:
There is no single 1975 or 1991 on this page. The foundational political literacy is longer: Ethiopian imperial incorporation of Oromo country, 20th-century state violence, the Oromo Liberation struggle as literacy for the desk not a speech, the 1974 revolution and the Derg, flight through Sudan and Kenya and the Gulf, U.S. resettlement, secondary migration to Minnesota, and unrest in the 2010s–2020s that sent another wave.

### Foundational events

Do not referee Ethiopian politics in a waiver meeting. Do not pick a side as DHS. Intra-Ethiopian tension in Minnesota rooms is real. Listen if they name it. Do not file it as a risk score.

### Who you meet

The desk in 2026 meets first-wave elders and U.S.-born children — English-dominant with peers, still translating for parents, still unable to get Afaan Oromoo in a lobby that offered Somali or Amharic.

If you only know “Ethiopian refugee,” you will miss this household.

Arabic may be religion, not the interview. Confirm the variety (Borana, Guji, Wollo, others). Gender match may be requested in maternal and intimate care.

Names: Oromo names are not Amharic names. The database that invents a last name, or that assumes three Somali names, is a gate that follows the person.

Hour caps, exception processes, and life-sharing matches without language are not culturally neutral.

Child welfare: help-seeking that becomes a report is part of why people wait. Mandated reporting still exists. So does the duty not to treat a whole community as a risk score. FGC: Minnesota law stands; this is not the Somali page; do not invent a rate.

Notices and comment: an eList and an English PDF is not how this community was reached. Empty follow-up cells are theater.

Workforce: Oromo staff are not the interpreter pool and not the community. Staff are colleagues, not the curriculum. Do not treat  them.

Legislation, funding, rule: you cannot advocate for a channel you will not study. This cultural intelligence exists so the 40% has a household in it — not a paternalistic program designed in a building that filed Oromo under Somali or under Ethiopian as a synonym.

sections.heading: A Note on This Guide
sections.body:
This brief is about Bosniak / Bosnian Minnesota as a people-page. The CLAS ten language block says Serbo-Croatian (Bosnian). That is operations. It is how the building batches a notice. It is not the name of the household in the lobby.

### Who this is

Bosniak names the Muslim peoplehood of Bosnia and Herzegovina. Bosnian can also mean a citizen of a state that Dayton wrote as three constituent peoples — Bosniak, Croat, Serb. Croatian and Serbian households in Minnesota are adjacent. They may share a mutually intelligible language. They do not share this war story by default. Ask. Do not file them here because the interpreter catalog used a hyphen.

### Who this is not

This is not a Census “white” mash and not a Balkan blob. It is not Somali Islam with a different flag. It is not Russian, not Albanian, not Kosovar, not Ukrainian. Shared continent is not shared culture. Shared Islam is not shared culture. A full mosaic is not a stereotype. A stereotype is when this page becomes the person in the lobby.

### How to read this

There is no Minnesota Compass cultural-community count for Bosnian. That absence is a finding, not a reason to invent 40,000. Between 1993 and 2003 more than 2,300 primary Bosnian refugees resettled in Minnesota; they were part of about 140,000 Bosnian and Herzegovinian refugees who came to the United States (MSP Magazine, looking back at Minnesota’s refugee history). Primary placement is not the community. Secondary migration happened. Date the number you use. A rate is not the person.

The diversity inside this people is the point. A Srebrenica widow, a man who will not name the camp, a Catholic Croat neighbor who speaks the same language and not the same memory, a less-observant Bosniak who drinks coffee and does not keep Ramadan, a woman who covers, a woman who does not, a U.S.-born nurse who uses English with friends and Bosnian with an elder — share a language family and do not share a Tuesday.

Always defer to the person in front of you. This page is a hypothesis you still test on this family.

sections.heading: Origins and the Founding of a People
sections.body:
Bosniak peoplehood is older than 1992 and older than the refugee file. South Slavic speakers in the Dinaric and Bosnian lands lived under medieval kingdoms, Ottoman centuries (from the 15th century), Austro-Hungarian rule after 1878, royal and then socialist Yugoslavia, and the 1992 independence of Bosnia and Herzegovina. Islam in this land is Ottoman-era and European. That sentence is literacy. It is not a piety rank.

### History for the meeting

Bosniak, Croat, and Serb in Bosnia are not three languages you can hear from across a lobby. They are political names on a mutually intelligible South Slavic speech. The 1990s war made the names lethal. The desk that treats them as flavor has already failed the household.

### What people brought

What people brought: family, coffee, a language with a literature, Islam as heritage for most Bosniaks (sometimes as daily order, sometimes as a name without a public mark), Catholic and Orthodox streams in adjacent households, and a memory of neighbors who became a front. What they met in Minnesota: an English form, a language block that says Serbo-Croatian (Bosnian), and often one interpreter labeled “former Yugoslav.”

There is no Bosniak nation-state in the simple sense the checkbox wants. Dayton wrote a state with two entities and three constituent peoples. Do not referee that constitution in a waiver meeting. Listen if they name home.

sections.heading: The Geography of the Bosnian World
sections.body:
Homeland is Bosnia and Herzegovina — Sarajevo, Tuzla, Zenica, Banja Luka, Mostar, Bihać, the Drina towns, the eastern enclaves. Srebrenica is a place-name and a crime. Do not put it on a small-talk map.

### Homeland

The 1992–1995 war produced camps and exile in Croatia, Serbia, Montenegro, Germany, Austria, Scandinavia, and then the United States. St. Louis became a large U.S. Bosnian hub. Chicago, New York, and other cities hold communities. Minnesota received a notable resettlement in the mid and late 1990s. Minnesota is not St. Louis. Do not copy a Missouri story onto this desk and call it local.

### Minnesota

In Minnesota: Twin Cities pattern. Islamic Community of Bosniaks in Minnesota has been a named Minneapolis door. Greater Minnesota households exist because work and kin exist. Do not assume one neighborhood. Do not assume the person in front of you has been back. Do not assume they want to go.

sections.heading: 1992–1995, Srebrenica, Dayton — Foundational Event
sections.body:
If the Great Migration is the foundational demographic event of modern Black America, and 1991 of Somali Minnesota, 1992–1995 is the foundational event of Bosnian Minnesota.

### Foundational events

Yugoslavia broke. Bosnia and Herzegovina declared independence. War followed: siege of Sarajevo, ethnic cleansing, camps, mass rape as a method of war, and on 11 July 1995 the genocide at Srebrenica — more than 8,000 Bosniak men and boys killed after a UN “safe area” failed. That is public record (ICTY, International Court of Justice). It is literacy for the desk. It is not a speech you give the family. Do not ask a survivor to narrate the pit.

### Who you meet

Dayton, December 1995, stopped the shooting and froze a political map. Camps and temporary protection in Europe came first for many. U.S. resettlement followed in the mid and late 1990s. Minnesota’s primary-refugee arrivals between 1993 and 2003 were more than 2,300. Secondary migration after that is real and not a Compass cell.

The desk in 2026 does not only meet that first wave. It meets their children — U.S.-born, English-dominant with peers, still translating for a parent who will not tell the war to a stranger and still cannot get the right language in the lobby. If you only know “refugee,” you will miss them.

sections.heading: Family
sections.body:
Family is larger than a nuclear English form. Elders often speak. Kumovi — godparent ties — can be as binding as blood in some households. Who cares for a child, an elder, or a disabled adult may be a network the waiver checkbox does not have a box for.

### Who is in the household

War and exile also broke families. Missing men. Split siblings. A neighbor who is now the household. Camp years and then a U.S. apartment. Ask who should be in the room. Do not reconstruct a family tree as icebreaker.

### Who speaks

Women’s labor — factory, care work, professional second generation — sits next to a household in which an elder man may still be named as head. Both can be true in the same room.

Do not use 1995 as a family personality. Do not skip mandated reporting and call it culture. Minnesota law still stands.

sections.heading: Minnesota and Bosnian History
sections.body:
Minnesota received a notable Bosnian resettlement in the mid and late 1990s. That is why this page has to be as complete as the Hmong and Somali intelligences — because this department will meet this community on waivers, child welfare, health care, cash, food, aging, and employment, including the elder who still needs the language and the adult child who does not think of themselves as a refugee.

### Places

Places, not a blob: Twin Cities; a Minneapolis Bosniak civic and religious life some families name; Greater Minnesota when work pulled people. Do not invent a Little Sarajevo on a case note. Ask this family where they live.

### Partners

Partners: Islamic Community of Bosniaks in Minnesota; mosques and churches families actually name; resettlement-era voluntary agencies as history, not a current partner list; CECLC as a department door — not the whole community.

Bosnian staff are not unpaid interpreters and not the community. Identity is not a staffing plan. A Bajram greeting is optional professional courtesy. It does not make you the expert.

sections.heading: Bosniak / Bosnian — the heart of a people
sections.body:
To be Bosniak in Minnesota is to be a European Muslim people whose public mark is often quieter than Somali Minnesota, carrying a war the United States watched on television and then filed under the 1990s. In this building it sits inside another fact: many Bosnian Minnesotans are white in a U.S. racial order that will delete 1995 and call them assimilated, or Muslim in a room that treats everyone the same that will copy the Somali page and get the covering, the mosque, and the language wrong.

### In this state

Bosnian can mean the language, the passport, or the people-name. Bosniak is the ethnic name for the Muslim peoplehood. Use what this family uses. Do not lecture them on the difference as a greeting.

This guide is a working orientation. Individual variation always supersedes group generalization.

sections.heading: Core Concepts
sections.body:
Language as a political name. Bosnian, Croatian, Serbian — mutually intelligible, not interchangeable as identity. Book what they ask. “Former Yugoslav” is a closed door with a polite label.

### Islam as heritage for most Bosniaks

Often less publicly marked than Somali Minnesota. Do not assume hijab. Do not assume five daily prayers in the lobby. Do not assume the absence of a mark means the absence of faith — or of trauma.

### Family and kumovi

Who is in the room. Who signs.

### Coffee

Hospitality is a virtue. You still keep medical and legal time.

### Memory

Srebrenica and the siege are in the room for some people whether they speak them or not. You do not extract the memory. You do not deny it. You do not platform denial.

### Face

Direct refusal may be costly, or it may be blunt. Ask whether they agree. Do not take a smile as consent.

sections.heading: Religion and Healing
sections.body:
Islam for most Bosniaks — Sunni, Ottoman heritage, a European Muslim history. Practice in Minnesota ranges from daily order to a name on a form. Hijab is not the default public mark. Do not copy the Somali religion chapter onto this page. Do not assume mosque is the case plan. Do not assume Friday prayer sets the appointment grid the way it might for another household. Ask.

### Streams

Catholic Croat and Orthodox Serb streams exist in the broader language. Christmas dates differ. A “Bosnian” interpreter for a household that names itself Croatian or Serbian may still be the wrong political door even when the words are understood. Ask.

### Practice

Do not make an imam, a priest, or a pastor the case plan unless this family asked. Church or mosque can be the information channel. It is not “the community.”

Illness meaning after war may not be the DSM sentence. PTSD, unexplained pain, sleep, and alcohol sit in the same clinic as ordinary Minnesota chronic disease. You can hold both. You do not interrogate the pit to complete a field.

sections.heading: Greetings
sections.body:
Elders first. A handshake is common in many Bosnian Minnesota rooms — European-style, not a Somali right-hand rule you import. Some observant Muslim Bosniaks will not shake hands across gender. Follow this room. Nod if a hand is not offered. Do not force one. Do not make a lesson of it.

### Titles

Merhaba, dobro jutro, zdravo, selam — follow what they offer. English “hello” is ordinary in the second generation. Say the name. Ask how to say the -ić.

### This room

Do not open with the war. Do not open with “I have a friend from Bosnia.” Do not import the Black nod or Somali As-salāmu ʿalaykum as the default here. This is not those grammars unless this person uses them.

sections.heading: Naming Conventions
sections.body:
South Slavic: given name, then family name. -ić and -vić endings are common (Hodžić, Begović, Hadžić, Petrović — examples of a pattern, not a roll call). The ć is not optional decoration. Ask how to say it. Do not joke. Do not anglicize it on the file without being asked.

### How to file

Women may or may not take a husband’s family name in U.S. records. Ask how to file. Do not “correct” a mother and child who do not share a last name as a fraud signal until you have a reason.

Given names may be Bosnian, South Slavic Christian, Arabic-origin, or English in the second generation. The form that demands first-middle-last and a hyphen will invent a person if you force it.

Pronounce it. Ask. Write what they say.

sections.heading: Dates of Significance
sections.body:
Ramadan and Bajram (Eid al-Fitr, Eid al-Adha) for many Bosniak households. Lunar. Date them each year. They are operations for fasting, appointments, and an elder who will not drink water in your lobby. They are not a festival you attend as consultation.

### Calendar

Catholic Christmas (December 25) and Orthodox Christmas (January 7) in adjacent Croat and Serb streams — and in mixed families. Ask. Do not put “Balkan holiday” on a case note.

11 July — Srebrenica Genocide Memorial Day. Literacy for the desk. Not a day off the work. Not a prompt to ask who they lost.

1 March is Independence Day for some. Dayton’s anniversary is not a greeting. A calendar click is literacy. It is not community engagement.

sections.heading: Education
sections.body:
There is no Compass education rate on this page. Do not invent one. Interrupted schooling from siege, flight, and camps is structure for some first-wave adults — not a personality and not illiteracy in Bosnian.

### School and language

A parent who speaks fluent Bosnian and limited English is not illiterate. The English-only IEP is the gate. Put the language they ask for on the interpreter line. Latin script is not the same as English literacy. Cyrillic in a Serbian-identifying household is a different written door.

Second-generation educational mobility is real. So is an elder who still cannot run an exception form in English. Date a Minnesota figure when a controlling source exists. Until then: pattern, not a fake percent.

sections.heading: Etiquette
sections.body:
Coffee is hospitality. Bosnian coffee is not a delay tactic. Accept a little if offered. You still keep medical and legal time. Name the conflict instead of punishing the cup.

### In the home

Shoes off in some homes. Elders first. Direct speech is not always rudeness here; courtesy-yes is not always agreement either. Ask whether they agree with the plan. Confirm in the language they use.

### Time

Do not walk into a living room and hunt for war photographs as professional development. Do not comment on pork, alcohol, or covering as a piety audit.

On-time for appointments. Traffic and multi-household logistics are real. So is a no-show when the plan was never agreed. Ask. Confirm.

sections.heading: Language and Communication
sections.body:
Bosnian, Croatian, and Serbian are mutually intelligible with political names. The differences that matter on Tuesday are the name the household claims, the script, and whether the interpreter will walk in as “former Yugoslav.” That label is a closed door with a polite hyphen.

### Language

Script: Latin for Bosnian and Croatian; Cyrillic for much Serbian. Book what the household asks. CLAS ten writes Serbo-Croatian (Bosnian) on the language block. That is notice. It is not the interpreter. Staff who answer the number must be ready; the interpreter request must still name the variety.

Second-generation English is common. Elders may not have it. A long answer may be story. A short English yes may be exhaustion or courtesy. Do not take a smile as consent.

Do not make a Bosnian coworker the interpreter.

sections.heading: Other Considerations
sections.body:
Unvarnished, because Minnesota Nice is how a room that treats everyone the same deletes facts.

### Named harms

Genocide denial in Bosnia and in diaspora politics is current, not archival. Do not platform it in a lobby. Do not “both-sides” Srebrenica to keep a meeting calm. Literacy is not a debate club.

PTSD, unexplained pain, sleep, and alcohol use sit in this diaspora’s clinical literature. Alcohol is not a joke and not a Muslim impossibility. Islam and drinking can exist in the same extended family. You follow law. You still see a person, not a bottle with an ethnicity. LGBTQ Bosnians exist. Conservative family, mosque, and church climates can mean silence. You use the name. You do not out someone to kin and call it culture.

Do not mash this page with Somali Islam, FGC, or Maay. Those are other intelligences. Second generation is American. They may still need language for an elder. An English IEP that never reached the parent is still a gate.

Staff who share this community may add facts. They do not get to delete a fact because it is hard to say.

sections.heading: Health
sections.body:
War trauma is structure for some first-wave adults and for some children who grew up inside someone else’s silence. PTSD, depression, unexplained pain, and somatic complaint are patterns named in Bosnian diaspora clinical literacy. This page does not invent a Minnesota rate. Date a figure when a controlling source exists. Do not skip screening because “they don’t talk about that.”

### Access

Alcohol use is part of the unvarnished picture for some households — men more often in the stereotype, not a rule. Do not treat a Bosniak Muslim as impossible for a substance-use screen. Do not treat a screen as a nationality.

Believe reported pain. Do not ask them to narrate the pit to make the pain credible. Gender match may be requested in maternal and intimate care. Offer it.

Do not fold this history into Tuskegee, into Somali FGC, or into a generic “refugee trauma” slide that erases Srebrenica as a specific crime.

sections.heading: LGBTQ
sections.body:
Queer and trans Bosnian Minnesotans exist. Conservative family, mosque, and church climates can mean silence or exile. Some people live a public English life and a private Bosnian life.

### This person

You use the name they use. You do not out them to an elder as cultural humility. Minnesota’s Human Rights Act still applies.

So does the duty not to treat a whole people as a family-values exhibit or as automatically secular because they are European Muslims.

sections.heading: Hair, Dress, and Body
sections.body:
Do not assume hijab. Many Bosniak women in Minnesota dress like other European-origin Minnesotans. Some cover. Ask the woman, with gender match if she wants it.

### Dress

Do not rank covering as piety, oppression, or assimilation. Traditional dress is public at weddings and commemorations, not a daily uniform. Do not ask if they “still wear the costume.”

Do not touch hair. This is not the CROWN Act chapter and not the Somali hijab chapter. Follow this person.

sections.heading: Music
sections.body:
Sevdah / sevdalinka is the named urban song tradition. Coffee-house and wedding music, ilahija in some religious rooms, and popular turbo-folk that some families love and some families disdain — all live here.

### Variation

A playlist is not engagement. Do not ask a survivor for a soundtrack of Sarajevo under siege.

A funeral is not staff entertainment. Second-generation rooms will have American pop. Follow this room, not a souvenir.

sections.heading: Sports
sections.body:
Soccer is common public sport. Club names from home can be identity and can also be a war map you do not referee.

### Not the whole person

Basketball and ordinary school sport are real in the second generation. Sport clubs are not language access and not a case plan.

Do not assume the kid plays. A Saturday league is not how you reached the elder.

sections.heading: Literature
sections.body:
Written South Slavic literature is old — older than the refugee file, older than Dayton. Oral sevdah and family narrative sit next to novels the building may have heard of and many it has not.

### Literacy in the lobby

Second-generation English is a literature too. You do not need to quote a Nobel.

You need to know this is not a people without letters, and that the name of the language is political. The English form may still be unreadable to the parent who reads Latin Bosnian.

sections.heading: Art
sections.body:
Coffee culture, calligraphy, embroidery, contemporary Minnesota work. Stećci and mosque architecture are homeland history, not a Heritage Month table.

### Guest

Guest. A festival is not consultation. A commemorative exhibit is not a case plan.

Do not put a wedding photograph on a unit display. This is not a souvenir people.

sections.heading: Conflict, War, and the State
sections.body:
1992–1995, Srebrenica, camps, Dayton, dispersal, and a United States that resettled people and then mostly stopped saying the name — that is the political event.

### The badge

Genocide denial is current politics in the region and in some diaspora rooms. Do not platform it. Do not “hear both sides” of a genocide in a lobby.

A DHS badge is not automatically help. Do not use 1995 as a personality. Do not ask a veteran or a widow to narrate killing for your professional development. Mandated reporting still exists. So does the duty not to treat a whole community as a trauma score.

sections.heading: Work, Markets, and Government
sections.body:
Work, trades, small business, care, professional second generation, public employment. There is no Compass income or poverty rate on this page. Do not invent one. Pattern: people work. Pattern: an elder may still need the language the coworker does not get paid to provide.

### Work

Bosnian staff inside the department are not unpaid interpreters and not the community. Identity is not a staffing plan.

### Staff

Relationship may precede a signature. That is not permission to skip a notice. It is a reason the first visit may not be the decision.

sections.heading: Health-care and Human-service Encounters
sections.body:
Language label. Latin or Cyrillic. Who is in the room. Trauma without interrogation. Unexplained pain. Alcohol. An elder who needs Bosnian and an adult child who does not think they need an interpreter until the form gets legal.

### Language

Confirm what they ask to book. Offer gender match. Ask who should hear. Do not make staff the interpreter.

### The meeting

Believe reported pain. Do not open with the war. Mandated reporting still exists.

sections.heading: Adjacent Peoples — Do Not Mash
sections.body:
Not Albanian. Not Kosovar by default. Not Macedonian. Not Russian. Not Ukrainian. Not Somali. Not “Muslim” as a file. Not “former Yugoslav” as a people.

### Adjacent doors

Croatian and Serbian Minnesota households are adjacent. They may share the language and not the war story. If the household is Croatian, book Croatian and do not make them narrate Srebrenica. If Serbian, book Serbian; do not platform denial; do not assume they want this page.

Some households are mixed. Ask this household. Never one Balkan module.

sections.heading: Counts, Dated
sections.body:
Minnesota Compass has no Bosnian cultural-community profile. That is a finding. Do not invent 40,000.

### Counts

MSP Magazine, looking back at Minnesota’s refugee history: between 1993 and 2003, more than 2,300 primary Bosnian refugees resettled here, part of about 140,000 Bosnian and Herzegovinian refugees who came to the United States. Primary placement is not the community total. Secondary migration is real. ACS ancestry cells exist in some vintages; date a controlling source before you cite one. This page will not guess.

### What the count is not

CLAS ten includes Serbo-Croatian (Bosnian) on the standing language block. That is operations volume, not a census.

A missing rate is not permission to skip language access. A young second generation is not proof the elder can run an English exception form.

sections.heading: Doors and Sources
sections.body:
CLAS ten language block: Serbo-Croatian (Bosnian). Islamic Community of Bosniaks in Minnesota (Minneapolis). MSP Magazine on Minnesota’s refugee history (primary-refugee count, dated). ICTY and ICJ public record on Srebrenica. Dayton as political fact.

### Public doors

CECLC is a door, not the whole community. Learn on your own time. Do not make a Bosnian colleague your unpaid tutor.

### Learn on your own time

Pay the partner this household names. Report back. Guest.

sections.heading: How it hits DHS gates — the 40%
sections.body:
Workplace culture and service delivery are both candidates.

Language: the block says Serbo-Croatian (Bosnian). That is notice. An interpreter labeled “former Yugoslav” who is the wrong political name, or the wrong script, is a closed door with a polite label. Book what the household asks. Gender match may be requested in maternal and intimate care.

War as icebreaker: never. 1995 is literacy for the desk, not a speech and not a rapport trick. Do not ask a survivor to narrate the pit.

Names: ask how to say the -ić. Do not treat a spelling variant as fraud by default.

Hour caps, exception processes, and life-sharing matches without language are not culturally neutral. An English IEP for an elder is a gate.

Child welfare and disability: trauma is not a risk score. Mandated reporting still exists. So does the duty not to treat a whole community as a personality.

Notices and comment: an eList and an English PDF is not how this community was reached. Empty follow-up cells are theater.

Workforce: Bosnian staff are not the interpreter pool and not the community.

One Balkan blob is a closed gate. Adjacent Croatian and Serbian households are not this war story by default. Not Albanian, not Kosovar, not Russian, not Somali.

Legislation, funding, rule: you cannot advocate for a channel you will not study. This cultural intelligence exists so the 40% has a household in it — not a paternalistic program designed in a building that never learned the difference between a language block and a people.

sections.heading: A Note on This Guide
sections.body:
This brief is about Amharic-speaking Minnesota — Amhara households and other households that use Amharic as a first or working language — as a people-page. Amharic is on the CLAS fifteen interpreter cards. That is operations. It is not a census of who is Ethiopian, and it is not permission to treat Ethiopia as one people.

### Who this is

Amharic is not Oromo. Amharic is not Somali. Amharic is not Tigrinya. Amharic is a federal working language of Ethiopia. Many non-Amhara Ethiopians speak it as a second language of school, army, and office. If the household is Oromo, open Oromo and book Afaan Oromoo. If Tigrayan, book Tigrinya. If Somali — including people born in Ethiopia who name Somali ancestry — open Somali Minnesota. Compass counts those last households as Somali, not Ethiopian. Shared Horn is not shared culture. Shared Orthodox calendar is not shared politics.

### Who this is not

Minnesota Compass Ethiopian (ACS 2019–2023) is 40,324. About 89.4 percent Twin Cities, 10.6 percent Greater Minnesota. About 43.5 percent age 17 or younger. Foreign-born 61.7 percent. Language other than English (age 5+) 74.9 percent; English less than “very well” 30.4 percent. Median household income about $57,106 (2022 dollars, averaged). Poverty 13.0 percent. Renter 65.3 percent. Date the number. It is an umbrella. Census recodes some people who write Oromo into Ethiopian. It is not an Amharic speaker count. Minnesota Secretary of State voter materials include Amharic. Do not invent a population.

The diversity inside this door is the point.
