Compass: language other than English about 28.7 percent; LEP about 8.6 percent (age 5+). Date it. Low compared with Vietnamese or Hmong is not a skip. Newcomers and elders are inside that 8.6 percent. English-dominant later generation is inside the 71.3 percent English-only and still on this page.

Chinese and Korean mash is a closed door. An interpreter labeled “Asian” is a closed door.

A short English yes may be exhaustion, courtesy, or honorific indirectness. Do not take a smile as consent. Do not make a Japanese coworker the interpreter. Do not use a child.

sections.heading: Other Considerations — unvarnished, not Minnesota Nice
sections.body:
Unvarnished, because Minnesota Nice is how a room that treats everyone the same deletes facts.

### Named harms

Internment is U.S. literacy. EO 9066, 19 February 1942. Camps. 442nd. MIS at Camp Savage and Fort Snelling. Redress 1988. It is not a speech. It is not an icebreaker. It is not a personality. Skipping it because the room is uncomfortable is how treating everyone the same deletes a state act.

Model-minority is a weapon. 97.0 percent high school and 51.0 percent bachelor’s will be used to skip 8.6 percent LEP, 5.1 percent poverty, 36.3 percent cost-burden, disability, and mixed-household grief. That skip is the policy. Median household income about $67,817 is not the Indian or Chinese median. Do not import another Asian average onto this kitchen table.

Mixed-race Japanese Minnesotans exist. Company-transfer isolation exists. LGBTQ Japanese Minnesotans exist. Mental-health stigma exists in some streams. Do not invent a Minnesota suicide rate. Do not skip screening. Do not collect status you do not need. Do not skip mandated reporting and call it humility.

Employee groups may fact-check this page. They do not get a veto because internment is hard to say in a room that treats everyone the same.

sections.heading: Health
sections.body:
Book Japanese for the elder who needs it. 8.6 percent LEP (Compass, age 5+) is a gate, not a rounding error. An English consent form is not consent if they could not run it.

### Access

Believe reported pain. Do not invent “Asian stoicism.” Do not fold this into a generic Asian slide. Do not skip screening because HS+ is 97.0 percent or because the person is English-dominant.

Mental-health stigma is real in some families. Do not invent a Minnesota rate. Do not import a Japan national rate as a Minnesota rate. Naming a counselor is not the same as a family accepting one. A smile is not a PHQ-9. Gender match may be requested in maternal and intimate care. Offer it.

If they name a healer, a priest, or a butsudan, listen. Do not make that the case plan unless they asked.

sections.heading: LGBTQ
sections.body:
Queer and trans Japanese Minnesotans exist — in later-generation households, in transfer families, in mixed families, in churches, and in none of those. Conservative family climates can mean silence or exile. You use the name they use. You do not out them to an elder as cultural humility.

### This person

Minnesota’s Human Rights Act still applies. So does the duty not to treat a whole people as a family-values exhibit.

Do not assume a mixed or English-dominant household is affirming. Do not assume an immigrant household is not. Ask this person.

sections.heading: Hair, Dress, and Body
sections.body:
Kimono and yukata are public at Obon, some weddings, and some stages. They are not a daily uniform. Later generation and most mixed households look like Minnesota. Do not ask a woman in clinic whether she “still wears the costume.” Do not dress a child in kimono as DHS programming.

### Dress

Hair and head: follow this person. Do not touch.

Do not mash kimono with a qipao or a hanbok on the unit’s Heritage Month table. That mash is the adjacent-peoples failure.

sections.heading: Music
sections.body:
Gagaku, min’yō, enka, J-pop, church music, none. Not one soundtrack. J-pop is public culture, including among people with no other Japanese language. It is not consultation.

### Variation

A playlist is not engagement. Do not ask a staff person or a client to perform. Do not use a music video as the training.

A funeral is not staff entertainment.

sections.heading: Sports
sections.body:
Baseball is public culture for some families. Judo and kendo are public for some and a stereotype if you assume them. Do not assume them. School sport is ordinary for later generations.

### Not the whole person

Sport clubs are not language access and not a case plan. An elder in the stands who needs Japanese still needs Japanese. 8.6 percent LEP is not a skip because the child plays varsity.

A Saturday tournament does not replace an interpreter on Monday.

sections.heading: Literature
sections.body:
A long written vernacular. Hiragana, katakana, kanji. Japanese and Japanese American writers exist in both languages. Internment memoir and scholarship are a U.S. literary fact. You do not need to quote a novel. You need to know this is not a people without letters.

### Literacy in the lobby

Literacy in Japanese is not guaranteed for later generations or for mixed households. A Japanese-language notice can still be a closed door. An English notice can still be a closed door. Ask.

Do not put a proverb on a brochure and call it language access.

sections.heading: Art
sections.body:
Ceramics, ink, woodblock as literacy, Obon public art, and diaspora visual work. Guest. A kimono on a stage is not a case plan. A museum visit is not consultation. A tea ceremony is not a waiver design.

### Guest

Do not mash with Chinese calligraphy or Korean ceramics on an “Asian art” table.

Pay the door this person names. Do not extract a staff person’s child as New Year entertainment.

sections.heading: Internment, the Language School, and the State
sections.body:
Empire, 1941–45, Executive Order 9066 (19 February 1942), the camps, the 442nd, and the Military Intelligence Service Language School at Camp Savage and Fort Snelling — that is the political event. Redress: Civil Liberties Act of 1988. A DHS badge is not automatically help. A government that incarcerated families and trained their children as linguists in this state is not automatically safe in a lobby.

### The badge

Do not use internment as a personality or an icebreaker. Do not ask a person to narrate a camp, a lost farm, or a redress check for your professional development. Do not collect immigration status you do not need.

Filing this household as Chinese or Korean is a state act. It is a closed gate.

sections.heading: Work, Transfer, and Government
sections.body:
Professional work, company transfer, small business, public employment. Median household income about $67,817 (Compass, 2022 dollars) is an average — lower than some neighboring Asian spines. Poverty 5.1 percent is in the same row. About 37.9 percent live alone. Cost-burdened households about 36.3 percent. Do not staff a program as if every household were a four-person professional family, and do not import an Indian or Chinese median onto this table.

### Work

Japanese staff inside the department are not unpaid interpreters and not the community. Identity is not a staffing plan.

### Staff

Relationship may precede a signature in some rooms. That is not permission to skip a notice.

sections.heading: Health-care and Human-service Encounters
sections.body:
Japanese for the elder. English-dominant later generation who still needs this page. Name order on the wristband. A butsudan in the story. Internment memory you do not icebreak. Pain you must believe. A mixed child asked “what are you” in the waiting room.

### Language

Ask the language. Ask how to say the name. Offer gender match. Believe reported pain. Do not skip screening. Do not make staff the interpreter. Do not use a child. Mandated reporting still exists.

### The meeting

Do not mash this encounter with a Chinese or Korean interpreter. A smile is not consent. 8.6 percent LEP is not a rounding error.

sections.heading: Adjacent Peoples — Do Not Mash
sections.body:
Not Chinese. Not Korean. Not Hmong. Not Vietnamese. Not Filipino. Not “Asian American” as the file. Open those CIs for those households. Open this for a Japanese household. Some households are mixed. Ask this household.

### Adjacent doors

Oshōgatsu is not Chinese New Year as a file. It is not Seollal. Kimono is not hanbok and not qipao. Internment is a Japanese American story. It is not a speech you give a Korean or Chinese family, and it is not a speech you give this family.

Never one Asian module. Do not skip this page because the person is English-dominant. Foreign-born 17.3 percent is not “no culture.”

sections.heading: Counts, Dated
sections.body:
Minnesota Compass, ACS 2019–2023, Japanese cultural community: about 13,391; Twin Cities 76.8%; Greater Minnesota 23.2%; age 17 or younger 31.8%; 65+ about 8.6%; foreign-born 17.3%; English only (age 5+) 71.3%; language other than English 28.7%; English less than “very well” 8.6%; high school or higher (25+) 97.0%; bachelor’s or higher 51.0%; median household income about $67,817 (2022 dollars); poverty 5.1%; owner-occupied 60.3%; average household size 2.13; individuals living alone 37.9 percent; cost-burdened households 36.3 percent.

### Counts

Date Compass. Do not invent other rates. Counts disagree across ACS vintages and definitions (ancestry vs. birthplace vs. language). Date the number you cite.

### What the count is not

An 8.6 percent LEP rate is not zero. A 5.1 percent poverty rate is not zero. A 17.3 percent foreign-born share is not “no culture.” A 36.3 percent cost-burden rate is not a model-minority brochure. Median $67,817 is not another Asian spine’s median. A rate is not the person.

sections.heading: Doors and Sources
sections.body:
Minnesota Compass Japanese profile (ACS 2019–2023). Minnesota Historical Society: Military Intelligence Service Language School at Camp Savage and Fort Snelling. Japanese American Citizens League and Japan-related associations this person names. Buddhist temples and churches this person names. Pay the door this person names. Do not assign a temple.

### Public doors

CECLC is a door, not the whole community. Learn on your own time. Do not make a Japanese colleague your unpaid tutor. An eList and an English PDF is not how an LEP elder was reached. Book Japanese when they need it.

### Learn on your own time

A Fort Snelling visit is optional professional development. It is not consultation, and it is not an icebreaker.

sections.heading: How it hits DHS gates — the 40%
sections.body:
Workplace culture and service delivery are both candidates.

Language: 8.6 percent LEP is not “no language gate.” An elder who needs Japanese and gets English — or Chinese, or Korean — is a closed door. Gender match may be requested in maternal and intimate care. Later-generation people may want Japanese or may not. Ask. Do not use a child.

Names: family name first. -san is not a given name. The database that reverses order or “corrects” toward Chinese is a gate.

Hour caps, exception processes, and life-sharing matches without Japanese for the elder who needs it are not culturally neutral. An English IEP is still a gate for that parent.

Model-minority: 97.0 percent high school and 51.0 percent bachelor’s will be used to skip LEP, 5.1 percent poverty, 36.3 percent cost-burden, disability, and mixed-household grief. That skip is the policy. Do not import an Indian or Chinese income average onto this packet.

Internment: EO 9066 is U.S. literacy. Using it as an icebreaker is a closed door. Skipping it because the room is uncomfortable is how Minimization deletes a state act. A DHS badge is not automatically help.

Notices and comment: an eList and an English PDF is not how an LEP elder was reached. Empty follow-up cells are theater. Greater Minnesota is 23.2 percent.

Workforce: Japanese staff are not the interpreter pool and not the community. Staff are colleagues, not the curriculum. Do not treat  them.

Legislation, funding, rule: you cannot advocate for a channel you will not study. This cultural intelligence exists so the 40% has a household in it — not a paternalistic program designed in a building that never learned that internment is literacy, not a speech, and that Japanese is not Chinese.

sections.heading: A Note on This Guide
sections.body:
This brief is about Kenyan Minnesota as a state-name community of many peoples. Kikuyu (Gikuyu / Agĩkũyũ), Luo, Luhya, Kamba, Kalenjin, Kisii, Meru, Maasai, coastal Mijikenda, Kenyan Somali, and others are not one file. Book the language this household names. English and Kiswahili are official in Kenya. They are not the home language until this family says so. A “Kenyan interpreter” is not a language.

### Who this is

This is not Somali. If the household is Kenyan Somali and names Somali, open Somali Minnesota. Shared Horn and shared border are not shared culture. This is not Ethiopian. This is not Oromo as a synonym — Oromo people live in Kenya; if this household is Oromo, open Oromo Minnesota. This is not historic African American. Shared race in the United States is not shared culture.

### Who this is not

Minnesota Compass (ACS 2019–2023) puts Kenyan Minnesota near 20,967. About 77.3 percent Twin Cities, about 22.7 percent Greater Minnesota. About 44.1 percent age 17 or younger; about 4.6 percent 65+. About 66.6 percent foreign-born. Language other than English (age 5+) 65.8 percent; English less than “very well” 24.4 percent. Date the number. A rate is not the person.

The diversity inside this state name is the point. A Kikuyu Pentecostal nurse in the suburbs, a Luo Catholic household, a Luhya factory family in Greater Minnesota, a Kenyan Somali household that should have been booked Somali, a U.S.-born student who uses English with friends and Gikuyu with an elder, a Muslim coastal family — share a Compass row and do not share a Tuesday.

### How to read this

Always defer to the person in front of you. This page is a hypothesis you still test on this family.

sections.heading: Origins and the Founding of a People
sections.body:
Kenya is a state of many nations. Kikuyu highland peoplehood around Mount Kenya, Luo peoplehood on Lake Victoria, Luhya, Kamba, Kalenjin, Kisii, Meru, Maasai pastoral peoplehood, coastal Swahili and Mijikenda worlds, Kenyan Somali in the northeast — and others. There is no single Kenyan ethnicity. Ask which people they are. Do not lecture taxonomy they did not ask for.

### History for the meeting

English and Kiswahili as official languages are colonial and national history. They are literacy for the desk. They are not permission to skip the home language. Independence in 1963 ended British colony. Mau Mau is literacy, not a speech you give the family, and not every household’s story.

### What people brought

What people brought: ethnic language, English, Kiswahili, church and mosque, harambee as a named mutual-aid ethic in some rooms, kin obligation, a memory of colony and of a state that followed. What they met in Minnesota: an English form, one “East African” checkbox, and often Somali because the building already has that page.

Do not start with a safari sentence. Do not assume Nairobi as identity. Many people name a district, a people, a village.

sections.heading: The Geography of the Kenyan World
sections.body:
Homeland is not one map. Central highlands, Nyanza, Western, Rift Valley, the coast, the north. Nairobi is not the whole. A person may name Kiambu, Kisumu, Kakamega, Machakos, Eldoret, Mombasa — not the capital. Do not referee regional politics in a waiver meeting. Listen if they name a place.

### Homeland

The diaspora is global: Texas, Minnesota, Washington State, Maryland and D.C., Georgia, the Gulf, the UK. Minnesota is a real community, not the U.S. capital of it. Secondary migration, church networks, and healthcare work pulled people here.

### Minnesota

In Minnesota: Compass 77.3 percent Twin Cities, 22.7 percent Greater Minnesota. That Greater Minnesota share is larger than Ethiopian Compass and larger than Liberian Compass. Do not assume Minneapolis. Do not assume Cedar-Riverside — that hub is Somali unless this family lives there. Do not assume the person in front of you has been to Kenya.

sections.heading: Independence, Skilled Streams, and 2007–08 — Foundational Events
sections.body:
There is no single 1975 or 1991 on this page. Independence in 1963 is the political founding of the state. Later Minnesota streams are mixed: students, family, diversity visas, skilled work including healthcare, and displacement after 2007–08 post-election violence for some households. Do not file every Kenyan household as refugee. Do not file every Kenyan household as a nurse.

### Foundational events

2007–08 is named memory for some: killing, camps, flight. It is not a personality. It is not a reason to skip screening. It is literacy. You do not referee Kikuyu/Luo or other ethnic politics in a waiver meeting. You do not pick a side as DHS.

### Who you meet

Healthcare recruitment is a Minnesota labor fact in some rooms — LeadingAge and related pipelines have named Kenya as a nursing source. That is work. It is not a personality and not the whole Compass row.

The desk in 2026 meets first-generation professionals and U.S.-born children — English with peers, still translating, still unable to get Gikuyu or Dholuo in a lobby that offered Somali or “African.” If you only know “East African,” you will miss this household.

sections.heading: Family
sections.body:
Extended households and elder authority sit in many rooms. Harambee — pulling together, fundraising, mutual aid — is a hypothesis in some families, not a personality you assign. Compass average household size about 3.50. Who cares for a disabled adult or a child may be a brother, a cousin, a church mother, not the legally recognized caregiver on the checkbox. Hour caps and “natural supports” can dump unpaid work onto women in that network and call it culture.

### Who is in the household

Naming is already a who: English / Christian given names plus ethnic names; Luo naming is not Kikuyu naming. Do not invent a last name because the screen requires one. Do not assume three Somali names.

### Who speaks

Who speaks in the lobby may be a child with the best English. That child is not the qualified interpreter. CLAS still stands. Ask who should be in the room. Minnesota law still stands. Do not skip mandated reporting and call it humility.

sections.heading: Minnesota and Kenyan History
sections.body:
Minnesota holds a Kenyan Compass community large enough that this department will meet it on waivers, child welfare, health care, cash, food, aging, and employment — and large enough that the building has a habit of hearing East Africa and booking Somali. Compass: about 20,967 (ACS 2019–2023). Greater Minnesota is 22.7 percent. Do not write this people as a Minneapolis anecdote.

### Places

Places, not a blob: Twin Cities suburbs; Minneapolis and St. Paul pockets; Greater Minnesota towns with hospitals, factories, and housing. Churches — ethnic congregations and Kenyan fellowships — are public life. They are not consultation. A food visit does not make you the expert.

### Partners

Partners: churches families name; ethnic associations (Luo, Kikuyu, Luhya, and others as this household names them); professional and nursing networks as doors, not a staffing plan; CECLC as a department door — not the whole. Pay the partner this household actually uses.

Kenyan staff are not unpaid interpreters and not the community. Identity is not a staffing plan. A Jamhuri or harambee visit is optional professional development if you are invited. You are a guest. It does not make you the expert.

sections.heading: Kenyan Minnesota — the heart of a people
sections.body:
To be Kenyan in Minnesota is to be a state-name people of many nations, filed under East African, Black, and sometimes Somali by a building that has not studied. Peoplehood after colony and after 1963 is not a safari poster. Kikuyu, Luo, Luhya, and the rest do not share one Tuesday. You do not pick a side.

### In this state

In this building another fact sits on top: many of these households are Black in a U.S. racial order that will file them under Somali or under historic African American and get the language, the church, and the name wrong. Shared race is not shared culture. Shared Horn geography is not shared language.

Face, elder obligation, harambee as hypothesis, and not shaming the name travel into a waiver meeting. Harmony can look like agreement and then a plan nobody follows. Ask whether they agree. Do not take a smile as consent.

This guide is a working orientation. Individual variation always supersedes group generalization. Always defer to the person in front of you.

sections.heading: Core Concepts
sections.body:
Which people. Kikuyu, Luo, Luhya, Kamba, Kalenjin, Kisii, Meru, Maasai, Kenyan Somali, others. Ask. The Compass row is not the ethnic file.

### Which language

Gikuyu, Dholuo, Luhya languages, Kikamba, Kalenjin languages, Kiswahili, English, others. A “Kenyan interpreter” is not a language. A Somali interpreter is the wrong door unless this household is Somali.

### Harambee as hypothesis

Mutual aid, fundraising, pulling together. Staff do not use it as a guilt tool. If the family names it, you listen.

### Faith is plural

Protestant, Pentecostal, Catholic, AIC, Islam, none. Follow this room.

Do not referee Kikuyu/Luo or other ethnic politics in a waiver meeting. Do not assume Nairobi.

### Work and school as a family project

Nursing is a job, not a personality. A rate is not the person.

sections.heading: Religion
sections.body:
Christianity is the large public stream in Kenyan Minnesota: Protestant, Pentecostal, Catholic, African Independent / AIC churches. Islam lives on the coast, among Kenyan Somali, and in some other families. Traditional practice sits in some rooms and is not a souvenir. None is also a Tuesday. Ask. Do not assume Muslim like Somali.

### Streams

The church is a center of ritual, mutual aid, information, and often the first Minnesota network. It is not “the community.” Do not BCC one pastor and call it consultation. Do not make clergy the case plan unless this family asked.

### Practice

Funerals gather family and can run long. You still keep medical and legal time. You name the conflict instead of punishing it.

Arabic may be religion, not the interview, in Muslim rooms. Kiswahili may be church or market language, not the home language. Book the interview language.

sections.heading: Greetings
sections.body:
Elders first. English “hello” is ordinary in many professional rooms. Kiswahili habari and related forms live in some rooms. Do not perform tourism “jambo” as icebreaker. Ethnic greetings exist — ask, do not perform one you learned from a video.

### Titles

A hard handshake you assume is universal is already a closed door for some women and some elders. Many second-generation people will shake hands in English-language rooms. If a hand is not offered, nod. Do not force it.

### This room

Do not import Somali right-hand rules onto this page as default. In a Muslim Kenyan room they may apply. Follow this room. Do not assume the Black nod is this grammar.

Physical contact: ask the room. Cross-gender touch with elders is not a default. Say the name.

sections.heading: Naming Conventions
sections.body:
English and Christian given names are common — after mission schools and colonial record. Ethnic names sit beside them or instead of them. Kikuyu names are not Luo names. Luo names (Ochieng, Achieng, Odhiambo, and others) are not a joke and not a clan icebreaker you pulled from a coworker. Luhya, Kamba, Kalenjin naming each have their own grammar. Ask.

### How to file

U.S. forms want first-middle-last. Kenyan naming may not match. Do not invent a last name because the screen requires one. That invented name becomes a gate. Do not assume three Somali names.

Ask how to say it. Ask how to file it. Pronounce it. Women may or may not take a husband’s name in U.S. records. Mother and child may not match. That is not fraud until you have a reason.

sections.heading: Dates of Significance
sections.body:
Jamhuri Day — 12 December, Independence / Republic. Madaraka Day. Mashujaa Day. Schedule around the ones this family names when you can. A calendar click is not community engagement. Guest if invited.

### Calendar

Christmas and Easter on church calendars. Eid in Muslim rooms. Ethnic rites — Kikuyu, Luo, and others — some families name and some do not. Ask. Do not put them on a case note as color.

2007–08 post-election violence is memory for some, not a holiday. Do not put it on a file as color. Do not collect it as a risk score.

Do not put “African holiday” or Somali dates on this page by default. Ask this family.

sections.heading: Education
sections.body:
Compass (ACS 2019–2023): among Kenyan Minnesotans 25 and older, about 94.1 percent high school or higher; about 38.9 percent bachelor’s or higher. Date Compass. About 66.6 percent of the community is foreign-born. High attainment is a pattern. It is not proof the grandmother needs no interpreter. It is not permission to skip the IEP in the home language.

### School and language

A parent who speaks fluent Gikuyu or Dholuo and limited English is not illiterate. Many Kenyans were schooled in English. Some elders were not. The English-only form is still a gate. Book THIS language. The child is not the interpreter.

Second-generation educational mobility is real. So is a gap that a room that treats everyone the same will call “culture.” Do not treat a nurse in the family as proof the waiver household heard the form.

sections.heading: Etiquette
sections.body:
Elders first. Hospitality is a virtue in many rooms. Accept a little tea if offered. You still keep medical and legal time.

### In the home

Shoes off in some homes. Right hand for food in some rooms. Church time and harambee gatherings can run long. Do not photograph a family and call it rapport. Do not enter a prayer space as a tour.

### Time

On-time for appointments. Traffic and multi-household logistics are real. So is a courtesy-yes then no-show when the plan was never agreed. Ask whether they agree. Confirm in the language they use.

Do not use a child as the go-between and call it family values. Book the interpreter.

sections.heading: Language and Communication
sections.body:
Book the language this household names. Gikuyu (Kikuyu), Dholuo, Luhya languages, Kikamba, Kalenjin languages, Kisii, Kimeru, Kiswahili, English, and others. A “Kenyan interpreter” is not a language. Kiswahili is official and is not always home. A Somali interpreter is the wrong door unless this household is Somali. Arabic may be religion, not the interview.

### Language

Compass: among those 5 and older, about 65.8 percent speak a language other than English; about 24.4 percent speak English less than “very well.” Date the number. Many Kenyans use English at work. The IEP still has to reach the parent who does not.

A long answer may be story. A short English yes may be exhaustion or courtesy. Do not take a smile as consent. Ask whether they agree with the plan.

Do not use a child as the interpreter. Do not make a Kenyan coworker the interpreter.

sections.heading: Other Considerations — unvarnished, not Minnesota Nice
sections.body:
Unvarnished, because Minnesota Nice is how a room that treats everyone the same deletes facts.

### Named harms

Intra-Kenyan ethnic politics are real — Kikuyu, Luo, and others, including 2007–08 memory. Do not pick a side as DHS. Do not referee in a waiver meeting. Do not file politics as a risk score.

FGC exists in some Kenyan communities, including some Kenyan Somali and some other groups. Minnesota law stands. This is not the Somali page. Do not invent a Kenyan rate. Do not mash Somali prevalence onto this household. Follow mandated reporting. Still see a family.

Queer and trans Kenyan Minnesotans exist. You use the name. You do not out someone to kin and call it culture. Kenya’s own law climate is not Minnesota’s. Do not skip mandated reporting and call it humility.

Enforcement climate is structure for some. Do not collect status you do not need. Do not treat fear as noncompliance. Staff who share this community may add facts. They do not get to delete a fact because it is hard to say.

sections.heading: Health
sections.body:
Believe reported pain. Do not invent African stoicism. Do not fold this history into Tuskegee or into a Somali MDH slide. This is not those pages.

### Access

Hepatitis B screening for people born in Kenya is a U.S. public-health pattern — CDC has treated Kenya as a higher-prevalence birth country in screening guidance. Date the CDC page you cite. Do not invent a Minnesota rate. Do not skip screening because the person looks well.

Compass disability 5.2 percent — dated. Mental-health stigma is real in some families. 2007–08 and other trauma sit in some rooms. A smile is not a PHQ-9. No dated Kenyan-specific Minnesota autism rate belongs on this page. Do not invent one. Do not mash Somali ADDM here.

Distance running as a Kenyan stereotype is not a file, not a compliment, and not a clinical assumption. Gender match may be requested in maternal and intimate care. Offer it. Traditional medicine and church healing often sit beside biomedicine. Ask. Co-create. FGC: Minnesota law stands; do not invent a rate; do not skip care.

sections.heading: LGBTQ
sections.body:
Queer and trans Kenyan Minnesotans exist. Conservative family, church, and some mosque climates can mean silence or exile. Some people live a public English life and a private home-language life. You use the name they use. You do not out them to an elder as cultural humility.

### This person

Minnesota’s Human Rights Act still applies. Kenya’s law climate is not this state’s. Do not use this chapter to raid a household. Do not pretend the tension is not there.

Ethnic politics and church do not get a veto over this person. Always defer to the person in front of you.

sections.heading: Hair, Dress, and Body
sections.body:
Kanga, kitenge, Kikuyu and Luo ceremonial dress are public at weddings, Jamhuri, and some church stages. They are not a daily uniform. Second generation looks like Minnesota. Do not ask a woman in clinic whether she “still wears the costume.”

### Dress

Hijab and modest dress for some Muslim women; not all. Do not assume covering. Do not rank covering.

This is not the CROWN Act chapter — and anti-Blackness still sits on Black Kenyan bodies in U.S. clinics, schools, and traffic stops. Ask this person. Do not mash historic African American hair politics as a script, and do not ignore them. Do not touch.

sections.heading: Music
sections.body:
Benga, gospel, taarab on the coast, Luo and Kikuyu popular forms, diaspora pop, church choir. Named variation, not a playlist. Ethnic politics can sit inside a song. You do not put the wrong anthem on a speaker.

### Variation

A funeral is not staff entertainment. A playlist is not engagement. Do not request a political song as icebreaker in a waiver meeting.

Jamhuri stages are public life. They are not consultation and not a case plan.

sections.heading: Sports
sections.body:
Distance running as a public image of Kenya is not a personality, not a compliment you give a child in clinic, and not a file. Soccer shows up. School sport is ordinary for the second generation. Basketball too.

### Not the whole person

Do not assume the kid runs. Do not assume the kid plays. Do not make sport the only excellence you can see.

Sport clubs are social infrastructure for some. They are not language access and not a case plan. Greater Minnesota teams are still this people when they live there.

sections.heading: Literature
sections.body:
English and Kiswahili made modern written publics. Gikuyu and other ethnic literatures sit beside them. Oral forms are older. Ngũgĩ wa Thiong’o is literacy for the desk, not a speech you give the family in the lobby. Minnesota and U.S. Kenyan writers and journalists exist.

### Literacy in the lobby

You do need to know this is not a people without letters. Many people read English. Some elders read only a home language. A notice that exists only in English is a closed door. Ask.

Tones and names are not decoration. Write what they tell you.

sections.heading: Art
sections.body:
Kanga slogans, beadwork, wood carving as a public image of Kenya — not the whole, and not a safari souvenir you put on a Heritage Month table. Church art. Diaspora visual work. Ugali, chapati, chai, nyama choma are foodway, not consultation.

### Guest

Guest, not researcher. A church or harambee visit is optional professional development. It is not consultation. Do not photograph a family as tourism.

Heritage Month that mashes this with a Somali poster, an Ethiopian flag, or a historic African American exhibit has already mashed the adjacent peoples.

sections.heading: Colony, 2007–08, and Intra-Community Politics
sections.body:
British colony, Mau Mau as literacy for the desk not a speech, independence 1963, and 2007–08 post-election violence as named memory for some — that is the political event. Intra-Kenyan ethnic politics, including Kikuyu/Luo memory, live in Minnesota rooms. Do not referee. Do not pick a side as DHS.

### The badge

A DHS badge is not automatically help. Do not use 2007 as a personality. Do not ask a person to narrate killing for your professional development.

Enforcement climate in the United States is a different state and still a closed door for some. It changes who opens the door. That is not noncompliance. Do not collect status you do not need. Do not collect ethnic or political speech as a risk score.

sections.heading: Work, Markets, and Government
sections.body:
Healthcare and nursing as a Minnesota labor pattern in some rooms. Professional class, small business, factory, public employment. Compass median household income about $77,518; poverty 12.6 percent; renter 62.9 percent; about 89.9 percent of working-age adults employed — dated. A rate is not the person. Nursing is a job. It is not a personality and not the whole economy.

### Work

Kenyan staff inside the department are not unpaid interpreters and not the community. Identity is not a staffing plan.

### Staff

Relationship and harambee networks may precede a signature. That is not permission to skip a notice. It is a reason the first visit may not be the decision. Pay the partner this household names.

sections.heading: Health-care and Human-service Encounters
sections.body:
Which people and which language are the first closed door. An interpreter labeled Kenyan, Swahili, Somali, or African who is not the language this household speaks is a closed door. Book Gikuyu, Dholuo, a Luhya language, Kiswahili, or whatever they name. Still book a qualified interpreter. Do not use a child. Do not make staff the interpreter.

### Language

Who is in the room. A child pushed forward as English. A pastor in the story. Pain you must believe. A running stereotype in the chart. Intra-community tension in the waiting room. Deportation climate.

### The meeting

Offer gender match. Ask who should hear. Ask how to file the name. If they name traditional medicine or church healing, listen. Mandated reporting still exists. Believe reported pain. Do not invent African stoicism. Do not mix Tuskegee or Somali CI into this history.

sections.heading: Adjacent Peoples — Do Not Mash
sections.body:
Not Somali. If this household is Kenyan Somali and names Somali, open Somali Minnesota. Not Ethiopian. Not Oromo as a synonym — Oromo people live in Kenya; if this household is Oromo, open Oromo Minnesota. Not Ugandan. Not Tanzanian. Shared Kiswahili is not shared peoplehood. Not historic African American. Not Liberian. Not Nigerian.

### Adjacent doors

Never one East African interpreter. Never one Kenyan module. Never one Black module. Some households are mixed. Ask this household.

Shared Christianity is not shared culture. Shared Islam is not shared culture. Shared race is not shared culture.

sections.heading: Counts, Dated
sections.body:
Minnesota Compass, ACS 2019–2023, Kenyan cultural community: about 20,967; Twin Cities 77.3%; Greater Minnesota 22.7%; age 17 or younger 44.1%; 65+ 4.6%; foreign-born 66.6%; language other than English (age 5+) 65.8%; English less than “very well” 24.4%; high school or higher (25+) 94.1%; bachelor’s or higher 38.9%; median household income about $77,518 (2022 dollars, averaged); poverty 12.6%; owner-occupied 37.1%; renter-occupied 62.9%; average household size 3.50; disability 5.2%; working-age employment 89.9%.

### Counts

Date Compass. Do not invent other rates. Counts disagree across ACS vintages and definitions (ancestry vs. birthplace vs. language). Date the number you cite.

### What the count is not

A young age structure is not a personality. High bachelor’s is not proof the elder heard the form. Greater Minnesota 22.7 percent is a channel. Language and child-as-interpreter are gates. A rate is not the person.

Minnesota Compass Kenyan profile (ACS 2019–2023). Churches and ethnic associations this family names — Luo, Kikuyu, Luhya, and others as they name them. Professional and nursing networks as doors, not a staffing plan. CECLC is a door, not the whole community.

### Public doors

If this household is Somali, open Somali Minnesota. If Oromo, open Oromo Minnesota. Book the language they name.

### Learn on your own time

Learn on your own time. Do not make a Kenyan colleague your unpaid tutor. Do not BCC a church and call it consultation. Pay partners. Report back. Guest at Jamhuri if invited — it is not consultation.

sections.heading: How it hits DHS gates — the 40%
sections.body:
Workplace culture and service delivery are both candidates.

Language: an interpreter labeled Kenyan, Swahili, Somali, or African who is not Gikuyu, Dholuo, a Luhya language, or whatever this household names is a closed door. Kiswahili is official and is not always home. Still book a qualified interpreter. Do not use a child. Gender match may be requested in maternal and intimate care.

Names: English plus ethnic names. The database that invents a last name, or that assumes three Somali names, is a gate that follows the person.

Hour caps, exception processes, and life-sharing matches without language are not culturally neutral.

Child welfare and disability: help-seeking that becomes a report is part of why people wait. Mandated reporting still exists. So does the duty not to treat a whole community as a risk score. FGC: Minnesota law stands; this is not the Somali page; do not invent a rate.

Notices and comment: an eList and an English PDF is not how this community was reached. Empty follow-up cells are theater. Greater Minnesota is 22.7 percent — a Minneapolis meeting is not the whole channel.

Workforce: Kenyan staff are not the interpreter pool and not the community. Staff are colleagues, not the curriculum. Do not treat  them. Nursing is a job, not a staffing plan for language.

Somali mash and Black mash: opening Somali because East Africa, or historic African American because both are Black, is a closed door.

Legislation, funding, rule: you cannot advocate for a channel you will not study. This cultural intelligence exists so the 40% has a household in it — not a paternalistic program designed in a building that heard “Kenyan” and booked Somali.

sections.heading: A Note on This Guide
sections.body:
This brief is about Korean Minnesota as two households that share a Compass row and do not share a Tuesday: immigrant Korean families — including elders who need Korean in the lobby — and Korean adoptees, a population that is Minnesota history. Adoptee households are often white Minnesota families and Korean-born adults. That is not the same as an immigrant Korean household and not “no culture.” Do not skip this page because the person is English-dominant. Do not ask an adoptee to represent “the Korean community.”

### Who this is

This is not a Census “Asian” mash. It is not Chinese. It is not Japanese. It is not Hmong. It is not Vietnamese. Shared continent is not shared culture. Seollal is not Chinese New Year as a file and not Hmong New Year. A full mosaic is not a stereotype. A stereotype is when this page becomes the person in the lobby.

### Who this is not

Minnesota Compass (ACS 2019–2023) puts Korean ancestry near 27,204. About 74.6 percent Twin Cities, 25.4 percent Greater Minnesota. About 37.1 percent age 17 or younger; 65 and older only about 2.7 percent. Foreign-born about 43.7 percent. Among those 5 and older: English only about 82.4 percent; language other than English about 17.6 percent; English less than “very well” about 7.9 percent. High school or higher (25+) about 95.7 percent; bachelor’s or higher about 59.2 percent. Median household income about $79,524 in 2022 dollars. Poverty 4.4 percent. Owner-occupied about 64.2 percent. Average household size about 2.29. Individuals living alone about 37.4 percent. Date the number you use.

CAAL and community sources have estimated Minnesota among the highest concentrations of Korean adoptees of any state — often cited near 15,000 historically, sometimes 15,000–20,000 in later community reporting. Date it as community/CAAL. Compass does not split adoptee vs immigrant. AKConnection has said Minnesota holds on the order of 10 percent of Korean adoptees worldwide. Pattern: this state is a hub. A count is not the person.

### How to read this

Always defer to the person in front of you. This page is a hypothesis you still test on this family.

sections.heading: Origins and the Founding of a People
sections.body:
Korean peoplehood is older than 1945, older than the war, and older than the adoption file. Kingdoms on the peninsula, Hangul (promulgated in the fifteenth century; suppressed and revived), honorific speech, and clan surnames are literacy for the desk. They are not a lecture you give a parent who came in for a waiver.

### History for the meeting

Japanese occupation (1910–1945) and the Korean War (1950–1953) are the modern political break. The peninsula divided. The Republic of Korea and the Democratic People’s Republic of Korea are not a mash you referee in a lobby. Most Minnesota immigrant households name the South. Do not test them. Do not ask an adoptee to narrate a war they were not asked to remember.

### What people brought

What people brought: language, church or temple or neither, education as mobility and as pressure, foodways, a memory of occupation and war. What adoptees met: a Minnesota family, often Lutheran or Catholic, a file, and a country that later argued about whether the passport was real. What they met in this department: an English form, one “Asian” checkbox, and often an assumption that LEP at 7.9 percent means you can skip Korean.

sections.heading: The Geography of the Korean World
sections.body:
Homeland is the peninsula — not a Seoul tourism map, and not Pyongyang as a personality. The Republic of Korea is the sending country for most Minnesota immigrant and adoptee files. The North is a political fact in the news and in some families. You do not referee it.

### Homeland

Global diaspora: Los Angeles, New York, China, Central Asia, and a Minnesota concentration that is unusual because of adoption. Compass: about 74.6 percent Twin Cities, 25.4 percent Greater Minnesota. Suburbs, university areas, and Greater Minnesota church-and-farm towns that received adoptees are all on this page.

### Minnesota

Do not assume Minneapolis. Do not assume they have been to Seoul. An adoptee raised in a western Minnesota town is still this people. An immigrant elder in a first-ring suburb is still this people.

sections.heading: War, Church, 1965, and the Adoption Pipeline — Foundational Events
sections.body:
Japanese occupation, then the Korean War (1950–1953), broke families and filled GI and missionary channels. Minnesota’s Lutheran and other churches sat on those channels. Adoption of Korean children into Minnesota homes is this state’s history, not a side note. MNopedia documents the pipeline. Peaks in the 1980s–1990s sit in today’s adult population. Compass does not split them.

### Foundational events

Hart-Celler (1965) opened skilled and family immigration. Later waves brought students, professionals, and church-sponsored families. Immigrant Korean Minnesota built congregations — Presbyterian especially — that are civic hubs. That hub is not the adoptee’s church unless they say so.

### Who you meet

The Child Citizenship Act of 2000 (signed October 30, 2000; effective February 27, 2001) granted automatic citizenship to certain foreign-born children, including adoptees, who were under 18 on the effective date. It was not retroactive for people already 18. Adoptee Citizenship Act bills (introduced from 2015, reintroduced 2018, 2019, 2021, 2024; 2025 Protect Adoptees and American Families Act in the same line) have tried to close the gap. Date the law that exists. Date the advocacy. Do not invent this person’s status. Do not collect status you do not need.

sections.heading: Family
sections.body:
Immigrant streams: family-name-first, generation names, obligation to elders as a hypothesis. Households can be multi-generation or Compass-small (average size about 2.29). About 37.4 percent live alone. Ask who should be in the room.

### Who is in the household

Adoptee households: often white Minnesota parents, siblings who may not be Korean, and an adult who is Korean-born. Kin search may point to Korea, to a closed file, or to no one. Do not assume Korean relatives in the metro. Do not assume the adoptive family is the barrier or the solution. Ask this person.

### Who speaks

Marriage, in-law duty, and who holds the child’s medical decision may not match the English form. Minnesota law still stands. Do not skip mandated reporting and call it culture.

Do not use an adoptee’s family as a lesson about “good Minnesota parents.” Do not use an immigrant family as a lesson about “strict Asians.”

sections.heading: Minnesota and Korean History
sections.body:
This department will meet this community on waivers, child welfare, health care, aging, adoption-adjacent adult services, student households, and employment. Compass: about 74.6 percent Twin Cities, 25.4 percent Greater Minnesota. Greater Minnesota is not an afterthought — the adoption pipeline placed children in towns that still hold adults.

### Places

Korean churches — Presbyterian especially, also Methodist, Catholic, and others — are civic hubs for some immigrant families: language, jobs, information. They are not “the community.” Adoptees may be Minnesota Lutheran or Catholic with no Korean congregation. Do not send them to a Korean church as programming.

### Partners

AKConnection, established in 2000, has been a Minnesota networking organization for adult Korean adoptees. Peer adoptee-led groups exist. Korean Association groups exist. Pay the door this person names. Korean staff are not unpaid interpreters and not the community. Identity is not a staffing plan. Do not use an adoptee coworker as the culture unit.

Seollal and Chuseok are public in some congregations. Guest if you go. A church lunch is not consultation.

sections.heading: Two households in one Compass row
sections.body:
To be Korean in Minnesota is often to be asked whether you were adopted, or whether you “speak it,” as if those were the only two rooms — and to be filed under a checkbox that also holds Chinese, Hmong, and Japanese histories this household does not share.

### In this state

Immigrant Korean Minnesota and Korean adoptee Minnesota share a war and a peninsula and do not share a kitchen, a church, or a language on Tuesday. Do not ask an adoptee to represent “the Korean community.” Do not ask an immigrant elder to explain an adoptee’s grief. Do not skip this page because the person in front of you sounds like Minnesota.

Face, education pressure, and family reputation travel into some immigrant meetings. Adoptee grief, citizenship anxiety, and a body that does not match the family photograph travel into others. Harmony can look like agreement. Ask whether they agree. Do not take a smile as consent.

This guide is a working orientation. Individual variation always supersedes group generalization.

sections.heading: Core Concepts
sections.body:
Language. Korean. Hangul. Honorific speech. Book Korean for immigrant elders. Adoptees may want Korean for a parent visit or may not. Ask. 7.9 percent LEP is not zero.

### Name

Family name first. Kim, Lee/Yi, Park/Pak, Choi, Jung. Do not “correct” Lee. Adoptee American names are names.

Adoptee is not “no culture.” English-dominant is not a skip. Do not use an adoptee coworker as culture.

### Church as hub — some immigrant families

Minnesota Lutheran/Catholic — some adoptees. Neither is the case plan unless they asked.

### Model-minority

A weapon that hides LEP elders, 4.4 percent poverty, disability, and adoptee grief.

### North/South

Literacy. Not a referee job.

sections.heading: Religion
sections.body:
Protestant Christianity, especially Presbyterian, is large in the immigrant stream. Catholic, Buddhist, and none also live here. Church can be the civic hub: Korean language, jobs, a ride, a funeral. It is not “the community.” Do not make a pastor the case plan unless this family asked.

### Streams

Adoptees may be Minnesota Lutheran, Catholic, evangelical, or none, with no Korean congregation. Do not assign a Korean church as cultural programming. Do not assume no faith.

### Practice

Do not treat Buddhist practice as souvenir. Do not treat church as the evolved version. Sunday is operations for some immigrant households. You still keep medical and legal time.

sections.heading: Greetings
sections.body:
A bow or nod with elders is ordinary in many immigrant rooms. A handshake is ordinary in many professional rooms and in most adoptee rooms. Follow this room. Do not force a bow you saw in a video. Do not force a hug.

### Titles

Honorific speech in Korean marks age and status. You do not need to perform it. You need to book an interpreter who can. English “hello” plus the name is ordinary.

### This room

Do not import Chinese, Japanese, Hmong, or Somali greeting rules onto this page.

Physical contact: ask the room. Cross-gender touch with elders is not a default.

sections.heading: Naming Conventions
sections.body:
Family name first in Korean: Kim, Lee (Yi / Rhee), Park (Pak), Choi, Jung (Jeong). Generation names may sit in a two-syllable given name. U.S. forms reverse the order. The same person can appear as Kim Min-jun and Minjun Kim. That is a system failure, not a fraud signal until you have a reason.

### How to file

Lee is not a misspelling. Do not “correct” it to Li or to a Chinese romanization. Do not mash with Chinese Chen or Japanese names.

Adoptees often carry an American given name and family name from the adoptive household. They may or may not use a Korean name. Ask. Do not demand the “real” name. Do not announce a Korean name in a waiting room as cultural humility.

Pronounce it. Ask. Do not joke that there are “too many Kims.”

sections.heading: Dates of Significance
sections.body:
Seollal — Korean Lunar New Year. Family, food, sometimes hanbok. Related lunar calendar, different people from Chinese New Year and Hmong New Year and Tết. Do not put “Asian holiday” on a case note.

### Calendar

Chuseok — harvest / ancestral remembrance. Literacy. Not a file.

Korean War, 1950–1953, and memorial days. Literacy for the desk. Not a speech you give the family. Not a day off the work.

Adoptee gathering days, camps, and reunions are literacy, not consultation. Child Citizenship Act effective February 27, 2001 — law history, not this person’s status unless they name it.

A calendar click is not community engagement.

sections.heading: Education
sections.body:
Compass (ACS 2019–2023), among Korean Minnesotans 25 and older: about 95.7 percent high school or higher; about 59.2 percent bachelor’s or higher. English only about 82.4 percent among those 5 and older. LEP about 7.9 percent. The average is not the elder in front of you.

### School and language

7.9 percent is low compared with Vietnamese or Hmong on Compass. It is not “no language gate.” An English IEP, an English waiver exception, and an English comment PDF still close the door for that elder and for a new arrival.

Education pressure in some immigrant streams is a hypothesis in research and in some households. It is not this teenager. It is not an excuse to skip mental-health screening. Adoptee school histories include Minnesota classrooms that had no Korean peer. Do not mash those stories.

A parent who reads Hangul and limited English is not illiterate. Book Korean.

sections.heading: Etiquette
sections.body:
Elders first in many immigrant rooms. Two-handed offering of a card or a cup in some rooms. Shoes off in some homes. Follow this room. Do not perform a drama of respect you saw online.

### In the home

Adoptee households may run on Minnesota Lutheran or Catholic manners — shoes on, first names, a casserole. That is culture too. Do not correct it toward a Seoul script.

### Time

Accept a little food if offered. Keep medical and legal time. Do not photograph a home altar or a family wall of adoption papers.

Courtesy-yes then no-show happens when the plan was never agreed. Ask whether they agree. Confirm in the language they use.

sections.heading: Language and Communication
sections.body:
Korean. Hangul. Honorific speech. Book Korean for immigrant elders and for anyone who asks. Adoptees may want Korean for a clinic visit with a parent, for a trip, or not at all. Ask. Do not assign a tutor as programming.

### Language

Compass: language other than English about 17.6 percent; LEP about 7.9 percent (age 5+). Date it. Low compared with Vietnamese or Hmong is not a skip. New arrivals and elders are inside that 7.9 percent. English-dominant adoptees are inside the 82.4 percent English-only and still on this page.

Cantonese, Mandarin, Chinese, and Japanese mash is a closed door. An interpreter labeled “Asian” is a closed door.

A short English yes may be exhaustion, courtesy, or honorific indirectness. Do not take a smile as consent. Do not make a Korean coworker the interpreter. Do not make a an adoptee coworker the interpreter as the culture.

sections.heading: Other Considerations
sections.body:
Unvarnished, because Minnesota Nice is how a room that treats everyone the same deletes facts.

### Named harms

Adoptee citizenship gaps were a real U.S. legal harm. The Child Citizenship Act of 2000 covered qualifying children under 18 on February 27, 2001, and was not retroactive for those already 18. Adoptee Citizenship Act advocacy (bills from 2015 through 2024; 2025 Protect Adoptees and American Families Act in the same line) has tried to close the gap. Date the law. Date the advocacy. Do not invent this person’s status. Do not collect status you do not need. Do not treat fear as noncompliance.

North/South politics are in the news and in some rooms. Do not referee. Do not fly a flag as inclusion.

Mental health and suicide risk is a documented conversation in Korean and adoptee communities. Do not invent a Minnesota rate. Do not skip screening. Do not make it a personality.

LGBTQ Korean Minnesotans exist. Model-minority hides LEP elders and adoptee grief. 4.4 percent poverty is not zero. 7.9 percent LEP is a gate.

Staff who share this community may add facts. They do not get to delete a fact because it is hard to say.

sections.heading: Health
sections.body:
Book Korean for the elder who needs it. 7.9 percent LEP (Compass, age 5+) is a gate, not a rounding error. An English consent form is not consent if they could not run it.

### Access

Mental health and suicide risk is a documented Korean and adoptee conversation in research and in community advocacy. Do not invent a Minnesota rate. Do not import a South Korea national rate as a Minnesota rate. Do not skip screening because “they don’t talk about that” or because the person is high-attaining or English-dominant. Do not make it a personality.

Believe reported pain. Do not fold this into a generic “Asian stoicism” slide. Gender match may be requested in maternal and intimate care. Offer it.

If they name a pastor, a healer, or an adoptee therapist, listen. Do not make that person the case plan unless they asked.

sections.heading: LGBTQ
sections.body:
Queer and trans Korean Minnesotans exist — in immigrant churches, in secular professional households, and in adoptee communities that have their own maps. Conservative Presbyterian and other church climates can mean silence or exile. You use the name they use. You do not out them to an elder or a pastor as cultural humility.

### This person

Minnesota’s Human Rights Act still applies. So does the duty not to treat a whole people as a family-values exhibit.

Do not assume an adoptee household is affirming because it is white and English-speaking. Do not assume an immigrant household is not. Ask this person.

sections.heading: Hair, Dress, and Body
sections.body:
Hanbok is public at Seollal and Chuseok for some immigrant families and at some adoptee cultural events. It is not a daily uniform. Second generation and most adoptees look like Minnesota. Do not ask a woman in clinic whether she “still wears the costume.” Do not dress an adoptee in hanbok as DHS programming.

Hair and head: follow this person. Do not touch.

Do not mash hanbok with a qipao or a kimono on the unit’s Heritage Month table.

sections.heading: Music

Church music is ordinary in immigrant Presbyterian streams. K-pop is public culture, including among people with no other Korean language. Pansori and traditional forms exist. Not one soundtrack.

### Variation

A playlist is not engagement. K-pop is not consultation. Do not ask a staff person or a client to perform.

Do not use a music video as the training.

sections.heading: Sports
sections.body:
Soccer, baseball, and ordinary school sport are ordinary. Taekwondo is public culture for some families and a stereotype if you assume it. Do not assume it.

### Not the whole person

Sport clubs are not language access and not a case plan. Adoptee sports look like Minnesota high school. Immigrant church leagues are not consultation.

An elder in the stands who needs Korean still needs Korean. 7.9 percent LEP is not a skip because the child plays varsity.

sections.heading: Literature
sections.body:
Hangul made a national written vernacular. Korean and Korean American writers exist in both languages. Adoptee memoir and scholarship are a Minnesota literary fact (MNopedia’s trail; Winona State and other scholars). You do not need to quote a novel. You need to know this is not a people without letters.

### Literacy in the lobby

Literacy in Hangul is not guaranteed for adoptees or for a second generation. A Korean-language notice can still be a closed door. Ask.

Do not put a proverb on a brochure and call it CLAS.

sections.heading: Art
sections.body:
Ceramics, ink, church-stage dance, Seollal public art, and adoptee-made work are public. Guest. A hanbok on a stage is not a case plan. A museum visit is not consultation.

### Guest

Do not mash with Chinese calligraphy or Japanese woodblock on an “Asian art” table.

Pay the door this person names. Do not extract a staff person’s child as New Year entertainment.

sections.heading: A Note on This Guide
sections.body:
This brief is about Lao people as a people of Laos — the lowland Lao state history, the Mekong, Theravada wats — and as a Minnesota community counted by Compass as Lao (non-Hmong). This is not Hmong. If the household is Hmong, open Hmong Minnesota and put White Hmong or Mong Leng on the interpreter line. If Lao, book Lao. Do not guess from the war.

### Who this is

This is not a Census “Asian” mash. It is not Thai. It is not Khmer. It is not Vietnamese. Shared continent is not shared culture. The Secret War sits next door. The Hmong alliance with the CIA is a neighboring story, not this people as a footnote. A full mosaic is not a stereotype. A stereotype is when this page becomes the person in the lobby.

### Who this is not

Minnesota Compass (ACS 2019–2023) puts Lao (non-Hmong) near 15,191. About 71.6 percent Twin Cities, 28.4 percent Greater Minnesota. About 21.9 percent age 17 or younger; 13.0 percent 65+. About 49.1 percent foreign-born. Language other than English (age 5+) 71.8 percent; English less than “very well” 36.1 percent. Date the number you use. A rate is not the person.

The diversity inside this people is the point. A person who came through the camps after 1975, a Christian family, a wat household that keeps phi, a U.S.-born nurse, a Greater Minnesota worker the building forgot, a college student who uses English with friends and Lao with an elder — share a people and do not share a Tuesday.

sections.heading: Origins and the Founding of a People
sections.body:

French colonial rule made a border and a school. Independence, the American war in Laos, and 1975 are the modern political sequence. They are not the origin of the people.

### History for the meeting

Lao is related to Thai. Related is not interchangeable. A Thai interpreter is not the default. Isan (northeastern Thai) is a neighboring variety some families will name. Ask. Do not guess.

### What people brought

Hmong people in Laos are a different people. Highland life, clan, and the CIA alliance are the Hmong page. Do not file Lao as the leftover of that war.

What people brought: Lao language, Theravada and phi, kinship, farming, and a memory of a state that changed hands. What they met in Minnesota: an English form, one “Asian” checkbox, and often a Hmong interpreter because the building already has that page.

sections.heading: The Geography of the Lao World

sections.heading: 1975, the Pathet Lao, and the Camps — Foundational Event

Resettlement.

Do not tell a Lao family the Hmong war story as if it were theirs. Do not tell a Hmong family this page is close enough. If the household is Hmong, open Hmong Minnesota.

The desk in 2026 meets the first wave and their children — U.S.-born, English-dominant with peers, still translating for parents, still unable to get Lao in a lobby that offered Hmong.

This brief is about Lebanese people as a people with a country in the Levant and a Minnesota community that is historic and recent. This is not the Arabic language door. That door is /ci/arabic — a CLAS ten- and fifteen-language line onto many peoples. Do not open it as a synonym for this people-page. This is not Somali. ### Who this is

A full mosaic is not a stereotype. A stereotype is when this page becomes the person in the lobby. Minnesota Compass (ACS 2019–2023) puts Lebanese ancestry near 6,959. About 81.0 percent Twin Cities, about 19.0 percent Greater Minnesota. ### How to read this

The desk in 2026 meets an English-dominant third-generation parish household, an elder who needs Levantine Arabic, and a recent arrival. Some Lebanese Christian streams use French or English given names and a family surname the database can already see. Some people have Westernized on U.S. forms. Ask.

### How to file

Do not invent a last name because the screen requires one. That invented name becomes a gate.

Pronounce it. Ask. Do not joke about long names. Do not assume three Somali names. Do not assume a hyphen.

Women may or may not take a husband’s family name in U.S. records. Ask how to file. Do not “correct” a mother and child who do not share a last name as a fraud signal until you have a reason.

sections.heading: Dates of Significance
sections.body:
Ask this family. Christmas and Easter — Western, Maronite, Orthodox — in Christian rooms. Muslim lunar dates — Ramadan, Eid al-Fitr, Eid al-Adha — in Muslim rooms. Independence 22 November. 1975 is literacy, not a holiday. 4 August 2020 is memory for some later rooms.

### Calendar

11 September 2001 is structure in this country, not a holiday and not a personality. Gaza-era harassment is current structure. Neither is a calendar click that makes you engaged.

Do not put “Arab holiday” or “Muslim holiday” on a case note without asking. A calendar click is literacy. It is not community engagement.

sections.heading: Education
sections.body:
Compass (ACS 2019–2023): among Lebanese Minnesotans 25 and older, about 97.9 percent high school or higher; about 50.5 percent bachelor’s or higher. Date Compass. About 8.5 percent of the community is foreign-born. High attainment and a large U.S.-born share are not “no language gate” for the household that needs Levantine Arabic.

### School and language

A parent who speaks fluent Arabic and limited English is not illiterate. Literacy in Modern Standard Arabic is not guaranteed for every dialect speaker. The English-only IEP is the gate when Arabic is home.

The child is not the interpreter. Do not skip the interpreter because Compass LOTE is 11.8 percent. Do not copy this attainment onto an Iraqi or Sudanese parent, and do not copy those pages onto this one.

sections.heading: Etiquette
sections.body:
Hospitality is a virtue in many rooms. Accept a little tea if offered. You still keep medical and legal time.

### In the home

Shoes off in some homes. Right hand for food in some Muslim rooms. Do not import a rule you learned on the Somali page as automatic.

### Time

Do not assume a woman will or will not cover. Do not photograph a family and call it rapport. Do not enter a prayer space as a tour.

On-time for appointments. Multi-household logistics are real. Courtesy-yes then no-show happens when the plan was never agreed. Ask whether they agree. Confirm in the language they use.

sections.heading: Language and Communication
sections.body:
Levantine Arabic if Arabic is the home language. Confirm whether it is. Compass: among those 5 and older, about 11.8 percent speak a language other than English. English less than “very well” is suppressed on the Compass Lebanese profile. Do not invent a LEP rate. A large historic share is English-dominant. The elder who is not still needs the line.

### Language

An interpreter labeled Arabic who speaks Maghrebi, or who tests the elder in fuṣḥā, can still be a closed door. Confirm dialect. Do not open Somali Minnesota by default because Arabic is on a card. On a Somali household, Arabic may be recitation — that is the other door.

A short English yes may be exhaustion or courtesy. Do not take a smile as consent. Do not make a coworker the interpreter. The child is not the interpreter.

sections.heading: Other Considerations — unvarnished, not Minnesota Nice
sections.body:
Unvarnished, because Minnesota Nice is how a room that treats everyone the same deletes facts.

### Named harms

Islamophobia and anti-Arab racism after 11 September 2001 and after Gaza are structure in this country and in this state. They hit Muslim Lebanese and they hit Christian Lebanese when the mash is “Arab.” They change who opens the door. That is not noncompliance.

Do not collect political speech as a risk score. Do not file a protest, a flag, or an opinion about Gaza or Hezbollah as a safety note. Enforcement climate is real for some later arrivals. Do not collect status you do not need.

Queer and trans Lebanese exist. You use the name. You do not out someone to kin and call it culture.

Do not assume hijab. Do not assume Muslim. Do not skip mandated reporting and call it humility.

Staff who share this community may add facts. They do not get to delete a fact because it is hard to say.

sections.heading: Health
sections.body:
No dated Minnesota-wide Lebanese autism, diabetes, or PTSD rate belongs on this page beyond Compass poverty 12.0 percent (ACS 2019–2023). Do not invent one. War trauma sits in some later streams. It is not a personality and not every household.

### Access

Gender match may be requested in maternal and intimate care. Offer it. Believe reported pain. Do not fold this page into Tuskegee or into a generic “stoicism” slide. Do not skip screening because Compass looks English-dominant.

Mental-health stigma exists in some families. So does a fierce wish for services. You can hold both. Confirm the language. Identification is not a community personality.

sections.heading: LGBTQ
sections.body:
Queer and trans Lebanese Minnesotans exist. Conservative church, mosque, and family climates can mean silence or exile. Some people live a public English life and a private home life. You use the name they use. You do not out them to an elder as cultural humility.

### This person

Minnesota’s Human Rights Act still applies. So does the duty not to treat a whole people as a family-values exhibit.

Do not use this chapter to raid a household. Do not pretend the tension is not there.

sections.heading: Hair, Dress, and Body
sections.body:
Hijab, niqab, and modest dress are ordinary for some Muslim women and not for others. Christian Lebanese dress is Minnesota dress plus, for some, church clothes. Do not assume covering. Do not rank covering as piety or oppression. Second generation looks like Minnesota. Do not ask whether they “still dress Lebanese.”

### Dress

This is not the CROWN Act chapter. Do not mash.

Do not touch. Do not police covering. Do not assume a covered woman cannot speak for herself — ask her, with a gender-matched interpreter if she wants one.

sections.heading: Music
sections.body:
Lebanese musical life is not one playlist. Levantine pop, dabke, Fairuz as public memory in some rooms, Maronite and Orthodox hymnody, and religious caution about some music in some families all exist.

### Variation

A playlist is not engagement. Do not request a dabke as icebreaker in a waiver meeting.

A liturgy is not staff entertainment.

sections.heading: Sports
sections.body:
Soccer is a common public sport in many streams. Basketball shows up in the second generation. Do not assume the kid plays. Do not make sport the only excellence you can see.

### Not the whole person

Sport clubs are social infrastructure. They are not language access and not a case plan.

World Cup loyalties are not a risk score.

sections.heading: Literature
sections.body:
Arabic is one of the world’s major literary languages. French and English letters sit in Lebanese streams as well. This is not a people without letters. Poetry is prestige in some rooms. The Qurʾan is recitation and scripture in Muslim rooms — not a literacy test you give a dialect-speaking elder in the lobby.

### Literacy in the lobby

MSA and dialect are not the same skill. A person who does not read fuṣḥā is not a person without letters. A U.S.-born adult who does not read Arabic is still this people-page.

You do not need to quote a poet. You need the language this person reads.

sections.heading: Art
sections.body:
Calligraphy in some rooms, church iconography in Christian streams, Levantine visual work, contemporary diaspora artists. Guest, not researcher.

### Guest

A museum visit is optional professional development. It is not consultation.

Do not put a camel or a keffiyeh on a Heritage Month table and call it this people. Do not mash with a Somali table because both might be Muslim.

sections.heading: War, the State, and the Arab-Module Trap
sections.body:
1975–1990 civil war, 2006, 2019–present economic collapse, 4 August 2020 port explosion, 11 September 2001 and what the United States did in its name, Gaza-era harassment, enforcement against some later arrivals — that is the political stack. Anti-Arab racism and Islamophobia are structure. They hit Christian Lebanese when the mash is “Arab.” They are not a personality.

### The badge

Do not collect political speech as a risk score. A flag, a protest, a sermon, an opinion about Gaza or Hezbollah is not a safety note.

A DHS badge is not automatically help. Do not use a war as a personality. Do not ask a person to narrate bombing for your professional development. Do not assume every Lebanese is last year’s arrival. Compass foreign-born 8.5 percent is the dated historic share.

sections.heading: Work, Markets, and Government
sections.body:
Professional class, small business, public employment, shift work. Compass bachelor’s or higher 50.5 percent and owner-occupied 74.5 percent are averages, not this kitchen table. Do not write one hustle onto the page.

### Work

Lebanese staff exist inside DHS and counties. They are not unpaid interpreters and not “the community.” Identity is not a staffing plan.

### Staff

Relationship may precede a signature. That is not permission to skip a notice. It is a reason the first visit may not be the decision. An English eList comment period is not how every stream was reached.

sections.heading: Health-care and Human-service Encounters
sections.body:
Confirm the language. Confirm whether Arabic is home language or liturgy or not in this house at all. Confirm Levantine if Arabic is the interview. Offer gender match. Ask who should hear. Do not force a handshake.

### Language

Believe reported pain. Do not close the file because English was thin. The child is not the interpreter.

### The meeting

Do not assume Muslim. Do not assume hijab. Do not open Somali Minnesota because Arabic is on a card. Mandated reporting still exists. So does the duty not to treat a whole people as a risk score.

Enforcement climate for some later arrivals: people skip clinic when a relative can be moved. That is not noncompliance. Do not collect status you do not need.

sections.heading: Adjacent Peoples — Do Not Mash
sections.body:
Not the Arabic language door as a people. Open /ci/arabic for a language request onto Lebanese, Iraqi, Syrian, Palestinian, Egyptian, Sudanese, Yemeni, Gulf, Maghrebi households. Open this for a Lebanese household.

### Adjacent doors

Not Somali. Not Persian / Farsi. Not Turkish. Not Oromo. Shared Islam is not shared culture. Shared Arabic is not shared culture. Not Syrian, Iraqi, Palestinian, or Egyptian as a synonym.

Compass Lebanese is one stream of what people call Arab Minnesota, not the whole. Some households are mixed. Ask this household. Never one Arab module. Never one Muslim module. Never a Somali default because Arabic is on the card.

sections.heading: Counts, Dated
sections.body:
Minnesota Compass, ACS 2019–2023, Lebanese cultural community: about 6,959; Twin Cities 81.0%; Greater Minnesota 19.0%; age 17 or younger 20.3%; 65+ 16.4%; foreign-born 8.5%; language other than English (age 5+) 11.8%; English less than “very well” suppressed on that profile — do not invent a LEP rate; high school or higher (25+) 97.9%; bachelor’s or higher 50.5%; median household income about $73,000 (2022 dollars, averaged); poverty 12.0%; owner-occupied 74.5%; average household size 2.14.

### Counts

Date Compass. Do not invent an “Arab Minnesota” total. Do not add this profile to Iraqi or Syrian guesses. Counts disagree across ACS vintages and definitions (ancestry vs. birthplace vs. language). Date the number you cite.

### What the count is not

Foreign-born 8.5 percent is not “no immigrant.” LOTE 11.8 percent is not “no language gate.” A rate is not the person. Lebanese numbers are not Iraqi, Syrian, Palestinian, or Somali numbers.

sections.heading: Doors and Sources
sections.body:
Minnesota Compass Lebanese profile (ACS 2019–2023). Adjacent, not this page: /ci/arabic — the language door. CLAS ten-language block and fifteen-language interpreter cards include Arabic. Confirm whether Arabic is the home language. Confirm Levantine.

### Public doors

Maronite, Orthodox, and other parishes families name. Mosques families name. CECLC is a door, not the whole. An eList is not how every stream was reached. Pay partners. Report back.

### Learn on your own time

Learn on your own time. Do not make a Lebanese colleague your unpaid tutor. Book a qualified interpreter when they need one. The child is not the interpreter. Do not open Somali Minnesota by default.

sections.heading: How it hits DHS gates — the 40%
sections.body:
Workplace culture and service delivery are both candidates.

Language: Levantine Arabic if Arabic is home. An interpreter labeled Arabic who does not speak this household’s variety is a closed door. MSA is not the kitchen. Arabic on a Somali or Oromo Muslim card may be recitation — book the interview language. Compass LOTE 11.8 percent is not “no gate.” Gender match may be requested in maternal and intimate care.

Names: the database that invents a last name, or that assumes three Somali names, is a gate that follows the person.

Hour caps, exception processes, and life-sharing matches without language are not culturally neutral.

Assuming Somali, assuming Muslim, assuming hijab, opening /ci/arabic as this people: those are closed doors that look like cultural competence.

Enforcement climate and post-9/11 and Gaza-era racism: people skip clinic, school, and waiver meetings. That is not noncompliance. Do not collect status you do not need. Do not collect political speech as a risk score.

Notices and comment: an eList and an English PDF is not how every stream was reached. Empty follow-up cells are theater. Greater Minnesota is 19.0 percent.

Workforce: Lebanese staff are not the interpreter pool and not the community. Staff are colleagues, not the curriculum. Do not treat  them.

Legislation, funding, rule: you cannot advocate for a channel you will not study. This cultural intelligence exists so the 40% has a household in it — not a paternalistic program designed in a building that treated Lebanese as a Somali default or as an Arabic list.

sections.heading: A Note on This Guide
sections.body:
This brief is about Liberian people as a West African people with a republic (1847), many ethnic nations inside it, and a Minnesota community built in large part after the civil wars. This is not historic African American / Black American. English as a shared official language is not shared culture. Compass African American includes some Liberian ancestry that other counts exclude. That mash is not this page. This is not Somali. This is not Nigerian as a synonym. Shared race in the United States is not shared culture.

### Who this is

Minnesota Compass (ACS 2019–2023) puts Liberian ancestry near 20,720. About 90.5 percent Twin Cities, about 9.5 percent Greater Minnesota. About 43.7 percent age 17 or younger; about 4.4 percent 65+. About 63.2 percent foreign-born. English only (age 5+) 80.3 percent; language other than English 19.7 percent; English less than “very well” 8.7 percent. Date the number. A rate is not the person.

### Who this is not

Brooklyn Park and Brooklyn Center are named in local knowledge as a concentration — among the largest Liberian communities outside Liberia in some public tellings. Confirm on this family. Do not assume that city. Greater Minnesota lives here too.

The diversity inside this people is the point. A Kpelle elder who uses Kolokwa, an Americo-Liberian professional, a Mandingo Muslim household, a U.S.-born nurse, a Greater Minnesota factory household, a person who lived DED for decades and naturalized after LRIF, a child who has never seen Monrovia — share a people and do not share a Tuesday.

### How to read this

Always defer to the person in front of you. This page is a hypothesis you still test on this family.

sections.heading: Origins and the Founding of a People
sections.body:
Liberia is older than the refugee file and older than 1989. A West African coast of many peoples — Kpelle, Bassa, Gio / Dan, Kru, Grebo, Vai, Mandingo, Krahn, Lorma, and others — and a republic declared in 1847 by settlers who included free Black Americans and Caribbean recaptives.
