Guest, not researcher. IgboFest is optional professional development if you are invited. It is not consultation. Do not photograph a family as tourism.

Heritage Month that mashes this with historic African American quilts, a Somali poster, or one “African” table has already mashed the adjacent peoples.

sections.heading: Colony, Biafra, and Intra-Community Politics
sections.body:
British colony, independence 1960, Biafra 1967–1970 as Igbo literacy for the desk not a speech, military rule, and current Nigeria politics — that is the political event. Intra-Nigerian tension, including Yoruba / Igbo / Hausa memory, lives in Minnesota rooms. Do not referee. Do not pick a side as DHS.

### The badge

A DHS badge is not automatically help. Do not use Biafra as a personality. Do not ask a person to narrate famine or killing for your professional development.

Enforcement climate in the United States is a different state and still a closed door for some. It changes who opens the door. That is not noncompliance. Do not collect status you do not need. Do not collect ethnic or political speech as a risk score.

sections.heading: Work, Markets, and Government
sections.body:
Professional class, nursing, entrepreneurship, shop, restaurant, public employment. Compass median household income about $88,194; poverty 6.8 percent; owner 53.8 percent; bachelor’s or higher 54.0 percent — dated. High income and high education are patterns. They are not a model-minority speech. They are not proof the gates closed. They are not permission to skip language access for the elder.

### Work

Nigerian staff inside the department are not unpaid interpreters and not the community. Identity is not a staffing plan.

### Staff

Relationship may precede a signature. That is not permission to skip a notice. It is a reason the first visit may not be the decision. Pay the partner this household names — MIND, an Igbo association, a church, whoever they use.

sections.heading: Health-care and Human-service Encounters
sections.body:
Which people and which language are the first closed door. An interpreter labeled Nigerian, African, or Somali who is not Yoruba, Igbo, Hausa, Pidgin, or whatever this household names is a closed door. Pidgin is a language. Still book a qualified interpreter. Do not use a child. Do not make staff the interpreter.

### Language

Who is in the room. A child pushed forward as Minnesota English. A title you skipped. A pastor in the story. Pain you must believe. High education in the chart used as an excuse to skip the interpreter. Deportation climate.

### The meeting

Offer gender match. Ask who should hear. Ask how to file the name. Use the title. If they name traditional medicine or church healing, listen. Mandated reporting still exists. Believe reported pain. Do not invent African stoicism. Do not mix Tuskegee or Somali CI into this history.

sections.heading: Adjacent Peoples — Do Not Mash
sections.body:
Not Somali. Not Liberian as a synonym. Not Ghanaian as mash — related coast, different state. Not Kenyan. Not Ethiopian. Not historic African American. Compass African American is not this page. Open historic African American for a Great Migration household. Open this for Nigerian.

### Adjacent doors

Yoruba, Igbo, Hausa and others are not one file. Never one African interpreter. Never one Nigerian module. Never one Black module. Some households are mixed. Some Nigerian families have historic African American in-laws. Ask this household.

Shared race is not shared culture. Shared English is not shared English. Shared Christianity is not shared culture. Shared Islam is not shared culture.

sections.heading: Counts, Dated
sections.body:
Minnesota Compass, ACS 2019–2023, Nigerian cultural community: about 18,141; Twin Cities 87.6%; Greater Minnesota 12.4%; age 17 or younger 29.9%; 65+ 8.2%; foreign-born 60.3%; language other than English (age 5+) 55.7%; English less than “very well” 7.6%; high school or higher (25+) 96.1%; bachelor’s or higher 54.0%; median household income about $88,194 (2022 dollars, averaged); poverty 6.8%; owner-occupied 53.8%; renter-occupied 46.2%; average household size 2.63; disability 8.9%.

### Counts

Date Compass. Do not invent other rates. Counts disagree across ACS vintages and definitions (ancestry vs. birthplace vs. language). Date the number you cite.

### What the count is not

A smaller young share than neighboring African Compass rows is not a personality. High bachelor’s and low LEP are not proof the elder heard the form. Language and child-as-interpreter are still gates. A rate is not the person.

sections.heading: Doors and Sources
sections.body:
Minnesota Compass Nigerian profile (ACS 2019–2023). Minnesota Institute for Nigerian Development (MIND) historically as umbrella. IgboFest as public life. Yoruba, Igbo, Edo, and other associations this family names. Churches and mosques this family names. CECLC is a door, not the whole community.

### Public doors

An eList is not engagement. Pay partners. Report back.

### Learn on your own time

Learn on your own time. Do not make a Nigerian colleague your unpaid tutor. Do not BCC a church and call it consultation. Guest at IgboFest or Independence Day if invited — it is not consultation. Book the language this household names.

sections.heading: How it hits DHS gates — the 40%
sections.body:
Workplace culture and service delivery are both candidates.

Language: an interpreter labeled Nigerian, African, or Somali who is not Yoruba, Igbo, Hausa, Pidgin, or whatever this household names is a closed door. Pidgin is a language, not broken English. Still book a qualified interpreter. Do not use a child. Gender match may be requested in maternal and intimate care.

Names and titles: Yoruba and Igbo names carry sentences. The database that shortens them or invents a last name is a gate. Skip a title and you have already closed a door.

Hour caps, exception processes, and life-sharing matches without language are not culturally neutral.

Child welfare and disability: help-seeking that becomes a report is part of why people wait. Mandated reporting still exists. So does the duty not to treat a whole community as a risk score. FGC: Minnesota law stands; do not invent a rate. Do not invent African stoicism.

Notices and comment: an eList and an English PDF is not how this community was reached. Empty follow-up cells are theater. High bachelor’s is not a mailing list. Greater Minnesota is 12.4 percent.

Workforce: Nigerian staff are not the interpreter pool and not the community. Staff are colleagues, not the curriculum. Do not treat  them.

Somali mash and Black mash: opening Somali because Africa, or historic African American because both are Black, is a closed door.

Legislation, funding, rule: you cannot advocate for a channel you will not study. This cultural intelligence exists so the 40% has a household in it — not a paternalistic program designed in a building that heard “Nigerian” and booked an African interpreter.

sections.heading: A Note on This Guide
sections.body:
This brief is about Puerto Rican Minnesota as a people — boricua, puertorriqueño, puertorriqueña — not as a Mexican variant, not as an immigrant file, and not as the Latino / Hispanic umbrella. U.S. citizens since the Jones Act (2 March 1917). Do not run an immigration script by default. Compass foreign-born is 1.3 percent because ACS does not count birth on the island as foreign. Spanish varieties exist. English-dominant households exist. This is not Mexican. It is not Guatemalan. It is not Salvadoran. Shared Spanish is not shared culture. A full mosaic is not a stereotype. A stereotype is when this page becomes the person in the lobby.

### Who this is

Open the Latino umbrella only as adjacent. That page is the mash and the CLAS Spanish line. This page is Puerto Rican. If you leave this door and file the household under “Latino” or under Mexican, or greet them with an ICE speech because the name is Spanish, you have left this door.

### Who this is not

Minnesota Compass (ACS 2019–2023) puts the Puerto Rican cultural community at 21,802. Twin Cities 67.1 percent; Greater Minnesota 32.9 percent — not an afterthought. About 38.2 percent age 17 or younger; 5.5 percent 65+. English only (age 5+) 62.2 percent; language other than English 37.8 percent; English less than “very well” 10.2 percent. Date the number you use. LEP 10.2 percent is not “no language gate.” A rate is not the person.

The diversity inside this people is the point. An island-born elder who uses Spanish, a Minnesota-born English-dominant kid, a Nuyorican household that moved west, a person displaced after Hurricane María, an Afro-Puerto Rican student, a Greater Minnesota worker the building filed as Mexican, a queer second-generation adult who uses English with friends and Spanish with a grandmother — share a people and do not share a Tuesday.

### How to read this

Always defer to the person in front of you. This page is a hypothesis you still test on this family.

sections.heading: Origins and the Founding of a People
sections.body:
Puerto Rican peoplehood is older than 1917 and older than the Minnesota file. Borikén. Taíno people, Spanish colonial rule, African enslavement in the sugar and later coffee economy — that three-root sentence is literacy for the desk. It is incomplete. It is not a speech you give the family. Do not start with a salsa tourism sentence or a Heritage Month flag.

### History for the meeting

1898: the United States took the island in the war with Spain. Colony. The Jones Act (2 March 1917) made Puerto Ricans U.S. citizens. Citizenship without treating the household as foreign is the first operational fact on this desk. They still cannot vote for president from the island. They can, if they reside in Minnesota. That is colonial status as literacy, not a lecture.

### What people brought

Spanish and English are both official on the island. Writing in both exists. Some elders read Spanish and not English. Some Minnesota-born adults read English and not Spanish. Some read both. Ask. Oral skill is not print.

What people brought: language (Caribbean Spanish and English), kinship, Catholic and later Protestant church, Afro-diasporic practice in some families, baseball, a memory of a colony that claimed them. What they met in Minnesota: an English form, one “Latino” checkbox, often one interpreter labeled Spanish, and a lobby that had already decided they were immigrants.

sections.heading: The Geography of the Puerto Rican World
sections.body:
Homeland is the island — municipalities people name, San Juan, Ponce, Mayagüez, the mountains, the coast. Vieques and Culebra are not trivia. Confirm the place if they name it. Do not referee San Juan versus the west in a waiver meeting. Listen.

### Homeland

The U.S. Puerto Rican map is New York (Nuyorican as a named diaspora), Chicago, Florida, Pennsylvania, and also Minnesota. Those hubs are not this map. Secondary migration, military, school, and work pulled people here. Hurricane María (2017) moved people again.

### Minnesota

In Minnesota: Twin Cities 67.1 percent, Greater Minnesota 32.9 percent (Compass ACS 2019–2023). Greater Minnesota is not an afterthought. Do not assume Minneapolis. Do not assume the person in front of you has been to the island. Do not assume a Spanish-surnamed household in a plant town is Mexican. A Greater Minnesota household is still this people.

sections.heading: Citizenship, Island, and Internal Migration — Foundational Facts
sections.body:
This is internal U.S. migration, not immigration. Jones Act, 1917. Operation Bootstrap in the mid-twentieth century pushed industrial policy on the island and labor to the mainland — New York, Chicago, and later other states. Nuyorican is a named diaspora. Minnesota is a later present. Do not run an immigration script by default because the name is Spanish.

### Foundational events

Hurricane María (September 2017) is displacement literacy for the desk. People left a wrecked grid. Some came here. That is not an immigrant wave. It is citizens moving inside the United States after a disaster. PROMESA and the fiscal control board are political literacy. They are not a speech you give the family.

### Who you meet

The desk in 2026 meets island-born elders, U.S.-mainland-born adults, Minnesota-born children, and mixed island–mainland households. Compass foreign-born 1.3 percent is the ACS fact: birth in Puerto Rico is not foreign-born. If you only know “immigrant,” you will miss them and you will harm them.

Enforcement climate in the wider Latino lobby still spills. A Puerto Rican citizen can still be asked for papers because the building mashed the file. That is the gate. Do not collect status you do not need.

sections.heading: Family
sections.body:
Kin networks often run island to mainland to Minnesota in the same month. Compass: average household size about 2.39 — smaller than some neighboring spines. Still not always a nuclear English form. Elders, adult children, and cousins who are household in practice sit in the same week. Who cares for a child may not match the waiver checkbox. Ask who should be in the room.

### Who is in the household

Do not treat this household as mixed-status by default. Citizenship is the fact. Do not collect status you do not need. Do not treat unmatched last names or a grandmother as caregiver as fraud until you have a reason. Hour caps and “natural supports” language can dump unpaid work onto women in that network and call it culture.

### Who speaks

Who speaks in the lobby may be a child. Even in an English-dominant household, a child is not the qualified interpreter for a Spanish-speaking elder — and an English-speaking adult is not a child to be skipped. CLAS still stands when Spanish is needed. Using a child as the go-between is a harm.

Minnesota law still stands. Domestic violence is not culture. Do not skip mandated reporting and call it humility.

sections.heading: Minnesota and Puerto Rican History
sections.body:
Minnesota holds a Puerto Rican community large enough that this department will meet it on waivers, child welfare, health care, cash, food, aging, and employment. Compass: 21,802 (ACS 2019–2023). Twin Cities 67.1 percent; Greater Minnesota 32.9 percent — not an afterthought. Do not write this people as a New York anecdote and do not write them as a Mexican leftover.

### Places

Places, not a blob: Twin Cities corridors and suburbs; Greater Minnesota towns with work, school, and military ties. Public culture is not a sombrero mash. A festival visit does not make you the expert.

### Partners

Partners: parishes and cultural groups families name; rural partners when the household is Greater Minnesota — name the local one; do not assume Minneapolis. CLUES is a Twin Cities Latino door, adjacent, not automatic reach and not this people. CECLC is a department door, not the community. Pay the partner this household actually uses.

Puerto Rican staff are not unpaid interpreters and not the community. Identity is not a staffing plan. You are a guest at a public event if invited. It does not make you the expert.

sections.heading: Boricua — the heart of a people
sections.body:
To be Puerto Rican in Minnesota is to be a people with an island, a colony, and U.S. citizenship, filed under a checkbox that defaults Mexican and often immigrant. Face, kin, and not shaming the name travel into a waiver meeting. Harmony can look like agreement and then a plan nobody follows. Ask whether they agree. Do not take a smile as consent.

### In this state

Afro-Puerto Rican people exist. Colorism is real. Do not bleach this household into a mestizo Latino story, and do not mash them into historic African American because both are Black. Ask.

The Mexican default in this state is a count fact on another page. It is a harm on this one when staff copy Guadalupe, ICE, and “the interpreter” onto a citizen household that may be English-dominant.

This guide is a working orientation. Individual variation always supersedes group generalization. Always defer to the person in front of you.

sections.heading: Core Concepts
sections.body:
Citizenship. Jones Act 1917. Do not run an immigration script by default. Do not collect status you do not need. Foreign-born 1.3 percent on Compass is the ACS clothing of that fact.

### Boricua

Peoplehood word. Island and diaspora. Nuyorican is a named stream, not this whole map. Ask how this family names itself.

### Spanish and English both

English-dominant households exist (English only 62.2 percent). LEP 10.2 percent is not zero. Ask. Do not assume.

### Two surnames still common

The database that keeps one invents a person. English-style single last names exist in some U.S.-born households. Ask.

### Afro-Puerto Rican peoplehood

Not a footnote. Not the African American CI as the file.

### Colonial status

Literacy for the desk. Not a speech you give the family. María (2017) is displacement, not an immigrant wave.

sections.heading: Religion
sections.body:
Catholic majority in many streams — not all. Protestant and evangelical churches live here. Espiritismo and Santería live in some families. Do not exoticize. Do not assume. Do not treat Afro-diasporic practice as folklore or as a risk note. Our Lady of Guadalupe is Mexican Catholic literacy. Do not install it as the default on this page. Ask.

### Streams

Do not make a priest or a pastor the case plan unless this family asked. Do not BCC one parish and call it consultation.

### Practice

Three Kings (6 January) is larger than Santa in some rooms. Holy Week, funerals, and family obligation can collide with your calendar. You still keep medical and legal time. You name the conflict instead of punishing it. Do not photograph an altar.

Help that looks like a report is not help. Religious framing of disability, mental health, or gender can sit next to a fierce wish for services. You can hold both.

sections.heading: Greetings
sections.body:
Elders first. A handshake is common in many rooms. Many English-dominant second-generation rooms will move to a first name faster than a Mexican Spanish room. Follow this room. Do not force a first name on an elder because the form printed it.

### Titles

Titles — Señor, Señora, Don, Doña — until invited in some Spanish rooms. English “hello” is ordinary in others. Say the name. There may be two surnames. Do not assume a Spanish greeting is required, and do not assume English is a closed door to Spanish.

### This room

Do not import Somali right-hand rules or the Black nod onto this page. This is not those grammars. Cross-gender touch: follow this room. A hug from staff is not warmth if the household did not offer it.

sections.heading: Naming Conventions
sections.body:
Two surnames remain common: apellido paterno then apellido materno. A U.S. database that keeps one surname invents a person. That invented name then follows them through MHCP, child welfare, and school. It is a gate.

### How to file

English-style single last names exist in some U.S.-born and some mainland-raised households. Ask how to file. Ask how to say it. Pronounce it. Do not drop accents as a joke. Given names may be Spanish, English, or both. Some people use a middle given name as the call-name.

Women may or may not take a husband’s surname in U.S. records. Children may carry two surnames that do not match a parent’s U.S. “last name” field. That is not fraud until you have a reason.

Do not treat unmatched last names in a household as a fraud flag by default. Do not invent a hyphen and then punish the person when the hyphen moves.

sections.heading: Dates of Significance
sections.body:
6 January — Día de los Reyes / Three Kings. Larger than Santa in some Puerto Rican rooms. Literacy for scheduling. Not a costume for staff.

### Calendar

25 July is contested public memory: 1898 U.S. landing, and Constitution Day of the commonwealth. 19 November is marked in some public life. You do not referee independence versus commonwealth versus statehood on a case note. Listen if they name a day.

Hurricane María — September 2017 — is displacement literacy, not a holiday. Hispanic Heritage Month is the umbrella calendar. It is not this people’s day and not consultation. Not Cinco de Mayo. Not Mexican 16 September. Do not put “Latino holiday” on a case note. A calendar click is not community engagement and not a day off the work.

sections.heading: Education
sections.body:
Compass (ACS 2019–2023): among Puerto Rican Minnesotans 25 and older, about 93.9 percent high school or higher; about 38.6 percent bachelor’s or higher. Date Compass. Do not invent a dropout rate. English only (age 5+) 62.2 percent. LEP 10.2 percent is not “no language gate.” The IEP still has to reach the parent who does not read it — in English or in Spanish.

### School and language

A parent who speaks fluent Caribbean Spanish and limited English is not illiterate. A parent who is English-dominant is not “no culture” and not proof the elder in the household needs no interpreter. Ask. Do not use a child as interpreter.

Second-generation educational mobility is real. So is a gap that a room that treats everyone the same will call “culture” instead of a school that never learned the second surname, or that filed this student as “immigrant.” Puerto Rican students are not immigrant students by default. Do not collect status you do not need at enrollment theater.

sections.heading: Etiquette
sections.body:
Hospitality: food, drink, time. Accepting a little is courtesy. You still keep medical and legal clocks. Titles and elders in some rooms; faster first names in some English-dominant rooms. Follow this room.

### In the home

Do not walk into a living room and photograph an altar. Do not touch ritual objects. Do not ask an elder to explain “your culture” as entertainment, or to narrate María for professional development.

### Time

On-time for appointments. Social time can run long. Work, clinic, and court time should be treated as on time. Do not write a “Latino time” joke in a case note.

Do not use a child as the go-between. Ask whether they agree with the plan. Do not take a smile as consent.

sections.heading: Language and Communication
sections.body:
Ask. Do not assume they need a Spanish interpreter. Do not assume they do not. Compass: among those 5 and older, English only 62.2 percent; language other than English 37.8 percent; English less than “very well” 10.2 percent. Date the number. English-dominant households exist. Spanish-dominant elders exist in the same cousin-line.

### Language

Caribbean Spanish is not Mexican Spanish and not one interpreter accent test. Book a qualified Spanish interpreter if this household needs one. Spanglish is ordinary in some rooms. Register matters. Literacy in any language is not guaranteed: oral skill is not print.

A long answer may be story. A short English yes may be exhaustion or courtesy. Do not take a smile as consent. Ask whether they agree with the plan.

Do not use a child as the interpreter. Do not make a Puerto Rican coworker the interpreter. Do not greet this household with an immigration script.

sections.heading: Other Considerations — unvarnished, not Minnesota Nice
sections.body:
Unvarnished, because Minnesota Nice is how a room that treats everyone the same deletes facts.

### Named harms

Do not run an immigration script by default. Citizenship since 1917. Foreign-born 1.3 percent. SSN theater on the first screen is a gate even for a citizen when the building mashed Latino into ICE. Do not collect status you do not need.

The Mexican default in this state will talk over this household if you let the umbrella page do this page’s job. Colorism is real. Afro-Puerto Rican erasure under a mestizo Latino story is a named harm. Do not mash Afro-Puerto Rican people into the historic African American CI because both are Black, and do not bleach them.

Colonial status is structure: PROMESA, the board, María, the grid. It is not a personality. Machismo is a named harm, not a joke and not “that’s culture.” Domestic violence is not culture. You follow mandated reporting. You still see a family.

LGBTQ Puerto Rican Minnesotans exist. You use the name. You do not out someone to kin. Staff who share this community may add facts. They do not get to delete a fact because it is hard to say.

sections.heading: Health
sections.body:
Believe reported pain. Do not invent stoicism or “they are dramatic.” Compass (ACS 2019–2023) puts disability at 12.8 percent — higher than the Mexican, Guatemalan, and Salvadoran Compass profiles in the same vintage. Date it. Do not invent a why. Do not skip screening. Do not fold this history into Tuskegee (African American literacy) or into a generic immigrant-mistrust slide.

### Access

Uninsured and delayed-care patterns: date Minnesota figures when you have them. Do not invent a rate. Compass poverty is 12.0 percent — a poverty figure, not an uninsured rate. U.S. public-health literature has treated Puerto Rican communities on the mainland as a higher-prevalence group for asthma in some studies — date CDC or the study you cite. Do not invent a Minnesota rate.

Ask language in clinic. An English-dominant adult and a Spanish-dominant elder can sit in the same room. Do not use a child as interpreter. Do not run an immigration script at check-in.

Gender match may be requested in maternal and intimate care. Offer it. If they name a healer, a parish, or Espiritismo, listen. Do not make any of it the case plan unless they asked.

sections.heading: LGBTQ
sections.body:
Queer and trans Puerto Rican Minnesotans exist. Conservative family and parish climates can mean silence or exile. That is not every family. Afro-Puerto Rican queer people exist. Some people live a public English life and a private Spanish life. You use the name they use. You do not out them to an elder as cultural humility.

### This person

Minnesota’s Human Rights Act still applies. So does the duty not to treat a whole people as a family-values exhibit. Do not mash this chapter into the historic African American LGBTQ chapter. Do not use this chapter to raid a household. Do not pretend the tension is not there.

Face and parish climate do not get a veto over this person. Always defer to the person in front of you.

sections.heading: Hair, Dress, and Body
sections.body:
There is no Puerto Rican uniform. Second generation looks like Minnesota. Fiesta and bomba dress are public at celebration, not a daily costume, and not yours to request for Heritage Month. Do not ask a woman in clinic whether she “still wears the costume.”

### Dress

Afro-Puerto Rican hair is not the CROWN Act chapter copied over — and you still do not touch, still do not police, still do not treat tightness or looseness as a professionalism problem. Colorism is a hierarchy. Name it if it is in the room. Do not rank race off hair.

Do not touch. Quinceañera dress, baptism white, funeral black — celebration and devotion, not a case note.

sections.heading: Music
sections.body:
Salsa, bomba, plena, reggaeton, church music. Named variation, not a playlist. A Mexican mariachi default in this waiting room is the mash in speakers.

### Variation

A festival stage is not engagement. A playlist is not language access. Bomba and plena are public culture and Afro-diasporic literacy, not staff entertainment.

Knowing that music is public life will not write the waiver. It will stop you from treating one Heritage Month speaker as the community.

sections.heading: Sports
sections.body:
Baseball and softball show up especially in Caribbean households. Boxing has prestige in some streams. Basketball. Fútbol. School sport is ordinary for the second generation. Do not assume the kid plays. Do not make sport the only excellence you can see.

### Not the whole person

Leagues are social infrastructure. They are not language access and not a case plan. Greater Minnesota teams are still this people.

A Saturday game does not replace an interpreter on Monday if the elder needs Spanish.

sections.heading: Literature
sections.body:
Spanish- and English-language letters both exist. Nuyorican writing is a named U.S. literature. That fact does not mean the person in the lobby can read your form — in English or in Spanish. Literacy in any language is not guaranteed. English-dominant is not “no culture” and not proof the elder can read the exception process.

### Literacy in the lobby

You do not need to quote a poet in the lobby. You need the language this person reads. Print Spanish from Mexico or a machine translation is not automatically this household’s Spanish.

CLAS is qualified language, not Google and not a child.

sections.heading: Art
sections.body:
Bomba and plena as public culture. Contemporary diaspora visual work. Not a sombrero mash and not a Mexican ofrenda copied over.

### Guest

Guest, not researcher. A festival is not a case plan. A Heritage Month table that mashes this with mariachi has already mashed the adjacent peoples. Do not photograph an altar because it is pretty.

Knowing that this people has a public culture will not write the waiver. It will stop you from treating Puerto Rican Minnesota as a Mexican leftover without one.

sections.heading: Colony, Citizenship, and the State
sections.body:
1898, the Jones Act (1917), commonwealth status, PROMESA, and Hurricane María (2017) are the political literacy. This is not an ICE file by default. Internal U.S. migration. A DHS badge is not automatically help — island experience of federal power is mixed — and you still do not greet this household with an immigration script.

Do not use María or the colony as a personality. Do not ask a person to narrate the storm or the grid for your professional development. Status politics (commonwealth, statehood, independence) are real. You do not referee them on a case note.

Do not collect status you do not need. SSN theater on the first screen is a gate when the building mashed Latino into enforcement. Mandated reporting still exists. So does the duty not to treat a whole people as a deportation score they do not belong in.

sections.heading: Work, Markets, and Government
sections.body:
Service, professional second generation, public employment, a military stream as U.S. citizens, plants in some Greater Minnesota towns. Do not assume the worker in the plant is Mexican. Do not assume they need Spanish.

### Work

Parishes and cultural groups may be the trusted channel. Name the local one. Do not assume Minneapolis. Do not assume CLUES is this people. Relationship may precede a signature. That is not permission to skip a notice.

### Staff

Puerto Rican staff exist inside DHS and counties. They are not unpaid interpreters and not “the community.” Identity is not a staffing plan. Do not make a Puerto Rican colleague your unpaid tutor.

Remittance to kin on the island — including after disaster — is obligation for many, not a disposable luxury. Still not an immigration script.

Ask language. English-dominant households exist. Caribbean Spanish if they need it. A Mexican interpreter can still be a closed door. Do not use a child as interpreter. Do not make staff the interpreter. Do not run an immigration script at check-in.

Who is in the room. Gender match in maternal and intimate care if they want it. Titles in some rooms. Two surnames. SSN on the first screen: if you do not need it, do not demand it as theater. Citizenship is the fact. Do not collect status you do not need.

Child welfare and disability: Compass disability 12.8 percent — date it. Help-seeking that becomes a report is part of why people wait. Mandated reporting still exists. So does the duty not to treat a whole community as a risk score. Domestic violence is not culture. You follow law.

Notices and comment: an eList and an English PDF is not how this community was reached if the elder reads Spanish — and an English PDF is not automatically wrong if the household is English-dominant. Ask. Empty follow-up cells are theater. Greater Minnesota is 32.9 percent — a St. Paul meeting is not the whole channel.

Workforce: Puerto Rican staff are not the interpreter pool and not the community. Staff are colleagues, not the curriculum. Do not treat  them.

Latino mash: opening Mexican, or the umbrella, because the checkbox says Hispanic is a closed door. Opening an ICE script is a closed door.

Legislation, funding, rule: you cannot advocate for a channel you will not study. This cultural intelligence exists so the 40% has a household in it — not a paternalistic program designed in a building that never learned that Puerto Rican is citizenship.

sections.heading: A Note on This Guide
sections.body:
This brief is about Salvadoran Minnesota as a people — salvadoreño, salvadoreña — not as a Mexican variant and not as the Latino / Hispanic umbrella. Civil war (1980–1992) and Temporary Protected Status are literacy for the desk, not a speech you give the family. Spanish is not one Spanish. Voseo is ordinary in Salvadoran rooms. A Mexican interpreter can still be a closed door. This is not Mexican. It is not Guatemalan. It is not Puerto Rican. Shared Spanish is not shared culture. A full mosaic is not a stereotype. A stereotype is when this page becomes the person in the lobby.

### Who this is

Open the Latino umbrella only as adjacent. That page is the mash and the CLAS Spanish line. This page is Salvadoran. If you leave this door and file the household under “Latino” or under Mexican because that is the Minnesota default, you have left this door.

### Who this is not

Minnesota Compass (ACS 2019–2023) puts the Salvadoran cultural community at 17,571. Twin Cities 76.7 percent; Greater Minnesota 23.3 percent — not an afterthought. About 48.5 percent age 17 or younger. Compass suppresses 65+ in this vintage — do not invent it. Foreign-born 43.9 percent. Language other than English (age 5+) 79.1 percent; English less than “very well” 39.0 percent. Date the number you use. Compass does not split an indigenous-language count on this profile. Do not invent one. A rate is not the person.

The diversity inside this people is the point. A 1980s arrival who came through the war, a TPS holder whose status is a clock, a U.S.-born nurse, a Greater Minnesota factory household, an evangelical grandmother, a college student who uses English with friends and voseo with an uncle, a person who will not open the door because a relative can be moved — share a people and do not share a Tuesday.

### How to read this

Always defer to the person in front of you. This page is a hypothesis you still test on this family.

sections.heading: Origins and the Founding of a People
sections.body:
Salvadoran peoplehood is not a Mexican origin story with a different flag. El Salvador is the smallest mainland republic in Central America. Pipil / Nahua history was largely mestizo-ized by the colony and the coffee state; do not invent a Minnesota indigenous-language count Compass does not have, and do not copy K’iche’ from the Guatemalan page onto this one. Ask this household.

### History for the meeting

Spanish colonial rule, independence with the other Central American republics (15 September 1821), a coffee oligarchy, and the twentieth-century state that went to war with its own people — that is literacy for the desk. It is not a speech you give the family. Do not start with a pupusa, a volcano, or a Heritage Month sentence.

### What people brought

Writing in Spanish is the ordinary public literacy. Some elders read Spanish. Some do not. Some U.S.-born adults do not read Spanish either. Oral skill is not print. Salvadoran Spanish is not Mexican Spanish.

What people brought: language (including voseo), kinship, Catholic and later evangelical church, work knowledge, remittance as obligation, a memory of a war the United States funded. What they met in Minnesota: an English form, one “Latino” checkbox, often one interpreter labeled Spanish — usually Mexican — and a lobby that had not studied TPS.

sections.heading: The Geography of the Salvadoran World
sections.body:
Homeland is El Salvador — departments people name, San Salvador, the coast, the interior. Confirm the place if they name it. Do not referee Santa Ana versus San Miguel in a waiver meeting. Listen.

### Homeland

The U.S. Salvadoran map is California (Los Angeles among the named hubs), the D.C.–Maryland–Virginia corridor, Texas, New York, and also Minnesota. Those hubs are not this map. Secondary migration and family pulled people here.

### Minnesota

In Minnesota: Twin Cities 76.7 percent, Greater Minnesota 23.3 percent (Compass ACS 2019–2023). Greater Minnesota is not an afterthought. Do not assume Minneapolis. Do not assume a plant town is Guatemalan by default. Do not assume the person in front of you has been to El Salvador. A Greater Minnesota household is still this people.

sections.heading: Civil War, TPS, and Later Streams — Foundational Event
sections.body:
If 1975 is the foundational event of Vietnamese Minnesota, the Salvadoran civil war (1980–1992) is the foundational political event of Salvadoran Minnesota. Archbishop Óscar Romero was assassinated on 24 March 1980. The United States backed the government. People fled. That is literacy for the desk. It is not a speech you give the family. It is not an icebreaker. Do not ask a person to narrate killing for your professional development.

### Foundational events

Peace Accords, 16 January 1992. Later streams carry family reunification, work, disasters, and Temporary Protected Status — including after the 2001 earthquakes — as a clock that reorganizes Tuesday. TPS is structure. It is not a personality. It is not a reason to collect status you do not need, and it is a reason a form that feels like enforcement will empty the lobby.

### Who you meet

The desk in 2026 does not only meet a 1980s arrival. It meets U.S.-born children — Compass foreign-born 43.9 percent — translating for parents, mixed-status households, TPS holders, and a person who has lived here since childhood and still cannot get Salvadoran Spanish in the lobby. If you only know “immigrant,” you will miss them. If you only know “Mexican,” you will mash them.

Enforcement is current structure. When TPS is threatened, or raids are rumored, people skip clinic, school, and waiver meetings. That is not noncompliance.

sections.heading: Family
sections.body:
Familismo is a hypothesis, not a personality. Elders often speak first. Adult children may be in the same week as a waiver meeting, a shift, and a school conference. Compass: average household size about 3.79. Still not always a nuclear English form. Who cares for a child may not match the waiver checkbox. Ask who should be in the room.

### Who is in the household

TPS and mixed-status are structure: a U.S.-citizen child, a parent on TPS, a sibling without status, an aunt who works service. Do not collect status you do not need. Do not treat unmatched last names, a grandmother as caregiver, or a missing SSN as fraud until you have a reason. Hour caps and “natural supports” language can dump unpaid work onto women in that network and call it culture.

### Who speaks

Who speaks in the lobby may be a child with the best English. That child is not the qualified interpreter. CLAS still stands. Using a child as the go-between is a closed door and a harm. Book the interpreter. Ask who should be in the room.

Minnesota law still stands. Domestic violence is not culture. Do not skip mandated reporting and call it humility.

sections.heading: Minnesota and Salvadoran History
sections.body:
Minnesota holds a Salvadoran community large enough that this department will meet it on waivers, child welfare, health care, cash, food, aging, and employment. Compass: 17,571 (ACS 2019–2023). Twin Cities 76.7 percent; Greater Minnesota 23.3 percent — not an afterthought. Do not write this people as a Minneapolis anecdote and do not write them as a Mexican leftover.

### Places

Places, not a blob: Twin Cities corridors and first-ring suburbs; Greater Minnesota towns with work and housing. Pupusa shops and markets are public life. They are not consultation. A food visit does not make you the expert.

### Partners

Partners: parishes and evangelical churches families name; rural parish and worker centers — name the local one; do not assume Minneapolis. CLUES is a Twin Cities door, not the whole community. CECLC is a department door, not the people. Pay the partner this household actually uses.

Salvadoran staff are not unpaid interpreters and not the community. Identity is not a staffing plan. A fiesta or a Romero commemoration is optional professional development if you are invited. You are a guest. It does not make you the expert.

sections.heading: Salvadoreño — the heart of a people
sections.body:
To be Salvadoran in Minnesota is to be a people with a small country and a long memory of a war the United States funded, then building a life in a cold state that filed you under Latino and often under Mexican. Face, kin, remittance, and not shaming the name travel into a waiver meeting. Harmony can look like agreement and then a plan nobody follows. Ask whether they agree. Do not take a smile as consent.

### In this state

Spanish is not one Spanish. Voseo is ordinary. A Mexican interpreter who does not hear this household is a closed door.

The Mexican default in this state is a count fact on another page. It is a harm on this one when staff copy Guadalupe, norteño, and Mexican Spanish onto a Salvadoran household.

This guide is a working orientation. Individual variation always supersedes group generalization. Always defer to the person in front of you.

sections.heading: Core Concepts
sections.body:
Civil-war memory. Foundational for the community. Not a personality for the person in the lobby. Not an icebreaker.

### TPS

Temporary Protected Status as a clock. Structure. Not a reason to collect status you do not need. A reason a badge is not automatically help.

### Voseo

Salvadoran Spanish. Not Mexican Spanish. Book qualified Spanish AND ask.

### Familismo and respeto as hypotheses

Titles, elders, kin as the unit of decision. Not a license to skip mandated reporting. A courtesy-yes is not a signature.

### Two surnames

The database that keeps one invents a person.

### Remittance, church, work

Evangelical and Catholic both. A plant shift and a second-generation degree can sit in the same household. Do not make a priest or a pastor the case plan unless they asked.

sections.heading: Religion
sections.body:
Catholic and a large evangelical / Pentecostal stream both live in Salvadoran Minnesota. The parish or the iglesia may be the trusted channel for information, mutual aid, and a room people will enter when they will not enter yours. Romero is literacy for the desk — 24 March 1980 — not a piety ranking you assign in the lobby. Our Lady of Guadalupe is Mexican Catholic literacy. Do not install it as the default on this page. Ask.

### Streams

Do not make a priest or a pastor the case plan unless this family asked. Do not BCC one church and call it consultation. Do not treat evangelical growth as the evolved version of Catholic.

### Practice

Holy Week, funerals, and fiesta obligation can collide with your calendar. You still keep medical and legal time. You name the conflict instead of punishing it. Do not photograph an altar.

Help that looks like a report is not help. Religious framing of disability, mental health, or gender can sit next to a fierce wish for services. You can hold both.

sections.heading: Greetings
sections.body:
Elders first. A handshake is common in many rooms. A slight nod with an older person is safer than a hard first-name hello you assume is warmth. Follow this room.

### Titles

Titles until invited: Señor, Señora, Don, Doña. Use the last name you were given — and remember there may be two. Do not use a first name with an elder because the form printed it. Usted is respect with strangers and elders; voseo is ordinary among familiars. A qualified interpreter matches register. You do not correct it.

### This room

Do not import Somali right-hand rules or the Black nod onto this page. This is not those grammars. Cross-gender touch with elders is not a default. A hug from staff is not warmth if the household did not offer it.

sections.heading: Naming Conventions
sections.body:
Two surnames is the default in much of Salvadoran Spanish-language naming: apellido paterno then apellido materno. A U.S. database that keeps one surname invents a person. That invented name then follows them through MHCP, child welfare, and school. It is a gate.

### How to file

Ask how to file. Ask how to say it. Pronounce it. Do not drop accents as a joke. Given names may be Spanish, English, or both. Some people use a middle given name as the call-name. Ask.

Women may or may not take a husband’s surname in U.S. records. Children may carry two surnames that do not match a parent’s U.S. “last name” field. That is not fraud until you have a reason.

Do not treat unmatched last names in a household as a fraud flag by default. Do not invent a hyphen and then punish the person when the hyphen moves.

sections.heading: Dates of Significance
sections.body:
15 September — independence with the other Central American republics. Literacy for the desk. Not Mexican 16 September. Not Cinco de Mayo. Do not put a restaurant calendar on a case note.

### Calendar

24 March — Romero. Literacy. Not an icebreaker. Not a day you ask a survivor to speak to staff for professional development. 16 January 1992 — Peace Accords. Holy Week. Funerals and fiesta days will not be on your state calendar. Ask.

Hispanic Heritage Month is the umbrella calendar. It is not this people’s day and not consultation. A calendar click is literacy for scheduling. It is not community engagement and not a day off the work. Do not put “Latino holiday” on a case note.

sections.heading: Education
sections.body:
Compass (ACS 2019–2023): among Salvadoran Minnesotans 25 and older, about 62.1 percent high school or higher; about 17.0 percent bachelor’s or higher. Date Compass. About 43.9 percent of the community is foreign-born. Among those 5 and older, 79.1 percent speak a language other than English; 39.0 percent speak English less than “very well.” That is a language gate, not a culture clash. The IEP still has to reach the parent who does not read it.

### School and language

A parent who speaks fluent Salvadoran Spanish and limited English is not illiterate. Some elders read Spanish. Some do not. The English-only form is the gate. A Mexican-Spanish notice is not automatically this household’s Spanish. Do not use a child as interpreter.

Second-generation educational mobility is real. So is a gap that a room that treats everyone the same will call “culture” instead of language access plus enforcement fear plus a school that never learned the second surname. Do not treat a college student as proof the waiver household needs no interpreter.

sections.heading: Etiquette
sections.body:
Elders first. Titles. Accept a little food if offered. Hospitality is a virtue. You still keep medical and legal time.

### In the home

Do not walk into a living room and photograph an altar. Do not touch ritual objects. Do not ask an elder to explain the war as entertainment. Shoes: follow the household.

### Time

On-time for appointments. Shifts and multi-household logistics are real. So is a pattern of courtesy-yes then no-show when the plan was never agreed. Ask whether they agree. Confirm in the language they use. Do not write a “Latino time” joke in a case note.

Do not use a child as the go-between and call it family values. Book the interpreter.

sections.heading: Language and Communication
sections.body:
Spanish is not one Spanish. Salvadoran Spanish is not Mexican Spanish. Voseo is ordinary. Book a qualified Spanish interpreter AND ask this household. A Mexican interpreter from one region can still be a closed door. Register matters: usted with elders and strangers; vos among familiars. The interpreter matches the room. You do not correct it.

### Language

Compass: among those 5 and older, about 79.1 percent speak a language other than English; about 39.0 percent speak English less than “very well.” Date the number. This is a large language gate. Literacy in any language is not guaranteed: oral skill is not print. Compass does not split an indigenous-language count on this Salvadoran profile. Do not invent one, and do not copy Mixtec or K’iche’ onto this page unless this household names it.

A long answer may be story. A short English yes may be exhaustion or courtesy. Do not take a smile as consent. Ask whether they agree with the plan.

Do not use a child as the interpreter. Do not make a Salvadoran coworker the interpreter.

sections.heading: Other Considerations — unvarnished, not Minnesota Nice
sections.body:
Unvarnished, because Minnesota Nice is how a room that treats everyone the same deletes facts.

### Named harms

ICE, TPS, and enforcement climate are structure. Mixed-status households skip clinic, school, and waiver meetings when a relative can be moved or when TPS is a clock. That is not noncompliance. Do not collect status you do not need. SSN on the first screen is a gate.

The Mexican default in this state will talk over this household if you let the umbrella page do this page’s job. Spanish is not one Spanish.

Gang discourse in U.S. media — including MS-13 as a story that began among Salvadoran refugee youth in Los Angeles — is HISTORY and a named harm in enforcement. A last name is not a gang file. Do not score a Minnesota child on a cousin’s decade or a cable-news segment. Follow law. Still see a family.

Machismo is a named harm, not a joke and not “that’s culture.” Domestic violence is not culture. You follow mandated reporting. LGBTQ Salvadoran Minnesotans exist. You use the name. You do not out someone to kin. Staff who share this community may add facts. They do not get to delete a fact because it is hard to say.

sections.heading: Health
sections.body:
Believe reported pain. Do not invent stoicism. War trauma sits in some rooms. It is not a personality. It is not a reason to skip screening. It is a reason a government badge is not automatically help. Do not fold this history into Tuskegee or into a generic immigrant-mistrust slide.

### Access

Uninsured and delayed-care patterns sit here. Date Minnesota figures when you have them. Do not invent a rate. Compass poverty (ACS 2019–2023) is 5.9 percent — a poverty figure, not an uninsured rate, and not proof the gates closed. Disability 3.4 percent — date it. Do not invent a 65+ rate; Compass suppresses it in this vintage.

Fear of the lobby is a health access fact. A badge, a form that asks for SSN, a child called to interpret a diagnosis, an interpreter who does not speak this Spanish — these are clinical events. When TPS is threatened or enforcement spikes, people skip clinic. That is not noncompliance.

Parish prayer and biomedicine can both be in the household. If they name a healer or a pastor, listen. Do not make either the case plan unless they asked. Gender match may be requested in maternal and intimate care. Offer it. Do not use a child as interpreter.

sections.heading: LGBTQ
sections.body:
Queer and trans Salvadoran Minnesotans exist. Conservative family, parish, and evangelical climates can mean silence or exile. Some people live a public English life and a private Spanish life. You use the name they use. You do not out them to an elder as cultural humility.

### This person

Minnesota’s Human Rights Act still applies. So does the duty not to treat a whole people as a family-values exhibit. Do not use this chapter to raid a household. Do not pretend the tension is not there.

Face and parish climate do not get a veto over this person. Always defer to the person in front of you.

sections.heading: Hair, Dress, and Body
sections.body:
There is no Salvadoran uniform. Second generation looks like Minnesota. Fiesta dress is public at celebration, not a daily costume, and not yours to request for Heritage Month. Do not ask a woman in clinic whether she “still wears the costume.”

### Dress

Do not touch. Do not rank piety off clothing. Colorism is real inside Central American streams. Name it if it is in the room. Do not rank.

Quinceañera dress, baptism white, evangelical modesty — celebration and devotion, not a case note. Service and plant work may mean stained hands. That is labor. It is not a joke.

sections.heading: Music
sections.body:
Cumbia, church music, later pop. Named variation, not a playlist. A Mexican mariachi default in this waiting room is the mash in speakers.

### Variation

A festival stage is not engagement. A playlist is not language access. Church music is not staff entertainment.

Romero commemorations are public life in some rooms. They are not consultation and not a case plan.

sections.heading: Sports
sections.body:
Fútbol is common public sport. School sport is ordinary for the second generation. Do not assume the kid plays. Do not make sport the only excellence you can see.

### Not the whole person

Leagues and pickup games are social infrastructure. They are not language access and not a case plan. Greater Minnesota teams are still this people.

A Saturday tournament does not replace an interpreter on Monday.

sections.heading: Literature
sections.body:
Spanish-language letters exist. Roque Dalton is literacy for the desk, not a quote for a case note. That fact does not mean the person in the lobby can read your form — in English or in Spanish. Literacy in any language is not guaranteed. Oral Spanish is not print Spanish.

### Literacy in the lobby

You do not need to quote a poet in the lobby. You need the language this person reads — or hears. Print Spanish from Mexico or a machine translation is not automatically this household’s Spanish.

CLAS is qualified language, not Google and not a child.

sections.heading: Art
sections.body:
Public culture of markets, church, and fiesta. Pupusas are foodway, not consultation. Guest, not researcher. A food visit is not a case plan. Do not photograph an altar.

### Guest

Heritage Month that mashes this with mariachi or a Guatemalan huipil has already mashed the adjacent peoples.

Contemporary Salvadoran artists work in this country. Knowing that will not write the waiver. It will stop you from treating this people as a Mexican leftover without a public culture.

sections.heading: Civil War, TPS, and Enforcement Climate
sections.body:
The civil war (1980–1992), Romero, U.S. backing of the government, the Peace Accords, and TPS as a later clock — that is the political event. Later: policing, and deportation of people with records, including people who have lived here since childhood. A DHS badge is not automatically help.

### The badge

Do not use the war as a personality. Do not ask a person to narrate dying for your professional development. Gang discourse in U.S. enforcement — MS-13 as a Los Angeles refugee-youth story later exported — is a named fact. It is not a last-name score. Do not write it on a Minnesota child. Follow law. sections.heading: Work, Markets, and Government
sections.body:
Service, construction, food processing, restaurants, cleaning, childcare, professional second generation, public employment. A small-business owner and a waiver recipient may be the same household.

### Work

Parishes, iglesias, and worker centers may be the trusted channel. Name the local one. Do not assume Minneapolis. Do not assume CLUES reaches a Greater Minnesota town. Relationship may precede a signature. That is not permission to skip a notice.

### Staff

Salvadoran staff exist inside DHS and counties. They are not unpaid interpreters and not “the community.” Identity is not a staffing plan. Do not make a Salvadoran colleague your unpaid tutor.

Remittance to kin in El Salvador is obligation for many, not a disposable luxury. A budget that treats it as optional has already chosen a household type.

Language. Book qualified Spanish AND ask. Salvadoran Spanish / voseo. A Mexican interpreter can still be a closed door. Do not use a child as interpreter. Do not make staff the interpreter.

sections.heading: A Note on This Guide
sections.body:
This brief is about Thai people as a people of Thailand — the lowland state history, Theravada wats, a language related to Lao and not interchangeable with it — and as a Minnesota community Compass counts near 6,738 (ACS 2019–2023). This is not Hmong. This is not Lao. Camps in Thailand — Ban Vinai, Mae La, and others — held Hmong and Karen families after wars this people did not fight as those files. Do not file a Thai household under that war. If the household is Hmong, open Hmong Minnesota. If Lao, open Lao Minnesota. If Thai, book Thai.

### Who this is

This is not a Census “Asian” mash. It is not Khmer. It is not Vietnamese. Shared continent is not shared culture. Songkran is not Hmong New Year and not Tết. A full mosaic is not a stereotype. A stereotype is when this page becomes the person in the lobby.

### Who this is not

Minnesota Compass (ACS 2019–2023): about 6,738; Twin Cities 60.8 percent; Greater Minnesota 39.2 percent; age 17 or younger 37.5 percent; 65+ about 4.9 percent; foreign-born 37.4 percent; among those 5 and older, English only about 33.3 percent, language other than English about 66.7 percent, English less than “very well” about 30.6 percent; high school or higher (25+) about 86.4 percent; bachelor’s or higher about 29.5 percent; median household income about $72,888 in 2022 dollars; poverty 17.8 percent; owner-occupied 46.4 percent; average household size about 3.15; individuals living alone about 18.6 percent. Female about 59.7 percent. Date the number you use. A rate is not the person.

The diversity inside this people is the point. A wat household in the Twin Cities, a Greater Minnesota restaurant family, an Isan speaker, a Bangkok-origin professional, a U.S.-born child translating for a parent, a marriage-stream household far from a Thai-speaking neighbor — share a Compass row and do not share a Tuesday.

### How to read this

Always defer to the person in front of you. This page is a hypothesis you still test on this family.

sections.heading: Origins and the Founding of a People
sections.body:
Thai peoplehood is older than the name Thailand (1939), older than 1932, and older than the restaurant file. Siam; kingdoms; a modern nation that marks itself as never colonized by a European power — that national narrative is literacy for the desk. It is not a speech you give the family. It is not a virtue ranking against neighbors who were colonized.

### History for the meeting

Thai language is related to Lao. Related is not interchangeable. A Lao interpreter is not the default. Isan (northeastern Thai) is a neighboring variety some families will name. Ask. Do not guess. Do not mash Hmong into this origin because camps sat on Thai soil.

### What people brought

What people brought: language, Theravada practice or not, family obligation, foodways, a memory of a state that was not a camp. What they met in Minnesota: an English form, one “Asian” checkbox, a restaurant cliché, and often a worker who has already filed them under Hmong because the building only studied the war.

Writing is Thai script. Related to Lao — not interchangeable. Many elders read Thai. Some do not. Second generation may not read it at all. A notice in Lao, or in English only, can still be a closed door. Ask.

sections.heading: The Geography of the Thai World
sections.body:
Thailand is Bangkok, the north, the south, Isan, and the places families name. Isan is related to Lao language and music — not identical, not a Lao file, not a Hmong file. Do not draw one tuk-tuk on a case note. The Malay-Muslim south is a named geography some families will name. You do not referee.

### Homeland

A global diaspora: United States, Europe, the Gulf, East Asia. Minnesota is one map, not the map. Compass: about 60.8 percent Twin Cities, 39.2 percent Greater Minnesota. That Greater Minnesota share is large next to several neighboring spines. Towns with restaurants, campuses, and mixed households are on this page.

### Minnesota

Do not assume Minneapolis. Do not assume they have been to Bangkok. Do not file this household onto a Thai border-camp map. Ban Vinai and Mae La are Hmong and Karen geographies. Open those CIs for those households.

sections.heading: Students, Marriage, Work — Not the Camp File
sections.body:
Thai Minnesota is not a 1975 airlift community. Student, marriage, restaurant and small-business, professional, and family-reunification streams built what you will meet. Cold War U.S. presence in Thailand and later ordinary immigration are literacy. They are not a Hmong Secret War sentence and not a Karen camp sentence.

### Foundational events

Camps on Thai soil held other peoples. Ban Vinai, Mae La, and others are named on the Hmong and Karen spines. Filing a Thai family under that war is a closed door. Do not ask a Thai parent to narrate a camp they did not live. Do not skip this page because the building only trained on 1975.

### Who you meet

U.S.-born children sit in a young age structure — Compass 37.5 percent age 17 or younger. The desk meets a child with English and a parent who still cannot get Thai in the lobby. 30.6 percent LEP is the gate.

If you only know “restaurant,” you will miss the wat household, the Greater Minnesota marriage-stream family, and the professional who still needs this page.

sections.heading: Family
sections.body:
Elders often speak first. Filial obligation is a hypothesis, not a personality. Compass: average household size about 3.15. Multi-generation households exist. So do people who live alone (about 18.6 percent). Ask who should be in the room.

### Who is in the household

Female about 59.7 percent in this Compass row is a labor and marriage-stream fact. It is not a mail-order personality, not a joke, and not a reason to skip the man in the lobby. Hour caps and “natural supports” language can dump unpaid work onto women in that network and call it culture.

### Who speaks

Who speaks in the lobby may be a child with the best English. That child is not the qualified interpreter. Using a child as the go-between is a closed door and a harm. Book Thai.

Minnesota law still stands. Do not skip mandated reporting and call it humility. Who holds the child’s medical decision may not match the English form. Ask.

sections.heading: Minnesota and Thai History
sections.body:
This department will meet this community on waivers, child welfare, health care, cash, food, aging, and employment. Compass: about 6,738 (ACS 2019–2023). Twin Cities 60.8 percent. Greater Minnesota 39.2 percent is not an afterthought. Do not write this people as a Minneapolis restaurant anecdote.

### Places

Wats families name are centers of ritual, mutual aid, and information. They are not “the community.” Thai associations this person names are partners — name the local one. Pay the door this household actually uses. Thai staff are not unpaid interpreters and not the community. Identity is not a staffing plan.

### Partners

Restaurants are public life and a documented work pattern. They are not consultation. A dinner does not make you the expert. Songkran at a wat is optional professional development if you are invited. You are a guest. It does not make you the expert.

Thai staff are not unpaid interpreters and not the community. Identity is not a staffing plan. Greater Minnesota 39.2 percent — a Twin Cities wat is not the whole channel. Pay the partner this household actually uses. Report back.

sections.heading: Not Hmong, not Lao — the heart of a people
sections.body:
To be Thai in Minnesota is often to be filed under a checkbox that also holds Hmong, Lao, Chinese, and Indian histories this household does not share — and to be asked, in the same week, whether they came through “the camps,” as if Thailand were only a holding country for someone else’s war.

### In this state

Face, elder obligation, the wat, and the wai travel into some waiver meetings. Harmony can look like agreement and then a plan nobody follows. Ask whether they agree. Do not take a smile as consent.

LEP at 30.6 percent and poverty at 17.8 percent sit in the same Compass row as a restaurant cliché the building will use as culture. That skip is the policy. Greater Minnesota 39.2 percent is isolation for some households far from a Thai-speaking neighbor.

This guide is a working orientation. Individual variation always supersedes group generalization.

sections.heading: Core Concepts
sections.body:
Language. Thai. Related to Lao — not interchangeable. Book Thai. A Lao interpreter can still be a closed door. A Hmong interpreter is the wrong door.

### Wat and Theravada

Do not make a monk the case plan unless they asked. Do not mash Hmong txiv neeb onto this household.

### Wai

Head high, feet low. Do not touch the head. Follow this room.

### Songkran

Thai New Year in April. Not Hmong New Year. Not Pi Mai as a mash you do not ask.

### Not the camp file

Camps in Thailand are a Hmong and Karen story.

LEP 30.6 percent. Poverty 17.8 percent. Greater Minnesota 39.2 percent. Gates, not rounding errors.

sections.heading: Religion
sections.body:
Theravada Buddhism is the large public stream. The wat is a center of ritual, mutual aid, and information. It is not “the community.” Some Christianity, and none, also live here. Ask. Do not assume a wat. Do not assume no wat.

### Streams

Do not mash Hmong household religion or txiv neeb onto this page. Do not make a monk the case plan unless this family asked. Do not BCC one wat and call it consultation.

### Practice

Shoes off. Head high. Feet not toward a Buddha image. Do not photograph an altar. Funerals and holy days gather family. You still keep medical and legal time. You name the conflict instead of punishing it.

Spirit practice exists in some rooms beside Theravada. Do not treat that as folklore. Do not treat it as a case plan.

sections.heading: Greetings
sections.body:
The wai — palms together, a slight bow — is ordinary in some rooms, especially with elders. A handshake is ordinary in many professional rooms and in much of the second generation. Follow this room. Do not force a wai you saw in a video. Do not force a hug.

### Titles

Elders first. English “hello” plus the name is ordinary. Say the name. Ask how to say it. Nicknames are ordinary in Thai address; the form-name may not be the name they use.

### This room

Do not import Hmong, Lao, Somali, or Black greeting rules onto this page.

Physical contact: ask the room. Do not touch the head. Cross-gender touch with elders is not a default.

sections.heading: Naming Conventions
sections.body:
Given names are used in address. Family names sit last in modern Thai practice — the Surname Act of 1913 is literacy for the desk, not a lecture. Family names can be long. Nicknames are ordinary and may be the only name a teacher or a nurse hears. Ask which name they use day to day. Ask how to file. Ask how to say it.

### How to file

U.S. forms flatten a long given name, invent a first-last pair, and then fail to match a nickname. That is a system failure, not a fraud signal until you have a reason.

Do not assume a Hmong clan name. Do not mash with Lao naming. Women may or may not take a husband’s family name in U.S. records. Mother and child may not match.

The form that guesses will invent a person, and that invented name follows them through MHCP, school, and child welfare.

sections.heading: Dates of Significance
sections.body:
Songkran — Thai New Year — in April. Water, elders, wat, travel. Related mid-April new year to Lao Pi Mai, different people. Do not mash. Do not put “Asian holiday” on a case note. Schedule around it when you can. A calendar click is not community engagement.

### Calendar

Loy Krathong. Buddhist holy days (including Visakha). Thai Mother’s Day and Father’s Day in sending-country public life may matter in some rooms. Household dates will not be on your state calendar. Ask.

Do not mash Songkran with Hmong New Year, Tết, Chinese Lunar New Year, or Diwali. 1975 is a neighboring people’s date. It is not a Thai holiday and not an icebreaker for this family.

sections.heading: Education
sections.body:
Compass (ACS 2019–2023), among Thai Minnesotans 25 and older: about 86.4 percent high school or higher; about 29.5 percent bachelor’s or higher. Language other than English (age 5+) about 66.7 percent. LEP about 30.6 percent. Date Compass. This is not a model-minority skip community.

### School and language

A parent who speaks fluent Thai and limited English is not illiterate. The English-only IEP is the gate. The child is not the interpreter. Book Thai, not Lao, not Hmong.

Greater Minnesota 39.2 percent means some children sit in districts that have never booked Thai. Under-identification in schools is a pattern to watch, not a rate to invent. Do not treat a college student as proof the waiver household needs no interpreter.

sections.heading: Etiquette
sections.body:
Wai with elders in some rooms. Head high — do not touch the head. Feet low — do not point them at a person or a Buddha image. Shoes off in many homes and at the wat. Follow this room.

### In the home

Accept a little food if offered. Hospitality is a virtue. You still keep medical and legal time. Do not photograph an altar. Do not touch ritual objects.

### Time

Courtesy-yes then no-show happens when the plan was never agreed. Ask whether they agree. Confirm in Thai if that is the language they use.

Do not use a child as the go-between and call it family values. Book the interpreter.

sections.heading: Language and Communication
sections.body:
Thai. A tonal language with its own script. Related to Lao — not a Lao interpreter by default. Isan speakers may name that variety. Ask. Not Hmong. An interpreter labeled Asian, or Lao, or Hmong, is a closed door. Book Thai. Still book a qualified interpreter.

### Language

Compass: among those 5 and older, about 66.7 percent speak a language other than English; about 30.6 percent speak English less than “very well.” Date the number. This is a language gate, not a rounding error. Compare it with Korean or Filipino LEP on Compass if you need the building to see it. Do not invent a rate.

A short English yes may be exhaustion, courtesy, or respect. Do not take a smile as consent. Ask whether they agree with the plan.

Do not use a child as the interpreter. Do not make a Thai coworker the interpreter.

sections.heading: Other Considerations — unvarnished, not Minnesota Nice
sections.body:
Unvarnished, because Minnesota Nice is how a room that treats everyone the same deletes facts.

### Named harms

The camp mash is a closed door. Camps in Thailand are a Hmong and Karen story. Filing a Thai family under Ban Vinai or Mae La is how a building that only studied 1975 erases this people. Do not do it.

Restaurant labor is work, not a personality and not a joke. Hours, pay, and a Greater Minnesota town with one Thai family are labor facts. Do not write “Thai food” as ethnicity.

Poverty 17.8 percent is not zero. LEP 30.6 percent is a gate. Owner-occupied 46.4 percent is not a model-minority brochure. Female 59.7 percent is not a mail-order cliché. Do not invent that personality.

LGBTQ Thai Minnesotans exist. Do not import a Bangkok nightlife cliché onto a waiver meeting. Visa climate changes who opens the door. Do not collect status you do not need. Do not skip mandated reporting and call it humility. Staff who share this community may add facts. They do not get to delete a fact because it is hard to say.

sections.heading: Health
sections.body:
Book Thai. 30.6 percent LEP (Compass, age 5+) is a gate. An English consent form is not consent if they could not run it. A Lao interpreter can still be a closed door.

### Access

Believe reported pain. Do not invent “Asian stoicism.” Do not fold this into a Hmong or Chinese slide. Do not skip screening because the person works in a restaurant or smiles.

Mental-health stigma is real in some families. Do not invent a Minnesota rate. Do not import a Thailand national rate as a Minnesota rate. Naming a counselor is not the same as a family accepting one. A smile is not a PHQ-9. Gender match may be requested in maternal and intimate care. Offer it.

If they name a monk, a healer, or a wat, listen. Do not mash a Hmong txiv neeb onto this household. Do not make clergy the case plan unless they asked. Poverty 17.8 percent is in the same row as the health encounter.

sections.heading: LGBTQ
sections.body:
Queer and trans Thai Minnesotans exist. Conservative family and wat climates can mean silence or exile. Public Thai discourse about gender — including kathoey as a word some people use and some people refuse — is not this person’s file and not a waiting-room lesson. You use the name they use. You do not out them to an elder or a monk as cultural humility.

### This person

Minnesota’s Human Rights Act still applies. So does the duty not to treat a whole people as a nightlife exhibit. Do not import a Bangkok cliché onto a waiver meeting.

Do not assume a wat household is not affirming. Do not assume a restaurant household is. Ask this person.

sections.heading: Hair, Dress, and Body
sections.body:
Traditional dress is public at Songkran, some weddings, and at the wat. It is not a daily uniform. Second generation looks like Minnesota. Do not ask a woman in clinic whether she “still wears the costume.”

### Dress

Head is high. Do not touch the head. Hair and head: follow this person.

Do not mash this dress with Hmong New Year clothing, a sinh as a Lao mash you did not ask, or a qipao on an “Asian” table.

sections.heading: Music
sections.body:
Luk thung, mor lam (Isan — related to Lao music, not Hmong qeej), pop, Buddhist chant at the wat. Named variation, not a playlist.

### Variation

A playlist is not engagement. A khene is not a Hmong qeej and not staff entertainment. Do not ask someone to perform.

Songkran stages are public life. They are not consultation and not a case plan.

sections.heading: Sports
sections.body:
Muay Thai is public culture for some and a stereotype if you assume it. Do not assume it. School sport is ordinary for the second generation. Do not assume the kid fights. Do not make sport the only excellence you can see.

### Not the whole person

Sport clubs are not language access and not a case plan. An elder in the stands who needs Thai still needs Thai. 30.6 percent LEP is not a skip because the child plays.

A Saturday tournament does not replace an interpreter on Monday.

sections.heading: Literature
sections.body:
Thai script and a written tradition. Related to Lao script — not interchangeable. This is not a people without letters. You do not need to quote a poem in the lobby.

### Literacy in the lobby

You do need to know that a notice that exists only in English is a closed door for the parent who reads Thai. A notice in Lao the Thai elder did not ask for is also a closed door. Ask which language they read.

Do not put a proverb on a brochure and call it language access.

sections.heading: Art
sections.body:
Wat mural and sculpture, dance, and the public culture of Songkran and restaurants. Foodway is not consultation. A restaurant visit is not a case plan.

### Guest

Guest, not researcher. A wat visit is optional professional development if you are invited. It is not consultation. Do not photograph an altar.

Heritage Month that mashes this with Hmong paj ntaub or a Chinese lion dance has already mashed the adjacent peoples.

sections.heading: The State, the Camps Next Door, and This Desk
sections.body:
Never-colonized as a national narrative, 1932, Cold War U.S. presence, and a United States that met Thai people as students, spouses, workers, and neighbors — that is this political file. Camps on Thai soil held Hmong and Karen people. That is a neighboring story. Telling a Thai family the Secret War as if it were theirs is a state act. It is a closed gate.

### The badge

A DHS badge is not automatically help. Do not collect immigration status you do not need. Do not treat fear as noncompliance. Do not use a restaurant, a marriage, or a camp as a personality.

Filing this household as Hmong, as Lao, or as a Census Asian mash is a closed door.

sections.heading: Work, Wats, and Government
sections.body:
Restaurant and small business, professional streams, public employment. Restaurant labor is a documented pattern. It is work. It is not a personality, not a joke, and not the whole economy. Do not write “Thai food” as ethnicity.

### Work

Median household income about $72,888 (Compass, 2022 dollars) is an average. Poverty 17.8 percent is in the same row. Owner-occupied 46.4 percent. Female about 59.7 percent. Do not staff a program as if every household were a model-minority brochure, and do not staff it as if every household were a restaurant.

### Staff

Thai staff inside the department are not unpaid interpreters and not the community. Identity is not a staffing plan. Relationship may precede a signature in some rooms. That is not permission to skip a notice.

sections.heading: Health-care and Human-service Encounters
sections.body:
Thai on the interpreter line — not Lao, not Hmong, not “Asian.” 30.6 percent LEP. A child pushed forward as English. A monk or a wat in the story. Pain you must believe. Poverty 17.8 percent. A nickname the wristband does not have. Greater Minnesota isolation.

### Language

Confirm Thai. Still book a qualified interpreter. Do not use a child. Offer gender match. Ask who should hear. Ask which name they use. Do not make staff the interpreter.

### The meeting

Believe reported pain. Do not invent Asian stoicism. Do not mash txiv neeb. Mandated reporting still exists. A smile is not consent.

sections.heading: Adjacent Peoples — Do Not Mash
sections.body:
Not Hmong. Not Lao. Not Khmer. Not Vietnamese. Not Chinese. Not Karen. Not “Asian American” as the file. Open those CIs for those households. Open this for a Thai household.

### Adjacent doors

Camps in Thailand are a Hmong and Karen story. Do not file Thai families under that war. Isan is related to Lao — related is not interchangeable. A Lao interpreter can still be a closed door. Some households are mixed. Some people name Isan. Ask this household.

Never one Asian module. Never one “Southeast Asian” interpreter. If Hmong, open Hmong Minnesota. If Lao, open Lao Minnesota. If Thai, this page.

sections.heading: Counts, Dated
sections.body:
Minnesota Compass, ACS 2019–2023, Thai cultural community: about 6,738; Twin Cities 60.8%; Greater Minnesota 39.2%; age 17 or younger 37.5%; 65+ about 4.9%; foreign-born 37.4%; English only (age 5+) 33.3%; language other than English 66.7%; English less than “very well” 30.6%; high school or higher (25+) 86.4%; bachelor’s or higher 29.5%; median household income about $72,888 (2022 dollars); poverty 17.8%; owner-occupied 46.4%; average household size 3.15; individuals living alone 18.6 percent. Female about 59.7 percent.

### Counts

Date Compass. Do not invent other rates. Counts disagree across ACS vintages and definitions. Date the number you cite. Some age bands on the Compass table are suppressed — do not fill them in.

### What the count is not

A 30.6 percent LEP rate is a gate. A 17.8 percent poverty rate is not zero. Greater Minnesota 39.2 percent is not an afterthought. A 29.5 percent bachelor’s rate is not a model-minority skip. A rate is not the person.

sections.heading: Doors and Sources
sections.body:
